Excipiendas esse persecutiones, mercaturam, studia, negotia; nam si in persequutionibus non licuisset se illuc conferre, incurrerent in culpam sanctissimi vates Vrias & Ieremias, qui secundùm Aben Efram Deut. xv. inviti illuc fugere coacti sunt: Quod etiam nobis pro Apologia esse potest contra Iudæos clamitantes Iosephum non absque crimine esse, quòd Iesum in Ægyptum abduxerit. Quod mercatores & alios quibus negotia incumbunt attinet, eos ipse Maymonides excusat. Soli itaque illi contra Canonem iverunt, qui rebus Domi & in patria integris, à regibus Ægypti, honoribus & libertate quævis in religione & sacris sentiendi, ad stabilem sedem figendam illecti fuerunt; & quibus mortuis deinde secundùm sententiam R. Eleasaris, vix alia beatitudinis & remissionis peccatorum spes fuit, nisi quam expectarunt ex appulsu in terram Israeliticam, & ex tactu glebæ friabilis; Quæ certè admodùm ficulnea & miserà fuit. §. Tempore Christi Ægyptus præter modum Iudæis repleta erat, idque partim ob migrantes illuc sub Iochanane filio Kareα Ierem. xliii. partim quia Onias noñ ita pridem templum ibi ædificaverat ; ad quod magna copia confluebant. vid. Ioseph. Antiq. lib. 13. 16. Talmud utrumque in Menachoth c.13. & Succah c. 5. Hierof. Ioma sol.43: 4. de Alexandrina Ecclesia vid. Infra. §. Profestionis Salvatoris nostri in Ægyptum,apud Iudæos vestigia quædam supersunt, sed admodum corrupta & depravata. Bab. Sanhed. sol.107. 2. dicitur : Cùm Iannai Rex occideret Rabbinos, abierunt R. Iehosua Ben Perachiæ & Iesus ad Alexandriam in Ægypto &c. Et paulò ante. Elisæus duabus manibus avertit Gehazi.& R.Iofua fil.Perachiæ, ambabus manibus repulit Iesum. Item in Schabb. 104. Nonne Ben Sadta prastigias attulit ex Ægypto in incifura quæ in carne eius? ubi per Ben Sadta Christum intelligunt, quamvis Commentator id neget.
units.tr: to slaughter sheep, but shepherds of sheep were also held in the utmost contempt and abhorrence. According to the Jews, Joseph did not want his bones left in Egypt, for these reasons. First, because it would have been very grievous to them to be carried to the land of Canaan for resurrection by that subterranean and troublesome revolution [גלגול], since the Jews deny that any resurrection will take place outside the holy land (see Kethubot sol. iii.1). Maimonides gives the reason in Hal. Melachim: כל השוכן בארץ ישראל עונותיו מחולין [kol hashokhen be'eretz Yisra'el 'avonotav mechulin], that the iniquities of all who dwell in the land of Israel are forgiven, as it is said (Isa. 33:24): "And the inhabitant shall not say, I am sick; the people that dwell in it shall be relieved of their iniquity" [שנאמר ובל יאמר חליתי]. From this, according to Maimonides, they further conclude that whoever enters the land of Israel, even to the measure of four cubits, is already worthy of eternal life; but whoever is buried in it has his sins atoned for, and his place of burial becomes to him like the altar of atonement (Deut. 32:43), since it atones for his land and his people. It is indeed better if someone, while still alive, betakes himself to the holy land; but if this cannot be done, we have the example of the patriarchs themselves that it is useful even after death. The commentator on Maimonides, moreover, brings forward something from the Jerusalem Talmud that contributes to a fuller clarification of this matter. Bar Kria, he says, walked with R. Eleazar in the public roads [באיסטרין], and they saw coffins brought in from foreign places. R. Kria said to Eleazar: What use is it to them (carried here at such great expense)? Indeed, I apply to such people that passage of Jeremiah 2:7: "You have made my heritage an abomination; while you were living you defiled it, and now you come and defile the land after you are dead." Eleazar replied: As soon as they come into this region, they take a clod of crumbled earth [נושלין גוש עפר] and place it in the coffin, relying on the saying of Deut. 32:43, "his land will be merciful to his people." Unless we are altogether inauspicious in our conjecture, those coffins were brought from Egypt, and R. Kria could not otherwise have applied that passage of Jeremiah well; for those who had gone there to settle permanently [להשתקע], according to Maimonides, did the same thing. And if they had held the land of Canaan in contempt and abhorrence, it was because the works of its inhabitants were מקולקלות יותר מכל ארצות [mekulkalot yoter mikol artzot], more corrupt and defiled than the works of all other nations, and partly because that nation had most miserably afflicted the holy people with profane acts. Hence that rule: מותר לשכון בכל הארץ חוץ מארץ מצרים [mutar leshakhen bekhol ha'arets chuts me'eretz Mitzrayim], it is permitted to dwell in the whole world except Egypt. R. Urian, weighing this, added the following objection in the margin of Hal. Melach. c.5: יש תמיה על קהילות שוכנים שם ועל רבינו המחבר שהלך לגור שם [yesh temihah 'al kehillot shokhenim sham ve'al rabbenu hamechaber shehalakh lagur sham]: It is strange, therefore, that one should be astonished at the congregations dwelling there, and likewise at our author (Maimonides), who went there to live. This is indeed true, for Maimonides spent many years at the Egyptian court, and indeed as royal physician, as may be seen from the letters he wrote to Samuel Ibn Tibbon. But Doctor Urian ought also to have observed that there is no rule so general that it does not admit its exceptions. We therefore reply that the force of this canon has in some way ceased since the Jews were driven from their homes and the sanctuary was laid waste. Second, the cases of persecution, trade, studies and business must be excepted; for if it had not been permitted to betake oneself there in times of persecution, the most holy prophets Urijah and Jeremiah would have incurred guilt, who, according to Ibn Ezra on Deut. 15, were forced to flee there against their will. This can also serve us as an apology against the Jews, who cry out that Joseph was not without guilt in having led Jesus into Egypt. As for merchants and others whose affairs keep them there, Maimonides himself excuses them. Therefore only those went there against the canon who, while their affairs at home and in their country were intact, were enticed by the kings of Egypt, with honours and with freedom to hold whatever views they liked in religion and worship, to fix a permanent residence there; and for whom, after death, according to the opinion of R. Eleazar, there was scarcely any other hope of blessedness and forgiveness of sins, except what they expected from being brought into the Israelite land and from touching the crumbled clod of earth. This was indeed a very fig-leaf and wretched hope. §. In the time of Christ, Egypt was filled with Jews beyond measure, partly because of those migrating there under Johanan son of Kareah (Jer. 43), and partly because Onias not long before had built a temple there, to which a great crowd flocked. See Josephus, Antiq. bk. 13, ch. 16; the Talmud on both in Menachoth c.13 and Succah c.5; Hierof. Ioma sol. 43.4. On the Alexandrian Church, see below. §. Some traces of our Saviour's flight into Egypt survive among the Jews, but they are very corrupted and distorted. Bab. Sanhed. sol. 107.2 says: When King Jannai was killing the rabbis, R. Joshua Ben Perachiah and Jesus went away to Alexandria in Egypt, etc. And a little before: Elisha pushed away Gehazi with both hands, and R. Joshua son of Perachiah repulsed Jesus with both hands. Likewise in Schabb. 104: Did not Ben Stada bring magic tricks from Egypt in an incision in his flesh? where by Ben Stada they understand Christ, although the commentator denies it.

units.la: ÆTAS primorum hominum quorum mentionem facit Sacra Scriptura non fuit communis indifferenter omnibus, sed illa freti sunt tantùm illi qui exprimuntur in S. Scriptura, idque propter accuratam alimenti rationem & diætam, vel per modum aliquem miraculosum More Nevoch. II. 47. §. Maymonidi subscribit etiam Don Abarbanel ad Gen.c.v. ubi singulares illos homines ad longam illam ætatem provectos per miraculum docet, duplicem potissimùm ob finem. Primò ad multiplicanda individua speciei, ut illis tanto citius mundus habitabilis redderetur. Secundò ad perficiendam speciem humanam in scientiā tiis artibus & disciplinis, quæ sint perfectio hominis. Illam verò perfectionem adipisci non potuisse nisi per experimenta,quæ non nisi longâ ætate rectè fieri possunt. Ex mente verò Maymonidis & Nachmanidis tres longævitatis patrum causas Abarbenel recensét; 1a. est quia origini mundi propiores fuerunt , adeóque maiore corporis robore instructi : 2a. quia ante diluvium aer purus fuit , post diluvium verò corruptus factus nocuerit hominum vitæ. 3a. quia cibis & alimentis temperantiùs usi fuerint quàm homines sequentium temporum.
units.tr: The age of the first men, whom Sacred Scripture mentions, was not shared equally by all. Only those named in Scripture attained it, and that because of their careful regimen and diet, or through some miraculous means. More Nevoch. II. 47. §. Don Abarbanel also agrees with Maimonides on Gen. 5, where he teaches that those singular men who reached that great age did so by a miracle, chiefly for two purposes. First, to multiply the individuals of the species, so that the world might be inhabited all the sooner. Second, to bring the human species to perfection in knowledge, in the arts and in the disciplines, which are the perfection of man. That perfection, however, could not be attained except through experiments, which can only properly be carried out over a long life. Following the thought of Maimonides and Nachmanides, Abarbanel lists three causes of the patriarchs' longevity. First, they were closer to the origin of the world and so were endowed with greater bodily strength. Second, before the flood the air was pure, but after the flood it became corrupt and harmed human life. Third, they used foods and nourishments more temperately than men of later ages.

units.la: AGADOT sunt historici discursus, instar illorum quos fingunt & formant aliquando Poëtæ. R. Asarias Meor Ennáim cap. 15. Agadot hunc finem habent ut trahant animos hominum ad audiendum. ibid. Lectio historiæ paschalis à Iudæis אגדה Agada vocatur, vid. Maiemon. par. de הגדה sect. 5. 10.
units.tr: Agadot are historical discourses, like those which poets sometimes invent and shape. R. Asarias, Meor Ennáim, ch. 15. The Agadot have this aim, to draw the minds of men to listen. Ibid. The reading of the Passover history among the Jews is called אגדה [Haggadah], see Maimonides, in the treatise on הגדה [Haggadah], sect. 5, 10.

units.la: AGRICVLTVRA, de Agricultura Iudæorum varia occurrunt in Peah, Demai, Kilaim, Scheviit. nos ex semente manipulum adducemus.
units.tr: Concerning agriculture among the Jews, various matters occur in Peah, Demai, Kilaim, Scheviit; we shall adduce a handful from the sowing.

units.la: §. Per agros satos tam communes quàm privatiores erant viæ & semitæ. Hinc in tract. Peah c. 2. ubi discutiunt quænam sint quæ agrum partiuntur, ita ut duplicem angulum pauperibus debeat, sic determinatur. Hæc partiuntur, fluvius, aqua ductus, via privata, via communis, semita communis, & semita privata. Id aliquâ ratione facit ad dilucidationem illius, quod de discipulis Matth. xii. 1 legimus.
units.tr: Through sown fields, both common and more private, there ran roads and footpaths. Hence in the tractate Peah, ch. 2, where they discuss what things divide a field, so that a double corner is owed to the poor, it is determined thus: These divide: a river, a watercourse, a private road, a common road, a common footpath, and a private footpath. This in some measure helps to clarify what we read of the disciples in Matt. 12:1.

units.la: §. De legibus seminum Heterogeneorum, atque anni septimi solutus est, 'qui seminat iuxta mare עג׳ משרה עג׳ סלעיםעג׳ טרשים /supra petras (i'ni 7a' πτρ'ώδη Matth. xiii. 5.) Scopulos & Saxofa. Hierof.Kilaim sol.27.1.Erat enim Palæstina in plurimis locis admodum saxosa, & tamen non omnino inidonea ad culturam, etiam in illis tractubus. De Seminandi ratione vid. Sementis.
units.tr: Concerning the laws of mixed seeds, and of the seventh year, it is settled that he who sows beside the sea עג׳ משרה עג׳ סלעים עג׳ טרשים [garbled] upon rocks ([Greek: petrōdē], Matt. 13:5), rocks and stony ground. Jerusalem Talmud, Kilaim, sol. 27.1. For Palestine was in very many places quite rocky, and yet not wholly unfit for cultivation, even in those districts. On the manner of sowing see Sowing.

units.la: §. Distinguitur ager in לבן שרה agrum album qui totus feritur, & שרה אילן Arboreum agrum, in quo nascuntur hic illic arbores aut fruticeta. Scheviit c. 2. MoedKaton c. 1. 3. 4. posterioris generis agrum forsan intellexit Christus per Ἀἀς ἀκαρίας Math.xiii.7.
units.tr: A field is distinguished as לבן שרה [a white field], a white field which is wholly tilled, and שרה אילן [a tree field], a field with trees, in which trees or thickets grow here and there. Scheviit ch. 2; Moed Katon ch. 1, 3, 4. Perhaps Christ meant the latter kind of field by [Greek: ta akantha], Matt. 13:7.

units.la: §. In usu habuerunt in agris & vineis areolas relinquere quas vocant מלבנות Peah. c.2. & עירוגות Kilaim c. 3. quando in illis areolis nihil fatum erat.vocarunt illas קרחה בשדה calvitiem in agro. Kilaim c. 4.
units.tr: In fields and vineyards they were accustomed to leave small plots, which they call מלבנות [mĕlabbĕnōt], Peah, ch. 2, and עירוגות [ʿirogot], Kilaim, ch. 3, when nothing had grown in those plots. They called them קרחה בשדה [a bald spot in the field], baldness in the field, Kilaim, ch. 4.

units.la: §. De agrorum fertilitate vid. Ifraelitica terra fertilitas.
units.tr: On the fertility of fields see The fertility of the land of Israel.

units.la: §. Quod Græcè vocamus Ζιζάνια Talmudicè ונין appellatur, & definitur à Glossa ad cap.i.v.1. Kilaim quod sit species quaedam tritici, quae in terra mutatur, & quoad formam & quoad naturam. Ager domini satus est totus tritico, id est hominibus, sed artibus.Diaboli magna pars hominum instar illius tritici quod ונין vocatur, in Zizaniam degenerat. Confer Matth. xiii. 25.
units.tr: What we call in Greek [Greek: zizania] is called in the Talmud ונין [zunin], and it is defined by the Gloss on ch. 1 v. 1 of Kilaim as a certain species of wheat, which is changed in the earth, both in form and in nature. The Lord's field is sown wholly with wheat, that is with men, but with the arts of the devil a great part of men, like that wheat called ונין [zunin], degenerates into tares. Compare Matt. 13:25.

units.la: §. Agrum siticulosum qui vocatur Talmud. בית השלחין irrigare licet in sefto, & in anno septimo, cùm ex fonte qui iam dudum fluxerit, tum tùm ex illo qui nunc demum fluere incepit; non autem aquâ pluviali, uti nec ex canali Moed Katon c.1.1. Ducunt in festo aquas ab arbore ad arborem, sed itâ ne irrigetur ager totus. Semina quæ non irrigata fuerunt ante festum, non irrigare licet in festo (quia in festo nihil agenduṁ quod multùm laboris requirit.) Licet in agris venari tempore festivo & in anno septimo Talpas & mures, modò illud non fiat per חפירה effossionem terræ, (quæ absque labore fieri non potest) Moed Katon. c.1.3.4.
units.tr: A thirsty field, which in the Talmud is called בית השלחין [a watered field], may be irrigated on a festival and in the seventh year, both from a spring which has long been flowing and from one which has only now begun to flow; but not with rainwater, nor from a canal, Moed Katon ch. 1, 1. They lead water on a festival from tree to tree, but in such a way that the whole field is not watered. Seeds which were not irrigated before the festival may not be irrigated on the festival (because on a festival nothing is to be done which requires much labour). It is lawful to hunt in the fields during the festal time and in the seventh year, moles and mice, provided that this is not done by חפירה [ḥăpîrâ], digging up the earth (which cannot be done without labour). Moed Katon ch. 1, 3, 4.

units.la: §. De Agro שלא נתקוץ non excanthato de quo superius diximus vid.etiam Schebhiit c.4.2.
units.tr: Concerning a field שלא נתקוץ [not cut off], not stubbled, of which we spoke above, see also Schebhiit ch. 4, 2.

units.la: §. quomodo intelligendæ sint formulæ loquendi Marc. v. 14. ἀνὴγγειλαν εἰς τὰς ἀγροὺς item cap. vi. 36. ἀπελθόντες εἰς τὰς κύκλῳ ἀγροὺς. an intelligendi sint operantes vel itinerantes in agris ? ᾿Αγρὸς stylo Palæstinæ vocatur הקלאי ; quando autem consulo Aruch in illa radice docet me ille הקלאים esse homines privatos degentes in agris, sparsis scilicet hic illic ædibus. Ita quoque Gloss. Bab. Beracot sol.37. 2. ubi mentio fit Cibi farinacei דחקלאי incolentium agros, notat per חקלאי esse intelligendos בני כפר incolas villarum. Hinc concludo in illis locis nec operantes nec itinerantes, sed in agris degentes intelligi debere.
units.tr: How the phrases of Mark 5:14 are to be understood, [Greek: aggeilan eis tous agrous], likewise ch. 6:36, [Greek: apelthontes eis tous kyklō agrous]: are those who are working or travelling in the fields to be understood? Agros, in the style of Palestine, is called חקלאי [ḥaqlāʾî]; but when I consult the Aruch under that root, it teaches me that those חקלאים [ḥaqlāʾîm] are men living privately in the fields, scattered here and there in houses. So also the Gloss on Bab. Beracot sol. 37.2, where mention is made of farinaceous food of those דחקלאי [dĕḥaqlāʾî] dwelling in the fields, notes that by חקלאי [ḥaqlāʾî] are to be understood בני כפר [bĕnê kĕfar], the inhabitants of villages. Hence I conclude that in those passages neither workers nor travellers, but men living in the fields, must be understood.

units.la: §. Angulus agri pauperibus relinquendus nullam habet determinationem שיעור mensuram, sed debet fieri pro ratione magnitudinis agri, multitudinis pauperum, & beneficentiæ. Si quis tamen aliquam mensuram determinare vult, sciet שאין מותחין לפאה משששים minus sexta parte agri non ordinandum esse. Ex Peah. c.1.2. angulus agri fieri potest in init o , medio , aut fine agri. ibid. v. 3. Angulus agri relinqui debet ex omnibus illis fructibus שהוא אוכל, quæ apta ad esum & licita sunt, ( nam de illis quæ sponte nascuntur,aut non adeò licita sunt, præceptum de angulo non sonat.) ונשמר quæ custodit (ad oppositionem illorum quæ publici juris sunt.) וגדולין מן הארץ quæ ex terra nascuntur, (ad oppositionem illorum quæ radices suas in terra non habent. ) quæ una vice legùntur, & quæ asservari possunt. In sequentibus arborum speciebus relinqui debet angulus בשקרים אגוזים תרובין אוגין תמרים זיתים דימונים גפנים Peah. c.1.4.5. Qui angulum non reliquit, ille ex decisio frumento anguli pretium pauperibus compensare potest, & à decimatione liber est donec frumentum ventilaverit. Peah. 1.5. quæ angulum agri determinare possunt ab init. huius seét, adduximus. Angulus agri relinqui debet etiam in illis montibus, qui aliàs jumentis ob asperitatem non arantur, sed simpliciter sarculis colunt Peah. c.2.1. Angulum in siliquis relinquunt, ubi se invicem respiciunt, in olivelo vero versus omnes mundi plagas. Qui in toto agro suo unam solùm seminis speciem adhibuit, etiamsi duo horrea replevisset, unum tamen solum angulum relinquit, qui duas species severit duos. Peah. c.2.4.5. Ab angulo liber est cuius agrum idololatræ aut latrones demessuerunt, aut Cameli aut alia animalia corruperunt. Si cùm iam dimidiam partem demessuit veniant depredatores, & alteram succidant,ab angulo liber est; fi vero depræda-tores partem demetunt, colligit ille deinde alteram, angulum relinquere debet. Si quis unam partem demetit, alteram vero vendit, emens pro toto angulum relinquere debet. Sic si quis unam partem demetit alteram vero sanctificat, ille qui à Quæstore templi illam partem redimit, angulum pro integro agro relinquere debet.Peah.c.2.7.8 Angulus agri relinquendus est, modò in fundo 4. pars cabi seri pollit, vel modo fundus duo seah producat, aut messor bis brachium suum replere possit. Peah.3.6. Vineæ palis aut arboribus incumbentibus angulum, Pater familias dividit, (non autem permittit ut unusquisque capiat quantum velit : idem facit respectu nucum, dactylorum. Peah.4.1. Angulum agri non demetunt falcibus messoriis, aut aliis eius generis instrumentis, ne pauperes se invicem dum unusquisque aliquid colligere studet vulnerent. Distribuunt autem angulum ter in die, mane, à meridie,& vesperi,quæ tempora vocant אבעיות à בעה pet it ; manè quidem distribuitur spicilegium propter pauperum infantes, qui mane cibo opus habent, à meridie vero propter pueros, vesperi autem propter senes, qui urbem non petunt, nisi tunc temporis. Peah c.4 4 5. vid Maym. in loc. Qui dicit,angulus hic agri sit N.viro pauperi & egeno, etiam illi totum dare potest, aliàs ille semper primum obvio pauperi relinquendus est. Angulo agri לקט וpicilegio & שכחה ( vid. de his f. 1. ) ille non frui debet, qui 200.sulfos (v. f.1.) possidet, aut qui 50. solùm habet, sed illis ad mercaturam & usuram uti scit. Quandiu aliquis pauper non ex cistula pecuniam acci­pit, potest fpicilegio frui, quamvis domi adhuc aliqua utensilia habeat, ex quorum pecunia vi­vere posset, sed fi pecuniam accipit cistulæ (vid. Eleemosyna.) dicunt ipsi vende fuppellectilem tuam pulchram, & tenuiorem tibi compara ואל תמעיט מחנות העניים nec deminue dona paupe& shy;rum. Qui privilegiis pauperum utitur illis vero non opus habet, aut qui quidem opus haberet sed ea negligit אינו מת מן הזקנה non morietur ex senectute, & ante suum fatum aliorumope indi­gebit. Peah.8.9. Comment.
units.tr: The corner of a field to be left for the poor has no fixed measure (mensura), but must be made in proportion to the size of the field, the number of the poor, and generosity. If anyone nevertheless wishes to fix some measure, he should know that שאין מותחין לפאה משששים [that one should not stretch the corner beyond a sixth] less than a sixth part of the field should not be assigned. From Peah ch. 1, 2: the corner of a field may be made at the beginning, middle, or end of the field. Ibid. v. 3: the corner must be left from all those fruits שהוא אוכל [that are eaten], which are fit for food and lawful (for the precept about the corner does not apply to those which grow spontaneously or are not really lawful); ונשמר [and kept], which is preserved (in contrast to those which are public property); וגדולין מן הארץ [and grown from the earth], which grow from the ground (in contrast to those which do not have their roots in the earth); which are gathered at one time, and which can be stored. For the following kinds of trees the corner must be left: בשקרים אגוזים תרובין אוגין תמרים זיתים דימונים גפנים [sycamores, walnuts, terebinths, figs, dates, olives, pomegranates, vines]. Peah ch. 1, 4, 5. He who has not left the corner may make up its price to the poor from the threshed grain, and he is free from tithing until he has winnowed the grain. Peah 1, 5. We have cited above, at the beginning of this section, what can determine the corner of a field. The corner must also be left on those hills which are otherwise not ploughed by draught animals because of their roughness, but are simply tilled with hoes. Peah ch. 2, 1. In pods they leave the corner where they face one another, but in an olive grove towards all the quarters of the world. Whoever has sown only one kind of seed in his whole field, even if he has filled two granaries, leaves only one corner; but whoever has sown two kinds leaves two corners. Peah ch. 2, 4, 5. He is free from the corner whose field idolaters or robbers have reaped, or whose field camels or other animals have damaged. If, when he has already reaped half, plunderers come and cut the other half, he is free from the corner; but if the plunderers reap part and he then gathers the other part, he must leave the corner. If someone reaps one part and sells the other, buying for the whole he must leave the corner. Likewise, if someone reaps one part and consecrates the other, the one who redeems that part from the treasurer of the temple must leave the corner for the whole field. Peah ch. 2, 7, 8. A corner of a field must be left wherever a fourth part of a cab of seed can be sown, or wherever the field can produce two seah, or wherever the reaper can fill his arm twice. Peah 3, 6. In vineyards where the vines lean on stakes or trees, the head of the household divides the corner (and does not permit each person to take as much as he wishes); he does the same with respect to nuts and dates. Peah 4, 1. They do not reap the corner with sickles or other such instruments, lest the poor wound one another while each strives to gather something. They distribute the corner three times a day, in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, which times they call אבעיות [ʾabʿiyyot], from בעה [baʿah], to seek. In the morning the gleaning is distributed for the little children of the poor, who need food in the morning; at midday for the boys; and in the evening for the old, who do not come to the town except at that time. Peah ch. 4, 4, 5; see Maimonides on the passage. He who says, "This corner of the field is for N., a poor and needy man," may give the whole of it to him; otherwise it must always be left for the first poor man who meets him. He who has 200 sela (see f. 1) or who has only 50, but knows how to use them for trade and usury, ought not to enjoy the corner of the field, the gleaning and the forgotten sheaves (see f. 1 on these). As long as a poor man does not take money from the alms-box, he may enjoy the gleaning, even though he still has some household utensils, from the sale of which he could live; but if he takes money from the alms-box (see Alms), they say to him: sell your fine furniture and buy yourself something humbler, ואל תמעיט מחנות העניים [and do not diminish the gifts of the poor]. He who makes use of the privileges of the poor, though he has no need of them, or who indeed would need them but neglects them, אינו מת מן הזקנה [shall not die of old age], and before his fated time he will need the help of others. Peah 8, 9. Commentary.

units.la: איש הר הבית Ifch har habbaith, Præfectus montis templi fecundùmR.Schemaia definitur משמרת על כל משמורים præfectus omnibus custodum excubiis. Illius officium erat perlustrare singulas custodias,& quando illud agebat præluceba nt ei faces: unumquemque autem custodem qui pedibus non insistebat, his verbis compellabat שלום עליך pax tibi. Si eum dormire animadvertebat, baculo percutiebat, imò aliquando vestimenta eius comburebat; Hinc etiam in usu erat apud ci­ves Hierosolymitanos quando aliquem cla­morem ex templo percipiebant, dicere מה קול בעודה קול בן לוי לוקה וכגדיו נשרפו Qua vox in atrio magno? vox Levita vapulantis, cuius ve& shy;stimenta comburuntur &c. Middot. c.1.2. Maymon. Hal.Bet Habech. c.8. sub med. de aliis templi officiariis vid. suo 1.
units.tr: Ifch har habbaith, the prefect of the Temple Mount. According to R. Schemaia he is defined as the overseer over all the watches [משמרת על כל משמורים]. His duty was to go round each of the guard posts, and torches lit his way while he did so. He addressed each guard who was not on his feet with the words Peace be upon you [שלום עליך]. If he saw a guard asleep, he struck him with a staff, and sometimes even set fire to his garments. Hence too it was the custom among the citizens of Jerusalem, when they heard some outcry from the Temple, to say: What is this voice in the great court? The voice of a Levite being beaten, whose garments are burnt, etc. Middot c.1.2. Maimonides, Hal. Beth Habechirah c.8, near the middle, on the other officers of the Temple; see his 1.

units.la: R. Akiba Natus est R. Akiba ex posteris Siserae ducis Iabin regis Tyri. Iud.c.4. Israelita deinde per proselytismum iustitiæ (uti vocant) factus in doctrina ita profecit, ut primò scholæ Lyddanæ, deindè etiam Iabhnenfis præses factus fuerit. De Akibæ actionibus in Lydda & Iafne plurima exempla reperiuntur: audax in primis erat illud facinus quo quadraginta hominum paria ad Synedrium itinerantia retinere ausus est, ut patet ex Rofch Hafchana c.1. à talibus enim testibus intercalatio mensis & anni dependebat, quæ ut accuratè fieret totius gentis commoditas requisivit: hinc sanè synedrium cùm adhuc Hierosolymis sedebat, homines lautis conviviis allexit, ut eò citiùs prima φάσει lunari cósspecta,se in פנים בית Iaafeki Atriu locum ad examen testium ordinatum conferrent, nec in itinere ullas moras necterent. Quo satis ostendit Senatus intercalationé nec negotium esse indifferens necsomnolente agendum.
units.tr: R. Akiba was born of the descendants of Sisera, captain of King Jabin of Tyre (Judg. 4). He was then an Israelite by the proselytism of righteousness, as they call it, and he advanced in learning so far that he became head first of the school at Lydda and then also of the school at Jabneh. Very many examples of Akiba's doings at Lydda and Jabneh are found. The boldest of his deeds was that by which he dared to detain forty pairs of men who were travelling to the Sanhedrin, as appears from Rosh Hashanah c.1. For the intercalation of the month and the year depended on such witnesses, and to make it accurate required the convenience of the whole nation. Hence, while the Sanhedrin still sat at Jerusalem, he enticed men with lavish banquets, so that as soon as the first lunar appearance was observed they would hurry to the hall in the house of Yaafeki appointed for the examination of witnesses, and would not delay on the journey. This shows well enough that the Senate regarded intercalation as no matter to be handled with indifference or drowsiness.

units.la: §. Disputavit Akiba cum Turno Russo(v.f.1.) & ipsi Sabbathum tribus argumentis adstruxit; primum desumpsit à fluvio סנטיין qui per omnes dies septimanæ fluit, sed Sabbatho quiescit, alterum verò à Pythonico, qui in Sabbatho non ascendit. Tertium àTurni Russi patris sepulchro, quod per totam septimanam fumigabat, & non nisi in Sabbatho cessabat. Sanhed.f.65.2. Gloss.
units.tr: Akiba disputed with Turnus Rufus (Russus, v.f. 1) and proved the Sabbath to him by three arguments. First, he took one from the river Sambation, which flows through all the days of the week but rests on the Sabbath. Second, from the Pythonic, which does not rise on the Sabbath. Third, from the grave of Turnus Rufus's father, which smoked through the whole week and ceased only on the Sabbath. Sanhedrin f.65.2, Gloss.

units.la: §. Periit Akiba in Betharana clade de qua legere poteris Bab. Gittin sol.57.1. Hierof.Taanith sol.68 4. & 69 1.
units.tr: Akiba perished in the slaughter at Bethar, of which you may read in Bab. Gittin fol. 57.1 and Jerusalem Taanith fol. 68.4 and 69.1.

units.la: ALEXANDER magnus in Palæstinam venit & à Simeone Iusto exceptus fuit, Historia exstat Ioma sol 69.1. Orarunt Cuthai Alexandrum Macedonem ut templum Dei nostri destruere possent ; annuit illis ipsis. Venerunt quidam atque id indicarunt Simeoni Iusto; qui induit statim vestes Pontificias, & cum praestantissimis Israelis manibus tenentes faces, per totam noctem Alexandro obviam processit. Cum ad Antipatridam pervenerunt ortus est sol: Dixit Alexander suis: Quinam isti? Responderunt, Iudaei qui in te rebellarunt, Cum autem videret Alexander Simeonem Iustum, descendit a curru, & coram ipso se incurvavit. Dixerunt ipsi, Rex tali us gloria, qualis tu, se coram Iudaeo incurvat. Respondit ipsis: figuram huic simile m vidi coram me in bello pugnantem. Deinde Iudaeos alloquutus est, Quare huc descendistis? Responderunt, ut preces ad Deum fundere-mus tui & regni tui causa, ne illud devastetur. &c.
units.tr: Alexander the Great came into Palestine and was received by Simeon the Just. The story is in Yoma fol. 69.1: The Cuthaeans asked Alexander the Macedonian that they might destroy the temple of our God, and he granted it to them. Some men came and reported this to Simeon the Just, who at once put on the priestly vestments and, with the most distinguished men of Israel holding torches, went out to meet Alexander through the whole night. When they reached Antipatris the sun rose. Alexander said to his men: Who are these? They replied: Jews who have rebelled against you. But when Alexander saw Simeon the Just, he got down from his chariot and bowed before him. They said to him: O king, do you, who have such glory, bow before a Jew? He answered them: I have seen the likeness of this man fighting before me in battle. Then he addressed the Jews: Why have you come down here? They replied: To pour out prayers to God for you and for your kingdom, that it not be laid waste, etc.

units.la: §. Alexander à Iudaeis Hierosolymam deductus, petiit à Simeone Iusto ut aliquod monumentum ipsi collocarent inter gradus & Altare. Renuit id Simeon propter praeceptum de nullo sculptili conficiendo; sed promisit Alexandro, cives Hierosolymitanos omnes filios illo anno nascituros de nomine ipsius Alexandros vocaturos esse. Vid. Zemach David Cl.Vorst. p. 59.
units.tr: Alexander, led up to Jerusalem by the Jews, asked Simeon the Just that they should set up some monument to him between the steps and the altar. Simeon refused, on account of the precept against making any graven image; but he promised Alexander that all the citizens of Jerusalem who would be born in that year would be called Alexander after his name. See Zemach David, Vorst, p. 59.

units.la: §. Postquam Alexander Hierosolymis prosectus est, egressus est ad ipsum Sanballetes Horonites, cum filiis Iehosuae Sacerdotis summi, & petiit ab Alexandro, ut Sacerdotes affines eius possent in monte Gerizim Sanctuarium aedificare. Rex annuit, & tunc exstructo templo in partes itum est, pars sequuta est Simeonem Iustum, alii vero Samaritanos. Iuchasin p.14.2.
units.tr: After Alexander had left Jerusalem, Sanballat the Horonite came out to meet him with the sons of Jehoiada the high priest, and asked Alexander that his priestly relatives might build a sanctuary on Mount Gerizim. The king consented, and when the temple had been built the people divided into parts: one part followed Simeon the Just, and the others followed the Samaritans. Iuchasin p. 14.2.

units.la: §. Hærente Alexandro in Palæstina accidit famosa illa disputatio inter Gi.rgesæos & Gaboah filium Pesi æ ex parte Iudæorum. Girgesæi enim suis sedibus fugati terrore Iosuæ in Africam se receperant, Alexandro autem in Iudæa versante apud ipsum cum Iudæis de repetundis experiri voluerunt. Respondit pro Iudæis Gaboah, & quidem tam feliciter, ut Girgesæi nullas exceptiones reperientes Iudicium & vadimonium defecerent. vid. cap. in Sanhed. p. 91. cap. ix.
units.tr: While Alexander was staying in Palestine, that famous dispute occurred between the Girgashites and Gaboah son of Pesi on the side of the Jews. For the Girgashites, scattered from their seats by the terror of Joshua, had withdrawn into Africa; but when Alexander was in Judea they wished to bring a suit against the Jews before him for extortion. Gaboah answered for the Jews, and so successfully that the Girgashites, finding no exceptions to take, gave up the judgment and the surety. See in Sanhedrin p. 91, ch. ix.

units.la: §. Alexander Solum Salomonis Regis, transuxit in Ægyptum Esth. 1.2.in Secundo Targum.De eius quæstionibus, quas 70. senibus proposuit vide Tamid. sol.31.2. sol.32.
units.tr: Alexander also transferred the throne of King Solomon into Egypt. Esth. 1.2, in the Second Targum. About his questions, which he put to the seventy elders, see Tamid fol. 31.2 and fol. 32.

units.la: ALEXANDRIÆ Iudæi splendidam Ecclesiam habuerunt,qui eam non vidit, non vidit unquam gloriam Israelis. Basilicæ instar erat, duplicatæ porticus. Erant aliquando illic qui numerum exeuntium ex Ægypto duplo excederent. Erant etiam in illa septuaginta cathedrae aureæ gemmataque, pro numero septuaginta seniorum. Suggestum etiam ligneum in medio collocatum, in quo stetit Episcopus Synagogæ. Confusim & mixtim non sederunt, sed unusquisque artifex cum professoribus eiusdem artificii, ita ut si advenieret peregrinus, cum eiusdem opificii mechanicis se posset commiscere, &c. Hierof.Succah. f.55.1.2. Gem. Babil.Succah sol. 51. 2. Probabile est Christi parentes in Ægypto asylum quærentes se huic magnæ Ecclesiæ coniunxisse, quia hac ratione etiam facile paupertati ipsorum, per communia Ecclefiæ subsidia, & eiusdem opificii, professorum auxilia subveniri potuit.
units.tr: At Alexandria the Jews had a splendid congregation, and whoever has not seen it has never seen the glory of Israel. It was like a basilica, with double porticoes. At times there were people there who exceeded twice the number of those who went out of Egypt. In it there were also seventy chairs of gold set with gems, corresponding to the number of the seventy elders. A wooden platform was placed in the middle, on which the bishop of the synagogue stood. They did not sit in confusion and mixed together, but each craftsman sat with the masters of the same craft, so that if a stranger came he could join the craftsmen of his own trade, etc. Jerusalem Succah f. 55.1.2; Babylonian Gemara Succah fol. 51.2. It is probable that Christ's parents, seeking refuge in Egypt, joined this great congregation, because in this way their poverty could easily be relieved by the common funds of the congregation and by the help of masters of the same trade.

units.la: Alienigenæ vid. Extranei.
units.tr: Aliens (Alienigenae): see Strangers (Extranei).

units.la: ALTARE debuit esse intra portionem Beniamininis, nam Bab.Ioma sol.12.1. quæritur, quid fuit in portione Iuda? Mons templi, Pastophoria, Atria: & quidnam in portione Beniaminis? Pronaon, templum & Sanctum Sanctorum. Prodiitque linea e portione Iudæ, & progressa est in portionem Benjaminis, atque in ea conditum est altare.
units.tr: The altar was to stand within the portion of Benjamin, for the Babylonian Yoma fol. 12.1 asks: What was in the portion of Judah? The mount of the temple, the pastophoria, and the courts. And what was in the portion of Benjamin? The porch, the temple, and the Holy of Holies. The line went out from the portion of Judah and extended into the portion of Benjamin, and the altar was founded in it.

units.la: §. Lapides altaris (ex nulla enim materia quàm ex lapidibus altare fieri debuit inquit Maymon.) debent ex illorum numero esse, qui vitium aut fissuram plane nullam habent, nullum opus super ipsos debuit factum esse; hinc in usu habuerunt illos desumere פן כתולת הקרקע ex terra virgine, loco scilicet illo ad quem nec aratra nec hominum perfossiones adhuc pervenerant. Etiam licitum erat lapides illos adhibere quos ex Mare mediterraneo מים גדול eruere poterant. Maymon. Hal. Beth Habech. c.1. in med.
units.tr: The stones of the altar (for Maimonides says the altar had to be made of nothing but stones) must be of those which have no flaw or crack at all, and no work was to be done upon them. Hence they were accustomed to take them from virgin ground [כתולת הקרקע], that is, from a place which neither plough nor human digging had yet reached. It was also permitted to use stones which they could dig out of the Mediterranean Sea [מים גדול]. Maimonides, Hal. Beth Habechirah c.1, in the middle.

units.la: §. Prohibitum fuit facere מדרגות gradus ad ascendendum super altare, quapropter in latere meridionali altaris ædificarunt ascensum in modum תל acervi, quo sensim ad summitatem ducebantur, hanc molem ascensus vocant נבש. Maymon.l.c.sub sin.
units.tr: It was forbidden to make steps [מדרגות] for ascending onto the altar. So on the south side of the altar they built an ascent in the form of a heap [תל], by which they were led gradually up to the top; this mass of ascent they call nevesh [נבש]. Maimonides, l.c., near the end.

units.la: §. Locus altaris mutari non debet, nam in illo offerre voluit Abraham Isaacum, David obtulit grassante peste sacrificium; in illo loco etiam ædificaverat Noachus altare suum postquàm arcâ egressus est.Imò ibi obtulerunt sacrificia Abel& Kain, & ipse Adamus. (v. supra)Maym.Beth Habeth. c.2.
units.tr: The place of the altar must not be changed, for Abraham wished to offer Isaac in it; David offered a sacrifice there when the plague was raging; in that very place Noah built his altar after he came out of the ark. Indeed Abel and Cain offered sacrifices there, and Adam himself. (See above.) Maimonides, Beth Habechirah c.2.

units.la: §. Cum Israele ex captivitate Babylonica tres Prophetæ ascenderunt, unus ipsis indicavit locum altaris, alter quæ mensuræ requirantur ad illud ritè conficiendum, tertius docuit ipsos omnigena sacrificia in illo offerri posse. Maymon l. c.
units.tr: When three prophets went up with Israel from the Babylonian captivity, one showed them the place of the altar, another told them the measurements required to build it properly, and the third taught them that all kinds of sacrifices could be offered on it. Maimonides, l.c.

units.la: §. De magnitudine, & latitudine altaris pluribus ipse Maym. recenset c. modò citato, inter alia refert altare Mosis, Salomonis, & ex captivitate Babyl. revertentium habuisse in altitudine decem cubitos; altitudo 3.cubitorum insumebatur in locum struis. Ibid. Cæterùm Altare quaquaversum fuit 32.cubitorum; post ascensum unius cubiti ita coarctabatur, ut in quadratura cubito uno minor esset. Post altitudinem aliorum 5. cubitorum iterum coarctebatur in cubitum,ita ut illic quaquaversum essent tantum 28.cubiti. Locus cornuum ab omni parte spatio unius cubiti deprimebatur, ita ut undiquaque iam solùm essent 26. cubiti. Locus ambulationis sacerdotum hinc inde unius cubiti,ita ut locus pyræ pateret undiquaque 24. cubitos. Ascensus ad altare erat longitudine 32. & latitudine 16. cubitorum. Middot. c.3.
units.tr: Concerning the magnitude and breadth of the altar Maimonides himself lists many details in the chapter just cited. Among other things he reports that the altar of Moses, of Solomon, and of those returning from the Babylonian captivity had a height of ten cubits, of which three cubits were taken up by the base of stones. The altar was thirty-two cubits on every side. After the ascent of one cubit it was narrowed so that it was one cubit smaller in its square. After a further height of five cubits it was narrowed again by one cubit, so that there it was only twenty-eight cubits on every side. The ledge of the horns was lowered by a space of one cubit on every side, so that on all sides there were now only twenty-six cubits. The walkway of the priests ran on either side for one cubit, so that the place of the pyre lay open on every side for twenty-four cubits. The ascent to the altar was thirty-two cubits long and sixteen cubits broad. Middot c.3.

units.la: §. Filum coccineum cingebat altare ad discernendum inter sanguinem superiorem & inseriorem: ut hac ratione Sacerdotes in spargendo sanguine ab errore cavere possent. Etenim hanc distinctionè olim observatâ tradunt,
units.tr: §. A scarlet thread went round the altar to mark the line between the upper and the lower blood, so that the priests might avoid error in sprinkling the blood. For they relate that this distinction was observed of old:

units.la: ut pecudis pro peccato & avis in holocauftum oblatæ sanguis supra filium : reliquorum verò sanguis infra filum spargeretur. vid. Cl. l'Empereur in Middot p. 100.
units.tr: the blood of a beast offered for sin, and of a bird offered as a burnt offering, was sprinkled above the thread, while the blood of the rest was sprinkled below the thread. See Cl. l'Empereur on Middot, p. 100.

units.la: §. Altaris Balis non habebat angulum versus ortum Brumalem, eò quòd ista portiuncula non effet intra portionem Iudæ (id est Benjaminis propter communionem enim utriufque tribus, aliquoties scriptura cùm de Iuda verba facit, Benjaminem vel eius saltem partem maximam, unâ intelligi vult. Sicuti videre est 1.Reg.12.20. collato cum cap.11. v.31.32. 2.Chron.11.3.10.12. & 13.)
units.tr: §. The southwest corner of the altar lacked a corner on the side toward the winter sunrise, because that little portion was not within the portion of Judah (that is, of Benjamin). Because the two tribes shared the territory, Scripture, when it speaks of Judah, sometimes means Benjamin too, or at least its greater part, as one may see at 1 Kings 12:20 compared with ch. 11:31–32, 2 Chron. 11:3, 10, 12, and 13.

units.la: §. I i cornu inter occidentem & austrum erant duo foramina per quæ sanguis descendebat in torrentem Kedron. Middot c. 3.
units.tr: §. At the two horns, between the west and the south, there were two openings through which the blood ran down into the brook Kidron. Middot ch. 3.

units.la: §. In Sancto Sanctorum erat lapis cui imposita erat arca וּלְפָנֵי & coram ipsa posita erat manna & baculus Aharonis. וּבְעֵת שִׁבְנָה שְׁלֹמֹה אֶת הַבַּיִת וַיֵּדַע שִׁסּוּוּ לִיחֹרֵב בְּנָה בוֹ מָקוֹם לִגְנוֹז בּוֹ הָאָרוֹן לְמֹשֶׁה בְּמִשְׁמְנִיּוֹת עֲמוּקוֹת וְעַקְלְקְלוֹת וַיֹּאשִׁיהוּ הַמֶּלֶךְ צִוָּה וַיְגַנּוּ בַּמָּקוֹם שְׁבָנָה שְׁלֹמֹה : Cum Salomo sanctuarium ædificabat, & ipsi probè notum erat, illud aliquando esse devastandum, ad præcautionem construxit locum in quo Arca abscon-deretur. Erat autem locus ille aufraclucfus & sinuosis viis munitus, & ibi arcam abscondere iussit Rex Iosias &c. in templo secundo verò non amplius fuit repositâ. Maym. Hal. Beth Habech. c. 4. Forsan illæ cavitates fuerunt ille locus ex quo soluta captivitate Babylonica Sacerdotes quidam ignem sacrum ad struem altaris incendendam præsentibus Nehemia
units.tr: In the Holy of Holies there was a stone on which the ark was placed, and in front of it were set the manna and Aaron's rod. [When Solomon built the house and knew that it would one day be laid waste, he made a place in it in which to hide the ark of Moses, in deep and winding recesses; and King Josiah commanded, and they hid it in the place Solomon had built.] Cum Salomo sanctuarium ædificabat… In the second temple, however, the ark was no longer put there. Maimonides, Hilkhot Beit ha-Behirah, c. 4. Perhaps those cavities were the place from which, after the Babylonian captivity had ended, certain priests brought out the sacred fire, in the form of a watery substance, to kindle the pile on the altar, in the presence of Nehemiah and Ezra, as Josephus ben Gorion relates in c. 17.

units.la: Esra sub aquosæ materiæ forma protulerunt, sicuti historiam refert Iosephi Ben Gorion c.17.
units.tr: Josephus ben Gorion, c. 17, relates this history.

units.la: §. Antequàm fato functus esset Simeon justus (quod contigit ante Christi nativitatem) ignis struis semper viguerat, at ipso mortuo vigor ignis non conservabatur, nisi Sacerdotes per totum diem ligna supplerent. Hieros. Ioma sol.43.3.
units.tr: Before the death of the just Simeon (which happened before the birth of Christ), the fire on the altar pile had always burned strongly; but after his death the fire did not keep its vigour unless the priests supplied wood through the whole day. Jerusalem Talmud, Yoma, fol. 43, col. 3.

units.la: §. Gradus sive ἀνάβασις altaris Sacerdotes ascendebant eâ parte quæ orientem spectat, & descendebant illâ quæ est versus occidentem, summus Sacerdos verò ascendebat & descendebat in die expiationis in medio. In omnibus anni diebus, quatuor iniacebant altari ligni strues, in die expiationis verò erant quinque. Ioma c.4.
units.tr: §. The time for cleansing the altar: see under the Feast of Atonement. At first, whoever wished to cleanse the altar did so. Then, when several wished to do it, they contended by a trial of fingers over who should enjoy that honour. At last, when one of them, while running, was thrown down from the steps of the altar by another and broke his foot, the Sanhedrin decreed that the man who was to cleanse the altar should be chosen by lot. Yoma ch. 2. The stones of the altar were wiped with a cloth every Sabbath evening, and the blood was washed off. Middot ch. 3–4.

units.la: §. Tempus purgandi altare vid. in Festo expiationis. In principio qui altare expurgare voluit expurgabat: Deinde cùm plures illud agere voluerunt, dimicatione digitorum decertarunt, qui illo honore frui deberet: Tandem cùm accidisset ut unus inter currendum ab alio à gradibus altaris deturbatus pedem fregisset, Synedrium constituit, ut ille qui altare purgare deberet sorte eligeretur. Ioma c.2. Lapides Altaris, mappâ, singulis Sabbathi vesperis detergebant, & Sanguinem eluebant. Middot c.3.4.
units.tr: §. The stones of the altar were neither to be cut with iron nor touched with it, lest the Israelites come to carve images on the stones. Abarbanel on Exodus; Cl. l'Empereur on Middot, p. 115. The stones of the altar, when the ascent was brought, were quarried from the valley of Beth Charem, below untilled ground (as we have said). Middot ch. 3–4.

units.la: §. Altaris lapides ferro nec scindi nec tangi debebant, ne Israelitæ, eò devenirent ut in lapidibus formarent imagines. Abarb. in Exod. Cl. l'Emper. in Middot p.115. Lapides tum altaris cùm ascensus allati sunt ex convalle בית כרם Beth Charem, infra terram incultam (ut diximus) effossi. Middot cap. 3. 4.
units.tr: §. The altar gives asylum only to one who lays hold of its top, and a priest must be there ministering who receives him. If anyone has fled to the altar, they do not leave him there, but they send attendants with him to a city of refuge. Maymonides, Hilkhot Rotze'ach, ch. 5.

units.la: §. Altare asylum non praestat nisi כנגד in summitate sua, & ibi sit Sacerdos ministrans qui ipsum recipiat. Si quis se receperit ad altare, ipsum ibi non relinquunt, sed Adiungentes ipsi custodes mittunt illum in asyli urbem: Maym. Hal. Rozeaeh c. 5.
units.tr: The altar gives asylum only at its horns [כנגד], in its top part, and a priest must be there ministering who receives the one who takes refuge. If anyone has fled to the altar, they do not leave him there, but the guards who come up to him send him to a city of refuge. Maimonides, Hilkhot Rotzeach, c. 5.

units.la: §. Nulla est differentia inter altare magnum & parvum כין בכה גדולה וקטנה nisi respectu aliorum paschalium; Haec est generalis regula, omne Sacrificium votivum & spontaneum offertur super altare (parvum secundum Gloss.) Sacrificium autem, quod nec votivum est, nec voluntarium, non offerri debet super altare. Megillah c. 1. 11.
units.tr: There is no difference between the great altar and the small altar [כין בכה גדולה וקטנה] except with respect to the other paschal offerings. This is the general rule: every votive and voluntary sacrifice is offered upon the altar (the small one, according to the Gloss). But a sacrifice that is neither votive nor voluntary must not be offered upon the altar. Megillah, c. 1, sect. 11.

units.la: §. De lignis pro altari vid. Ligna.
units.tr: On the wood used for the altar, see Ligna.

units.la: AMANAH secundum R. Salomo Cantic. iv. 8. est mons in ore terrae Israeliticae Aquilonari & apud Talmudicos vocatur אמנה טורי ; idem est cum monte Hor; extra illum montem non amplius erat terra Israelitica. Hierof. Scheviit. sol. 36. 4.
units.tr: AMANAH, according to R. Solomon on Song of Songs 4:8, is a mountain at the northern edge of the land of Israel; in the Talmudists it is called Amanah, the mountains (הרי אמנה). It is the same as Mount Hor; beyond that mountain there was no longer any land of Israel. Jerusalem Talmud, Sheviit, fol. 36, col. 4.

units.la: AMEN respondent post Israelitam benedicentem, sed non post Cutheum, nisi tota audita benedictione. Beracot c. 8. 8.
units.tr: They answer Amen after an Israelite who blesses, but not after a Samaritan, unless the whole blessing has been heard. Berakhot, c. 8, sect. 8.

units.la: §. In Liturgia publica in templo commemoratio regni Dei fuit pro Antiphono, quo vice Amen respondebatur à populo, orationibus finitis Sacerdotum. Nam תני לא היו עונין אמן בבית הקדש Traditio est, non respondsum suisse Amen in domo Sanctuarii. Quid ergo dixerunt? ברוך שם כבוד מלכותו לעולם Benedictum sit nomen gloriae regni eius in sempiternum. Hierof.
units.tr: In the public liturgy in the Temple, the commemoration of the kingdom of God took the place of the antiphon, to which the people answered in place of Amen when the prayers of the priests were finished. For there is a tradition (תני) that they did not answer Amen in the house of the sanctuary. What then did they say? "Blessed be the name of the glory of his kingdom for ever and ever." Jerusalem Talmud.

units.la: Beracot f. 13.3. Hinc in tractatu Ioma post recitatas varias oratiunculas, quas eo die fudit summus Pontifex, additur. Et respondit populus, Benedictum sit nomen gloriæ regni eius in sempiternum. vid. Bab. Ioma sol. 39. 1. 41. 2. sol. 66. 1. Hanc orationum Coronidem etiam retinuit in oratione Dominica ὡς σὺ βασιλεία.
units.tr: §. Amen is not only the word of one who confirms and assents, but also of one who swears an oath. An example of assent you have in the woman who was made to drink the bitter waters, for she had to answer Amen to everything the priest said to her (see f. 1). An example of an oath sworn by Amen you have in ch. 9 of Bava Kamma: [היכן פקדוני] Where is my deposit? He answers: It was stolen. I adjure you (whether the thing is so). He answers: Amen. Certainly this doubled word, if not an oath, is at least a solemn asseveration.

units.la: §. In Precibus privatis τὸ Amen etiam rarius usurparunt. Ex tractatu Béracot vero patet, precibus fusis à ministro in Synagoga & à Patrefamiliâs super cibum ut plurimum à Populo & familiaribus Amen fuisse additum: uti videmus illud adhuc hodie in cultu Ecclesiæ Romanæ fieri.
units.tr: In private prayers they used the word Amen even more rarely. But from the tractate Berakhot it is clear that after prayers poured out by the minister in the synagogue, and by the head of the household over food, Amen was usually added by the people and the members of the household. We see that this is still done today in the worship of the Roman Church.

units.la: §. Amen non solùm est confirmantis, assentientisque, sed etiam iuramentum præstantis; assentientis exemplum habes in muliere quæ aquis amaris potabatur illa enim ad omnia quæ Sacerdos ipsi dicebat Amen respondere debebat, (v. f. 1.) Exemplum iuramenti per Amen præstiti habes cap. ix. Bab. Kama היכן פקדוני אמר לו נגנב משביעך אני ויאמר אמן Vbi est depositum meum? Respondet furto ablatum est. Adiuro te (an res ita se habeat) Respondet, Amen. Duplicata certè hæc vox si Christo non iuramentum, tamen seria assleveratio est.
units.tr: Amen is not only a word of confirmation and assent, but also of swearing an oath. An example of assent you have in the woman who was made to drink the bitter waters, for she had to answer Amen to everything the priest said to her (see f. 1). An example of an oath sworn by Amen you have in chapter 9 of Bava Kamma: "Where is my deposit?" He answers, "It has been stolen." "I adjure you (whether the matter stands so)." He answers, "Amen." Certainly this doubled word, if not an oath to Christ, is still a solemn affirmation.

units.la: §. Quid in Beracot sol. 47. 1. per אמן השבועה אמן קשופה ואמן יתומה Per amen accelerationem, amen amputatum, & amen orbum intelligant Talmudici, apud Cl. Buxtorf. in L.T. reperies. Apud eundem vid. f. 169.
units.tr: What the Talmudists understand by "amen of acceleration, amen cut short, and amen bereaved" (אמן השבועה, אמן קשופה, ואמן יתומה), in Berakhot, fol. 47, col. 1, you will find in Buxtorf's Lexicon Talmudicum. In the same work see p. 169.

units.la: De Amentia vid. si quis mente excesserit. in M. Amici. Ad ostium tabernarum multi sunt fratres & amici, ad ostium locorum despectorum, neque fratres neque amici. Schabb. f.32.1: Non est foramen acus angustum duobus amicis, nec tota mundi capacitas sufficit duobus inimicis. Adag.
units.tr: On Amentia see if anyone has lost his mind, in M. Amici. "At the door of taverns there are many brothers and friends; at the door of disreputable places, neither brothers nor friends." Shabbat, fol. 32, col. 1: "The eye of a needle is not too narrow for two friends, nor does the whole breadth of the world suffice for two enemies." Proverb.

units.la: Rei Amissæ præconium vid. Bava Metzia sol. 28. 1.
units.tr: For the proclamation of a lost thing, see Bava Metzia, fol. 28, col. 1.

units.la: אמרכלין Amarcalin Fuerunt septem officiarii templi, qui habebant claves ad septem portas atrii, ita tamen ut nullus posset absque altero aperire. Schekalim. c. 5. Maymon. in Kele Mikd. p. 4. Alii addunt prope septem portas, fuisse septem conclavia, ad vasa & vestimenta sacra includenda, & hos septem operam dedisse, ut omnia rite ibi procederent. vid. Tosaph. ad Schekalim c. 5. & R. Salomoh in 2.Reg.12.
units.tr: אמרכלין, Amarcalin. There were seven officers of the temple who held the keys to the seven gates of the court, in such a way that no one could open them without another. Shekalim, c. 5; Maimonides on Kele ha-Mikdash, p. 4. Others add that near the seven gates there were seven chambers for enclosing the sacred vessels and garments, and that these seven took care that everything was done there properly. See Tosafot on Shekalim, c. 5, and R. Solomon on 2 Kings 12.

units.la: §. Ionathan in Paraphrasi legali voce אמרכול utitur primò ad denotandos principes & primarios 12. tribuum qui Mosi adsteterunt, ad populum numerandum. Num.1. Num.7.11. Secundò significat, seniores tribuum, qui manus imposuerant sacrificio congregationis pro peccato Lev.4.15. Targum in Cant.4.3. Immarcol sumit pro Principe qui cum rege versatur.
units.tr: In the legal Paraphrase Jonathan uses the word אמרכול, first to denote the princes and chief men of the twelve tribes who stood by Moses to number the people (Num. 1; Num. 7:11). Second, it signifies the elders of the tribes who laid their hands on the sacrifice of the congregation for sin (Lev. 4:15). Targum on Song of Songs 4:3: he takes Immarcol for a prince who attends the king.

units.la: §. Kimchi in 2. Reg.12.10. ita commentatur quid sint Amarcalin. פו שומרי Custodes utensilium vel vasum templi 3 פו enim est nomen generale & denotat indiscriminatim omnia vasa ad cultum adhibita. Ionathan פו שומרי interpretatur אמרכלין qui fuerunt summi Thesaurarii, & qui qui alios adhuc sub se habent &c:
units.tr: §. Kimchi, on 2 Kings 12:10, comments thus on what the Amarcalin are: "guardians of the utensils" or "of the vessels of the temple." The word pu is a general term and denotes indiscriminately all the vessels used in worship. Jonathan renders "guardians" as Amarcalin, "who were the chief treasurers, and who still have others under them," and so on.

units.la: § Etymologia אמרכל cst quasi כל על מר Dominus super omnia, nam in Talmud. Hierof. א aliquando abiicitur, aliquando verò, vel cum Chirek, sæpius cum patach effertur.
units.tr: § The etymology of Amarcal is, as it were, kol al mar, "Lord over all." In the Talmud of Jerusalem the aleph is sometimes dropped, and sometimes the word is pronounced with chirek, but more often with patach.

units.la: §. Probabile est hos officiarios fuisse perpetuos & ordinarios, ut etiam fuerunt summus Sacerdos, Sagan & Katholikin. (v. f. 1.) Sed aliquis dicere posset in Middot c. 1. legimus claves atrii magni fuisse in potestate בית אב וקני seniorum classis paterna (v. supra.) quomodo itaque nos claves illas attribuamus אמרכלין ? יג. Omnino verum esse seniores custodiæ habuisse claves, non autem primarió sibi commissas, sed ab Immarcalin, quibus nec possibile nec etiam honorificum erat semper reclusioni portarum præesse, pro temporere concreditas.
units.tr: §. It is probable that these officials were permanent and ordinary, as the high priest, the Sagan and the Katholikin were. (See note f. 1.) But someone might say that Middot ch. 1 tells us that the keys of the great court were in the power of "the house of the father and the elders," that is, the paternal class of elders (see above). How then shall we assign those keys to the Immarcalin? Answer: it is quite true that the elders of the guard had keys, but these were not entrusted to them primarily; they were given to them temporarily by the Immarcalin, for whom it was neither possible nor even honourable to preside at all times over the opening of the gates.

units.la: Amar in Talmudicis varia significat; aliquando simpliciter dixit; aliquando cecinit, cantavit ut Erach. cap. 2. לא היו אומרים בנגל וכינור אלא בפה Non sunt modulati nablio aut cithara sed ore, significat etiam constituit decrevit, ut in Gem. Sanhed. c.2. באותה שעה אמרו מלך לא דן Eo tempore decretum fecerunt, Rex (personas Synedrii) nec iudicare nec ab ipsis iudicari debere. Quod à studiosis observandum, ut eò facilius se ex pluribus locis extricent.
units.tr: Amar has various meanings in the Talmudic writings. Sometimes it simply means "said." Sometimes it means "sang, chanted," as in Erachin ch. 2: "They did not sing to the nebel or the kinnor, but with the mouth." It also means "established, decreed," as in Gemara Sanhedrin ch. 2: "At that time they decreed that the king (that is, the members of the Sanhedrin) should neither judge nor be judged by them." Students should note this, so that they may more easily extricate themselves from many passages.

units.la: <bl>Amuleta</bl>, carmina, infusurrationes fuerunt apud Iudæos maximè in usu, & quasi in deliciis. Exempla sunt innumera. Licuit ipsis quævis amuleta gestare diebus profestis, sed
units.tr: Amulets, charms and incantations were especially in use among the Jews, and were almost their delight. Examples are countless. They were allowed to carry any amulets on weekdays, but

units.la: in Sabbatho nullum licitum fuit nisi probatum fuerit, hinc est ille Canon Schab. c.6 2. Ne prodeat quis Sabbatho amuletum gestans שאינו מן non præscriptum fuerit à Medico probato; Amuleta talia vel fuerunt כתב של קמיע amuletum constans in aliqua schedula scripta, vel עקרין של קמיע amuleta ex radicibus confecta.
units.tr: on the Sabbath none was lawful unless it had been approved. Hence that canon in Shabbat ch. 6: "Let no one go out on the Sabbath carrying an amulet that has not been prescribed by an approved physician." Such amulets were either a "writing of an amulet," consisting of some written slip, or "roots of an amulet," amulets made from roots.

units.la: §. Omnibus diebus licuit recitare carmen super vulnus, recitare versiculum super alicuius filium, aut imponere super eum librum legis aut phylacteria ut dormiat, excepto Sabbatho, in quo hæc omnia prohibita erant. Hierof. Schabbat sol. 8. 2. vid. ibid. col. 3. ubi agitur de plurimis rebus quas gestare solebant pro remediis contra quosdam dolores, item de variis muflitationibus super vulnera.
units.tr: §. On every day it was lawful to recite a charm over a wound, to recite a verse over someone's son, or to lay upon him a book of the law or phylacteries so that he might sleep. Only on the Sabbath were all these things forbidden. Jerusalem Shabbat, fol. 8.2; see ibid. col. 3, where many things are discussed which they were accustomed to carry as remedies against certain pains, and likewise various rubbings over wounds.

units.la: §. Bab. Ioma sol. 84. Formam incantationis habes contra canem rabidum. Quomodo Dæmones ad cæcitatem incantandi sunt vid. Bab. Avoda Sarah sol. 12. 2. Hierof. Schabb. sol. 13. 4. & Avoda Sarah sol. 40. 4. legimus de Muflitationibus & incantationibus etiam in nomine Icfu. Quomodo autem præstigiis & miris magnis dediti fuerint Iudæi vid. Magica artes.
units.tr: §. Bab. Yoma, fol. 84: you have a form of incantation against a rabid dog. For how demons are to be charmed into blindness, see Bab. Avoda Zara, fol. 12.2; Jerusalem Shabbat, fol. 13.4; and Avoda Zara, fol. 40.4, where we read of rubbings and incantations, even in the name of Jesus. For how far the Jews were given over to sorceries and marvellous wonders, see Magic arts.

units.la: ANIMAL admirabile habuerunt in Palæstina, quod vivebat in agris sub terra, formâ & specie humanâ, voce etiam & sermone utebatur, sed qui intelligi non poterat. Agnoscitur autem ex herba quadam crassa & magna, cuius radix umbilico eius implicata est; Sine periculo præsentis mortis nemo ad ipsum accedere audus est; Venatores ergo istam herbam telis tantandiu petunt, donec ab umbilico eius divellatur, quo facto statim moritur: vocatur illud animal שרה אדני אש in Claim c.8. Simile quid fabulantur de Alrauna in his regionibus, quam dicunt opulentos reddere suos dominos. Quid in rei veritate sit compertum non habeo.
units.tr: The Jews had a remarkable ANIMAL in Palestine, which lived under the ground in the fields, of human form and appearance. It also used voice and speech, but such as could not be understood. It is recognised by a certain thick and large herb whose root is entwined about its navel. No one dares to approach it without danger of immediate death. Hunters therefore attack that herb with weapons for as long as it takes until it is torn from the animal's navel, whereupon it dies at once. That animal is called by the Hebrew phrase (transliterated sherah adonai esh) in Claim ch. 8. Something similar is told of the Alrauna in these regions, which they say makes its masters rich. What is actually true of the matter I do not know.

units.la: Anni dies primus pro ipso anno reputatur, (ita ut qui inchoaverit 12. annum habeatur, quasi iam duodecim annos natus esset.) Rosch Hashana f. 2. 2. Qui canon observandus in computationibus Chronologicis, praecipuè quando in aetatem Christi inquiritur, ut diversas de hac re sententias conciliare posumus.
units.tr: Years: the first day is reckoned as the year itself, so that one who has begun the twelfth year is regarded as if he were already twelve years old. Rosh Hashanah, fol. 2.2. This rule is to be observed in chronological computations, especially when the age of Christ is inquired into, so that we can reconcile the various opinions on this matter.

units.la: Anni quarti fructus praecipuè in vineis pingunt: Maasfer Scheni c.5.1. אותו רביעי בציין כרם בקומ אורלה בתרוסית ער שר Vineam quadriennem notant gleba aliquà terra colorata vero praeputiatam argilla. Sepulchra vero notantur calce. Glossa rem sic explicat: Vinea quadrienni appingunt notas aliquas è gleba terrae, ut noscant homines quod est vinea quadriennis, & de eà non comedant, quoniam ea sacrata est, ut dicit Dominus Levit. xix. 24. & oportet possessores eius fructum eius comedere Hierosolymis, ut decimam secundam. Vineam verò quae nondum Quadriennis est & quam praeputiatam nominant notarunt argillâ igne decoctâ, ne forte nota periret, & homines de ea comederent. Prohibitio enim de praeputiata maior est quam de vinea quadrienni, quapropter etiam quadriennis esui fuit idonea, praeputiata
units.tr: Years: the fruit of the fourth year is marked especially on vines. Maaser Sheni ch. 5.1: "They mark a vine of four years with some lump of coloured earth, but an uncircumcised vine with clay." Tombs are marked with lime. The gloss explains the matter thus: they mark a four-year vine with certain marks made from a clod of earth, so that people may know what a four-year vine is and not eat of it, since it is consecrated, as the Lord says in Lev. 19:24, and its owners must eat its fruit at Jerusalem, like the second tithe. But a vine that is not yet four years old, which they call uncircumcised, they marked with fired clay, lest the mark perhaps perish and people eat from it. For the prohibition concerning the uncircumcised is greater than that concerning the four-year vine; for this reason the four-year vine was fit to eat, but the uncircumcised

units.la: non item. Exhis lumen fæneratur locus Marci xii.2. Misit Dominus Vineæ ad Agricolas τῷ καιρῷ suo tempore &c. Certè illud tempus esse non potuit nisi anno quarto à prima eius plantatione, quoniam ante istum aunum apud Iudæos nullus erat fructuum usus. De redemptione fructus vineæ anni quarti vid. Sanhed. 1. 3.
units.tr: was not likewise. From this the passage Mark 12:2 gains light: "He sent to the husbandmen a servant at the time (τῷ καιρῷ), in its season," and so on. Surely that time could only have been the fourth year from its first planting, since before that year there was no use of its fruits among the Jews. On the redemption of the fruit of a fourth-year vine, see Sanhedrin 1.3.

units.la: Anni septimi fructus quandiu licet edere? Olivas edunt donec deficiat ultima in Tekoah; R. Eliefer dicit donec deficiat ultima in Gusch. Chalab. Ficus aridas comedunt donec deficiunt grossi in Bethene Bab. Pesachim f. 53. 1. Erubhin f. 28.2. ut hæc intelligas vid. ביעור. Videntur illa loca in rebus notatis admodum fertilia fuisse.
units.tr: How long may the fruits of the seventh year be eaten? They eat olives until the last one fails at Tekoah; R. Eliezer says until the last one fails at Gush Chalab. They eat dried figs until the large ones fail at Bethene, Bab. Pesachim fol. 53.1; Eruvin fol. 28.2. To understand these, see biur. Those places seem to have been very fertile in the things noted.

units.la: §. Tres regiones, Iudæa, Galilæa, & Peræa tenentur ad legem de anno septimo: Quodcunque possederunt ascendentes è Babylone, à terra Israelitica usque ad כוש Casib (locum quem ultimo subiugarunt,) non depascitur nec colitur: at quodcunque possederunt ascendentes ex Ægypto à Casib ad fluvium (Nilum) & ad Amanam depascitur sed non colitur, à Nilo & ab Amanah interius depascitur. Scheviit c. 6. 1.
units.tr: §. Three regions, Judea, Galilee and Peraea, are bound by the law of the seventh year. Whatever they possessed when coming up from Babylon, from the land of Israel as far as Casib (the place last subdued), is neither grazed nor cultivated. But whatever they possessed when coming up from Egypt, from Casib to the river (the Nile) and to Amana, is grazed but not cultivated; from the Nile and from Amanah inward it is grazed. Sheviit ch. 6.1.

units.la: §. In anno septimo in Ammonitica regione ut & Moabitica feritur & spicilegium relinquitur. Ievamot sol. 16.1. Illuc pauperes Israelitarum se in anno septimo ad necessitates suas sublevandas conferre poterant.
units.tr: §. In the seventh year, in the land of the Ammonites as well as Moab, the ground is sown and a gleaning is left. Yevamot, fol. 16.1. There the poor of the Israelites could betake themselves in the seventh year to relieve their needs.

units.la: §. De Anno septimo vid. Iubilæum.
units.tr: §. On the seventh year, see Jubilee.

units.la: De Anno sic loquitur in cap. 2. משנה Maymo- nides
units.tr: Concerning the Year, thus he speaks in chapter 2 of the Mishneh, Maimonides.

units.la: nides. Anni de quibus mentio fit in materia de pubertate filii & filiæ, item in aliis locis Sacræ Scripturæ אין לא שני הלבנ neque sunt anni Lunares, neque שני החמה Anni Solares: אלא שנים של סדר העבור שהן פשוטות ומעוברות על גי בית רין: Sed anni ex ordine intercalationis dispositi, sicuti Synedrium illos extendere & intercalare in usu habet. Hanc observationem applicare poteris disputationi de Annis Patriarcharum; cùm enim intercalationes fierent ob festa præcipuè, & à Synedrio, aut Lunares solùm aut ad summum annos solares habuerunt.
units.tr: Maimonides. The years mentioned in the matter of the puberty of a son or daughter, and also in other places of Holy Scripture, are neither lunar years [לא שני הלבנה] nor solar years [שני החמה], but years arranged by the order of intercalation, whether common or intercalated, as the Sanhedrin has the practice of extending and intercalating them [שנים של סדר העבור שהן פשוטות ומעוברות על פי בית דין]. You may apply this observation to the discussion of the Years of the Patriarchs; for since intercalations were made chiefly for the festivals, and by the Sanhedrin, they had either lunar years only or, at most, solar years.

units.la: De Anno vid. Menses in sin. lit. M.
units.tr: On the Year, see Months, under the letter M.

units.la: Vox ימים absolutè posita denotat annum. Sic Cainus dicitur de fructu terræ oblationem attulisse מקץ הימים in fine dierum, quod idem est ac בצאת השנה in fine anni, quo tempore Israelitæ etiam offerebant ex frugibus Exod.23. 16. Alia exempla sunt huius locutionis Genes. XXIV. 55. Maneat puella nobiscum ימים או עשור Dies aut decem; quod significat secundum Vzielidem, יומי שתא חדא או עשר ירחי per dies anni unius, aut per decem menses. Levit.xxv.29. Cùm quis vendiderit domum &c. ימים תהיה גאלתו Per dies erit redemptio eius, id est, ut explicatur hoc ipso versu. שנה תמימה per annum integrum. 1.Samuel.1.2. Ascendebat vir ille מימים ימימה ut adoraret in Silob, id est שנה כשנה Annuatim; 1.Samuel.xxvii.7. Fuit Numerus dierum quibus habitavit David in agro Philistæorum ימים ארבעה חדשי Dies [annus unus] & menses quatuor.
units.tr: The word ימים [yamim], used absolutely, denotes a year. So Cain is said to have brought an offering from the fruit of the earth מקץ הימים [at the end of days], which is the same as בצאת השנה [at the going out of the year], the time when the Israelites also offered from their produce (Exod. 23:16). Other examples of this expression are Gen. 24:55, "Let the maiden remain with us ימים או עשור [days or ten]," which means, according to Uziel, יומי שתא חדא או עשר ירחי [the days of one year or ten months]. Lev. 25:29: "When a man shall sell a house, etc., ימים תהיה גאלתו [within days shall be its redemption]," that is, as this same verse explains, שנה תמימה [a full year]. 1 Sam. 1:2: "That man went up מימים ימימה [from year to year] to worship in Shiloh," that is, שנה כשנה [year by year, annually]. 1 Sam. 27:7: the number of days David lived in the country of the Philistines was ימים ארבעה חדשי [a day, a year and four months]; that is, [one year] and four months.

units.la: DE ANGVLO agri vid. supra ap. Agriculturam &c.
units.tr: On the Angle of the field, see above under Agriculture, etc.

units.la: Angaria, Graece ἀγγαρεία non tam officii impulsum quàm violentiæ coactionem denotat. Bab. Ioma sol.35. 2. occurrunt R. Eleasaro Ben Harsum servi eius וע ואשר & ipsum angariant. Dixit iis, obsecro vos, dimittite me, ut abeam & discam legem &c. Glossa ענורת שר העיר אנגריא Angaria est servitus Politarchæ; ad quem servi subditos adigebant.
units.tr: Angaria, in Greek ἀγγαρεία, denotes not so much the impulse of duty as the coercion of violence. In Bab. Joma fol. 35.2, Rabbi Eleazar ben Harsum's servants are met with, who angariate him [ואשר ... ואנגריאו]. He said to them, "I beg you, let me go that I may depart and learn the Law," etc. The Gloss says: "Angaria is the servitude of the governor of the city," to whom servants compelled subjects to serve.

units.la: §. In Bab. Nedarim sol.32. 1. Dicit R. Eliezer. Quare punitus est Abrahamus pater noster, & afflicti sunt filii eius in Ægypto ducentis & decem annis? מפני שעשה אנגריא בתלמידי ? חכמים Quia angariavit discipulos sapientum, sicut dicitur Gen.xiv. 14. & Armavit Catechumenos suos.
units.tr: §. In Bab. Nedarim fol. 32.1, Rabbi Eliezer says: "Why was our father Abraham punished, and why were his sons afflicted in Egypt for two hundred and ten years?" Because [מפני שעשה אנגריא לתלמידי חכמים] he angariated the disciples of the sages, as it is said in Gen. 14:14, "and he armed his trained men [Armavit catechumenos suos]."

units.la: §. In Sotah sol. 10.1. Quæritur quare Asa punitus fuerit podagrâ? Respondetur, quia angariavit discipulos sapientum in generali illa congregatione de qua leg. 1, Reg.xv.22.
units.tr: §. In Sotah fol. 10.1, the question is asked why Asa was punished with gout. The answer: because he angariated the disciples of the sages in that general assembly of which 1 Kings 15:22 speaks.

units.la: §. Baya Metzia c. 6.1. mentio fit angariationis circa iumentum. חמור שנעשית אנגריא Asinus si angariatus fuerit &c. quo in loco Glossa etiam explicat si angariatus fuerit, per, Si eum arripiunt ad opus aliquod Regis. Ex quibus apparet, Christum Matth.v.41 nos hortari ad patientiam, sub iniuria, coaction, aut violentia, cui patrocinatur authoritas regalis, aut superiorum.
units.tr: §. In Baba Metzia ch. 6.1, mention is made of angaria in connection with a beast of burden: [חמור שנעשית אנגריא] "If a donkey is angariated," etc. In this passage the Gloss also explains "if angariated" as "if they seize it for some work of the King." From these things it appears that Christ, in Matt. 5:41, urges us to patience under injury, compulsion, or violence, which is backed by the authority of the king or of superiors.

units.la: §. Vocis אנגריא etiam mentio fit Hierof. Beracot p.1. col.4. sub sin.
units.tr: §. The word אנגריא is also mentioned in Hierosolymitan Berachot p. 1, col. 4, near the end.

units.la: אנשי מעמד Anfche madmad vid. Stationarii Viri.
units.tr: Anshe maamad [אנשי מעמד]: see Stationary Men.

units.la: D
units.tr: D

units.la: De Anathemate vid. Excommunicationem.
units.tr: On Anathema, see Excommunication.

units.la: ANIMA Deo fideiubet pro omnibus membris, ac proinde ex rectitudine eorum iudicatur. Sanhed. 91. 1. Buxt. Cosri 72. Anima hominis debet laudare Deum ad unamquamque respirationem, secundum illud Psal.150.6. Berefchit Rabbah f. 14.
units.tr: The soul stands as surety to God for all the members, and therefore is judged by their uprightness. Sanhedrin 91.1; Buxtorf, Cosri 72. The soul of man ought to praise God with every breath, according to Psalm 150:6. Bereshit Rabbah f. 14.

units.la: §. De anima pluribus disserit Cosri.
units.tr: §. Cosri discourses at more length on the soul.

units.la: ANTIGONUS Sochæus fuit Simeonis Iusti discipulus, sive traditionum & doctrinæ eius hæres. Etiamsi autem Antigonus præceptoris traditiones religiosissimè observarit, accidit tamen malo quodam fato, ut propter ipsius verba quæ inter docendum dixerat סרוו fecerint Zadok & Baithos, discipuli eius mali. Iuchasin p. 52. Verba eius fuerunt referente R. Nathan in Abhot cap. 5. אל תהיו כעבדים המשמשים את הרב על מנת לקבל פרוס Ne sitis sicuti servi, qui serviunt Domino (praemii causa,) sed sitis sicut servi, qui Domino famulantur absque consideratione praemii timorem Dei habentes. In quæ verba (notante Maym. in Avot cap.1.) Talem fecerunt glossam discipuli. Magister noster nos docet, non esse vel praemium vel poenam, nec ullam omnino expectationem. Post talem mentis depravationem deinde in schisma ruerunt se mutuo in perniciosa sententia confirmantes, atque utrique adhæsit aliqua turba, qui deinde Sadducæi & Baithosæi vocati sunt. (v. f.1.)
units.tr: Antigonus of Sokho was a disciple of Simeon the Just, or the heir of his traditions and teaching. Although Antigonus observed his teacher's traditions most scrupulously, it happened by some evil fate that, because of words he had spoken while teaching, his wicked disciples Zadok and Boethus turned aside [סרוו] and made a schism. Iuchasin p. 52. His words, as Rabbi Nathan reports in Avot ch. 5, were: "Do not be like servants who serve the master for the sake of reward [על מנת לקבל פרס]; but be like servants who serve the Lord without regard to reward, having the fear of God." On these words (as Maimonides notes on Avot ch. 1) his disciples made this gloss: "Our master teaches us that there is neither reward nor punishment, nor any expectation at all." After such a depravity of mind they fell into schism, confirming one another in a pernicious opinion; and some crowd clung to each of them, who were afterwards called Sadducees and Boethusians. (See f. 1.)

units.la: De Antemurali templi v. פיח in C. &c.
units.tr: On the Antemurale of the Temple, see [פיח] under C., etc.

units.la: בעל אוב Baal Ob, Vid. Pythomantia.
units.tr: Baal Ob: see Pythomancy.

units.la: אונו Ono, Vrbs distabat tribus milliaribus à Lydda. Dixit R. Iacob à Lydda & Onofunt tria milliaria &c. R. Simai & R. Zadok profeßi sunt interea : Latum annum in Lydda, & Sabbatizarunt in זמן &c. luchafin sol. 39. 2. Bab. Chetubhot f. 3. 2. Cholin sol. 56. 2. Megillah Hier. f. sol. 70. 1. R.
