But when does this hold? Namely, when the other things are equal. But if a bastard is a disciple of a wise man, and the high priest is unlearned, the bastard is to be preferred to him. The wise man is to be preferred to the king, for if the wise man dies, there is no one equal to him; but if the king dies, any Israelite may become king.

units.la: Horas cognoscendi modum apud gentes sui ævi describit Aruch in שעה צורו. Sapientes gentilium conficiunt coram Regibus imagines, quibus dant in manus 24. lapides; iisque supponunt pelvim magnam æream; finità horâ quâlibet, projicit imago lapidem unum in pelvim istam; cuius sonus per totam civitatem exauditur, & indè cognoscunt horas. De hoc שעה צורו Vid. Kelim 26. 4.
units.tr: Aruch, under שעה צורו [sha'ah tsuro], describes the way the gentiles of his age knew the hours. The wise men of the gentiles make images before kings, and give them 24 stones in their hands, and place beneath them a large bronze basin. At the end of each hour the image casts one stone into the basin, and its sound is heard through the whole city, and so they know the hours. On this, see Kelim 26.4.

units.la: Hospitibus peregrinantibus tria debentur ossicia, quæ Abraham instituisse dicitur, אכילה Cibus, שתיה potus, לויה Comitatus. Sotah 46.2.
units.tr: Three duties are owed to travelling guests, which Abraham is said to have instituted: אכילה [akhilah], food; שתיה [shetiyah], drink; לויה [levayah], escort (Sotah 46.2).

units.la: §. Qui Hospites peregrinantes sæpius excipiunt, suis conclavibus communiter hæc inscripta habent: יום ראשון אורח Primo die hospes, יום שני שורח D.e secundo molestia, יום שלישי Die tertio superfluus, יום רביעי הוא בורח Quarto debet esse fugitivus. Quinto die חמשי עלה קרח Abi calvaster, יום ששי מר צרח Sexto die hospes amare clamat. Vid. in hunc sensum quæ sunt in Midrasch Tehillim Psal.23.
units.tr: §. Those who often receive travelling guests commonly have these inscribed in their rooms: "On the first day, a guest (אורח); on the second, a nuisance (שורח); on the third, superfluous; on the fourth he must be a fugitive (בורח). On the fifth day: 'Go away, baldy' (קרח); on the sixth day the guest cries out, 'Bitter!'" (מר צרח). On the same sense, see what is in Midrash Tehillim on Ps. 23.

units.la: §. Quamvis aliquis hospes viator aliquid apud se habeat quod comedat, tamen debet à tabernario sive hospite suo aliquid emere, ut fructus aliquis inferatur hospitio. R.Salomoh Num. 20.17. Quivis debet hospiti suo urceum testaceum suum relinquere. Ioma sol.12.1. Vid. Hierosolyma.
units.tr: §. Although a traveller who is a guest may have food of his own to eat, he should still buy something from the innkeeper or his host, so that some profit comes to the inn. R. Solomon, Num. 20.17. Anyone should leave his earthen pitcher behind for his host. Yoma 12.1. See Jerusalem.

units.la: Hyperbole libenter utuntur Iudæi, ut in pluribus exemplis observavimus. v. g. Quando dicunt ערים גדולות ובצורות בשמים Vrbes magnæ & munitæ ad cœlum usque. Simile est quod in Bab. Ioma sol. 35. 2. legitur, Fuerunt Eleafari Ben Harsum mille urbes in arida & mille naves in mari. Id est, fuit Eleafar Paleftinæ potentissimus magnas. Eiusdem farinæ sermo est in Middot c. 3. Trecenti Sacerdotes occupabantur ad viam porticus removendam. Et Tamid.c.33. Hierichunte audire poterant strepitum porta templi,cum recludebatur, item sonum tinnnabuli &c. Quæ cùm plurimi legunt, statim exclamant, fabulæ! non animadvertentes שנה five לין הבאי hyperbolen inesse: Et nos Europæos etiam talibus hyperbolismis uti, cùm rei magnam vim aut excellentiam denotare volumus. Iudæi in suis introductionibus Talmudicis præcipuè in Halicot Olam nos admonent, se hyperbolicè loqui, & nos ipsos vel fabulosos vel mendaces esse volumus.
units.tr: The Jews willingly use hyperbole, as we have observed in many examples. For instance, when they say "cities great and fortified up to heaven" (Vrbes magnæ & munitæ ad cœlum usque). Similar is what is read in Bab. Yoma 35.2: Eleafar ben Harsum had a thousand cities on dry land and a thousand ships at sea. That is, Eleazar was the most powerful of the great men of Palestine. Of the same kind is the saying in Middot c. 3: Three hundred priests were busy clearing the road by the portico. And in Tamid c. 33: From Jericho one could hear the noise of the temple gate when it was opened, likewise the sound of the bell, etc. When many read these things, they at once cry out "fables!", not noticing that hyperbole (hyperbolen, [לשון הבאי]) is present. We Europeans too use such hyperbole when we wish to denote great power or excellence in a thing. The Jews, in their Talmudic introductions, especially in Halicot Olam, warn us that they speak hyperbolically, and they do not want us to take them for either fabulists or liars.

units.la: HYPOCRITÆ à Iudæis vocantur צבועים Tinctí vel Colorati, Bab. Sotah sol.22.2. Rex Iannai monuit ut caveat sibi בן הצבועים ab hominibus pietis, Pharisæos similantibus, quorum opera sunt sicut opera Zimri, at tamen exspectant mercedem Pinchasi. Gloss. Homines pietis ij sunt quorum forma externa non respondet naturæ ipsorum, quorumq; opera mala sunt ut opera Zimri, & tamen ab hominibus honorem Pinchasi efflagitant. De Hypocritis sanum exstat axioma in Bab. Ioma f.72.2. Discipulus Sapientum שאין תוכו כברו Qui idem non est ad intra quod est ad extra, non est discipulus sapiens.
units.tr: HYPOCRITES are called by the Jews tzevu'im ["dyed"], that is, Tinctí or Colorati, Bab. Sotah 22.2. King Jannai warned to beware of the son of the dyed ones, that is, of men who pretend to be pious, imitating the Pharisees, whose works are like the works of Zimri, yet who still expect the reward of Phinehas. The gloss says: Those are pious men whose outward form does not correspond to their nature, whose works are evil like the works of Zimri, and who nevertheless demand from men the honour due to Phinehas. There is a sound saying about hypocrites in Bab. Yoma 72.2: A disciple of the wise whose inside is not like his outside [שאין תוכו כברו] is not a wise disciple.

units.la: HYSSOPUS υσσωπος; ipsi respondet in Hebræo אזוב; Cuius fuerunt variæ species. אזוב ין. Hyssopus Græca, אזוב כוחי Hyssopus fucata
units.tr: HYSSOP (hyssopus, from Greek hyssopos); the Hebrew equivalent is ezov. There were various species of it: Greek hyssop [אזוב יון], Hyssopus Græca; dyed hyssop, Hyssopus fucata.

units.la: forsan coloris stibii אזוב רומי Hyssopus Romana, מרבי אזוב Hyssopus agrestis. Parah c.II.7. De Hyssopo hunc Canonem habemus loc. m. c. : כל אזוב שיש לו שם לוי פסול־ Quacunque hyssopus habet Epitheton non est idonea ad aspersionem immundi.
units.tr: Perhaps of the colour of antimony: Roman hyssop, Hyssopus Romana; wild hyssop, Hyssopus agrestis. Parah c. II.7. We have this rule about hyssop in the same passage: Whatever hyssop has an epithet is not fit for sprinkling the unclean.

units.la: §. Legimus in historia Evangelica spongiam aceto plenam, quà Christi sitim aditantes extinguere voluerunt, impositam fuisse Hyssopo, quæ Matth. & Marco tuit Calamus: quæri potest, an talis Hyssopus in Palæstina fuerit, quæ in Calamos creverit? R. talem aliquam Hyssopi speciem fuisse elici potest ex Succah sol. 13. 1. ibi enim inter mentionem Cannarum Calamorum, quibus sua tuguriola obtegere debebant in festo Tabernaculorum, etiam memoratur אזוב hyssopus, quæ certè in hunc finem ipsis parum profuisset, nisi cannarum in modum extensos Culmos habuisset. His adde Magistros expresse distinguere in Parah c.II.8. inter illum qui hyssopum colligit לאוכלין pro cibo, & illum לעצים שלקטו qui ipsam colligit pro ligno: Quæ præsupponunt aliquam saltem hyssopi speciem satis crassos culmos habuisse.
units.tr: §. We read in the Gospel history that a sponge full of vinegar, which those who approached Christ wished to use to quench his thirst, was put on a hyssopus, which in Matthew and Mark is a reed (calamus). It may be asked whether such a hyssop grew in Palestine, one which grew into reeds. I answer that some such species of hyssop can be inferred from Succah 13.1. There, among the mention of canes and reeds with which they had to cover their booths at the Feast of Tabernacles, ezov (hyssop) is also mentioned. This would certainly have been of little use for that purpose unless it had stalks extended like canes. To this add that the Masters expressly distinguish in Parah c. II.8 between the man who gathers hyssop [לאוכלין] for food, and the man who gathers it [לעצים שלקטו] for wood. These presuppose that at least some species of hyssop had fairly thick stalks.

units.la: §. Hyssopi fasciculus fiebat ex tribus stipitibus sive caulibus, quorum quisque habebat alios ramusculos, minimum tres. Parah cap. II. Hyssopus brevior ligabatur filo ad bacillum. Parah cap. 12. Non comedunt Hyssopum in Sabbatho, quia non est cibus hominum sanorum, id est cibus communis, sed Medicinalis. Schabbat folio 109. 2. in Mișna de
units.tr: §. A bunch of hyssop was made of three stalks, each of which had other little branches, at least three. Parah ch. II. A shorter hyssop was tied with thread to a stick. Parah ch. 12. They do not eat hyssop on the Sabbath, because it is not food of healthy people, that is, ordinary food, but medicinal. Shabbat folio 109.2, in the Mishnah, concerning

units.la: Hyffopi fpeciebus vide Cholin fol. 62. 2. Negaim cap. ult.
units.tr: For the species of hyssop see Chullin fol. 62.2 and Negaim, last chapter.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: ABHNE יבנה locus cuius mentio fit ii. Paral. xxvi. 6. & qui celeberrimus eft ob fedem Synedrii, quæ ante & poft vaftatas Hierofolymas ibi fuit. Præfedit illic primus Rabban Gamaliel, (de quo V. f.1.) & octodecim annis ante excidium urbis excepit cum filius eius Rabban Simeon. Excifis Hierofolymis præfedit ibi Iochanan Ben Saccai, (de quo v.f.1.)& poft eum R. Gamaliel Secundus. Poft hunc vero R. Akiba. Vid Iuchafin fol. 21. & fol. 57.1.& 53. Avot. R. Nathan c. 4. Rofch Hafchana c. 1. 7.
units.tr: Jabneh (Ἰαβνή), a place mentioned in 2 Chronicles 26:6, and the most famous for the seat of the Sanhedrin, which was there both before and after the devastation of Jerusalem. Rabban Gamaliel presided there first (on whom see V. f.1.). Eighteen years before the destruction of the city, he took over the office together with his son Rabban Simeon. After Jerusalem was overthrown, Johanan ben Zakkai presided there (on whom see v.f.1.), and after him Rabban Gamaliel the Second, and after him Rabbi Akiba. See Yuchasin fol. 21 and fol. 57.1, 53; Avot of Rabbi Nathan c. 4; Rosh Hashanah c. 1, 7.

units.la: §. Claruit hic locus præ omnibus Academiæ fedibus, exceptâ Tiberiade, ita ut illinc ortum Adagium כרם ביבנה Vinea Iafnenfis. Extiterunt Iabhne trecentæ ltudioforum claffes. Hierof. Taanit fol. 67. 4. Diftabat Iafne Azoto duabus Parfis (i. e. viii. m. paffuum.) Vocataque eft tandem איבלין Ievelin. Beniam. in itin. Cur Iabhne vocata fuerit vinea rationem reddit R. Salomoh in Iebhamot cap. 8. שהיו יושבין שורות שורות Quoniam Studiofi illic confederunt feriatim, inftar vinea quæ plantatur שורות שורות lineatim. (Marcus diceret φραγμα φραγμα.) de Iacobi Patriarchæ fepultura multa loquuntur Gemariftæ ad c. 2. Sotah ad ea verba, Iofeph meruit patrem fuum fepelire &c. R. Abhu inter alia ibi recenfet, Iofephum fuam coronam fufpendiffe feretro poftquàm ad locum אטר אשר perventum erat; Ifmaelitas etiam & filios Efau pariter aliquas coronas apposuisse, ita ut triginta sex coronæ numeratæ fuerint.
units.tr: This place was the most famous of all the seats of the academy, except Tiberias, so that the proverb "a vineyard of Jabneh" arose from it. Jabneh had three hundred classes of students (Jerusalem Taanit fol. 67.4). Jabneh lay two parasangs (that is, eight Roman miles) from Azotus. It was finally called Yavneel (Ievelin) (Benjamin, in his Itinerary). The reason why Jabneh was called a vineyard is given by R. Solomon in Yevamot c. 8: because the students sat down in rows, row after row, like a vineyard that is planted in lines (Mark would say "phragma phragma" [φραγμα φραγμα]). The Gemarists say much about the burial of the Patriarch Jacob, in their commentary on Sotah c. 2, on the words "Joseph was privileged to bury his father," etc. There R. Abhu recounts, among other things, that Joseph hung his crown on the bier after they had reached the place Atad; that the Ishmaelites and the sons of Esau likewise laid down some crowns, so that thirty-six crowns were counted.

units.la: Idololatria. Idololatra reus fit lapidationis, five עובר idolo cultum suum exhibuerit, five sacrificium obtulerit, five suffitum fecerit, five libaverit, five adoraverit, five illud sibi Deum fecerit, atque ipsum his verbis salutaverit אלי אתה Tu es Deus meus. At qui amplexatur, osculatur, converrit, collocat, lavat, ungit, vestit, violat interdictum (עובר בלא תעש.) Qui votum concipit in nomine eius, & qui id exsolvit in nomine eius violat interdictum. Qui se nudat coram בעל פעור Baal Peor is ordinarium illi cultum defert. Eadem ratio est si quis projicit אבן למרקוליס Lapidem Mercoli, nam is est cultus eius. Sanhed. c.7. §.6. Quomodo explicent dictum Exod.20.23. Non facietis Deos alienos &c. Vid.L.T.Buxt.p.187.
units.tr: Idolatry. An idolater is liable to stoning, whether he has worshipped his idol in its own manner, or offered sacrifice, or burned incense, or poured a libation, or adored it, or made it his god and greeted it with the words, "You are my God" [אלי אתה]. But one who embraces it, kisses it, sweeps it, sets it in place, washes it, anoints it, or clothes it, violates a prohibition (a negative precept). One who makes a vow in its name, and one who fulfils that vow in its name, violates a prohibition. One who uncovers himself before Baal Peor pays it the customary worship. The same rule applies if someone throws a stone to Mercolis (Mercury), for that is its worship (Sanhedrin c. 7, §6). On how they explain the saying in Exodus 20:23, "You shall not make gods of others," etc., see L. T. Buxtorf, p. 187.

units.la: §. Idololatriæ initium fuit tempore Enosi; vid. Stellas col. &c. In Ægypto Israelitæ ad idololatriam deflexerunt, excepta tribu Levi. Fundamentum Mandati de idololatria est, ne quis serviat ulli rerum creatarum; non Angelo, non sphæræ, non stellæ, non uni ex quatuor elementis. Multos libros composuerunt idololatræ de cultu suo, sed in illis secundum præceptum Dei legere non debemus, quia omnia ea quæ hominem ad idololatriam impellunt prohibita sunt.
units.tr: The beginning of idolatry was in the time of Enosh; see "Stellas," col., etc. In Egypt the Israelites turned aside to idolatry, except the tribe of Levi. The foundation of the commandment about idolatry is that no one should serve any of the created things: not an angel, not a sphere, not a star, not any one of the four elements. Idolaters have composed many books about their worship, but we must not read them according to the command of God, because all those things which drive a man to idolatry are forbidden.

units.la: §. Præceptum de idololatria tanti ponderis est, ac reliqua omnia mandata: hinc qui idololatriam suscipit negat totam legem omnefque Prophetas. Israelita qui idololatra est, aut Epicureus nequaquam pro Israelita habendus est. Vt quis idololatriæ reus fiat, sufficit confiteri idolorum cultum verum esse, etiamsi ipse idolis non serviat.
units.tr: The precept about idolatry is of as great weight as all the other commandments. Hence whoever takes up idolatry denies the whole Law and all the Prophets. An Israelite who is an idolater, or an Epicurean, must by no means be regarded as an Israelite. For a man to become liable for idolatry, it is enough that he confess the worship of idols to be true, even if he does not himself serve idols.

units.la: §. Idololatra lapidatur & suspenditur, si sciens volensque idola coluerit, aliàs si errore id fecerit, sacrificium expiationis determinatum offert. Senatus,omnes idololatrici cultus modos, scire debuit, ne lapidibus aliquem obruant idololatriæ causâ, antequàm iis constiterit hunc esse eius cultum. Simul ac aliquis diversi quid à vero numine dixerit Deum suum esse, etsi laterculus esset, capitis reus fit. Si quis habeat spinam infixam pedi suo, aut videat dispersos nummos ante idolum, ne se incurvet ad eam evellendam, aut eos tollendos ne videatur se idolo incurvare. Prohibitum est, imagines facere לוּי ad ornatum, etiamsi non fiant ad cultum, ne per eas seducantur simplices השועים : restringitur autem hoc solùm ad figuras & imagines בולשוח protuberantes, in palatiis aut triclinis, nam imagines משקעות deprejas & coloribus expressas facere licet. Maymon Hal Avoda Zarah. c. 1. & 2. & 3.
units.tr: An idolater is stoned and hanged if he worshipped idols knowingly and willingly; otherwise, if he did it in error, he offers the appointed sacrifice of atonement. The Sanhedrin ought to know all the modes of idolatrous worship, so that they do not stone anyone for idolatry before it has been established that this is his worship. As soon as anyone says that something other than the true God is his God, even if it were a brick, he is liable to capital punishment. If someone has a thorn stuck in his foot, or sees coins scattered before an idol, he must not bend down to pull the thorn out, nor pick up the coins, lest he appear to bow down to the idol. It is forbidden to make images for ornament, even if they are not made for worship, lest the simple be led astray by them. This prohibition, however, is restricted to figures and images standing out in relief, in palaces or dining rooms; for it is permitted to make images carved in intaglio (depressed) and images painted in colours. Maimonides, Hilchot Avodah Zarah, c. 1, 2, 3.

units.la: §. De variis Idolis, qualia sunt Moloch, Afima, Adrämelech, Nergal Nisroch, Succot Benot, Kephan, Thammus, Theraphin, Baal Zephon, Baal Peor (cuius cultus erat, ut se coram ipso detegerent) Cammosch vel Cemos, Astarot, Baalzebub, Dagon, & Gad; Vide Seldenum de Dis Syris, & Leusdenii Philolog. Mixtum.
units.tr: On the various idols, such as Moloch, Asima, Adrammelech, Nergal, Nisroch, Succoth-Benoth, Kephan, Thammuz, Teraphim, Baal-Zephon, Baal-Peor (whose worship consisted in uncovering themselves before him), Chammosch or Chemosh, Ashtaroth, Baalzebub, Dagon, and Gad: see Selden, De Diis Syris, and Leusden's Philologus Mixtus.

units.la: §. Apud Iudæos pro religione & præclaro facto ferè habitum fuit, Idolis atque Idololatriæ convitiari. Hierof. Avoda Zarah sol. 43. 3. Polluit Idololatria, sicut polluit fœmina menstruosa: sicut dicitur, Abjicies (ido um) sicut quid menstruatum, dicesque ei apage. Esai. xxx. 22. R. Lazar dicit, Dices ei, apage; illud quod vocant faciem Dei, vocent faciem canis. Illud quod vocant כוס עין fontem calicis, vocent עין קוץ Fontem tædii. Illud quod vocant גרייה fortunam, vocent גלייא fœtorem. Illud oppidum quod aliquando dictum est Bethel, postea dictum est Beth-Aven. Bab. Sanhed. sol. 93. 2. כל ליצנותא אסירא חוץ מליצנותא דע"ז Omnis irrisio prohibetur, præter irrisionem idololatriæ, Repetitur hoc etiam in Megillah sol. 25. 2. Vbi hoc additur. Licet Iudæo dicere Cuthæo שקליה לע"ז אנחיה כשי"ן ת"י Accipe idolum tuum, & repone sub clunibus.
units.tr: Among the Jews it was almost regarded as piety and a distinguished deed to revile idols and idolatry (Jerusalem Avodah Zarah fol. 43.3). Idolatry defiles just as a menstruous woman defiles, as it is said: "You shall cast it away like something unclean; you shall say to it, Begone!" (Isaiah 30:22). R. Lazar says: you shall say to it "Begone!"; what they call the face of God, let them call the face of a dog; what they call "the fountain of the cup" [כוס עין], let them call "the fountain of thorn" [עין קוץ]; what they call "fortune" [גד], let them call "stench" [גלי]. That town which was once called Bethel was afterwards called Beth-Aven (Bab. Sanhedrin fol. 93.2). "Every kind of mockery is forbidden, except the mockery of idolatry." This is repeated also in Megillah fol. 25.2, where this is added: a Jew may say to a Cuthean, "Take your idol and put it under your buttocks."

units.la: §. Inter nomina probrosa Idolis indita commune fuit זבור stercus Hierof. Beracot sol. 12. 2. אפילו אותם שפשטו ידיהם בזבול יש להם בטחון Etiam illis qui manus suas expanderunt in stercorario (idoleo) est ipse, ut iterum in Ecclesiam reducantur. Et paulò post, qui videt eos מובלין stercorantes (id est sacrificantes) idolo &c.
units.tr: Among the opprobrious names given to idols, "dung" [זבל] was common (Jerusalem Berakhot fol. 12.2): "Even those who have stretched out their hands in the dunghill (that is, the idol-house) have hope, so that they may be brought back again into the Church." And shortly after: whoever sees them "dunging" (that is, sacrificing) to an idol, etc.

units.la: §. Hæc sunt tempora Idololatrarum, (i.e. his temporibus cultum idolis præcipuè præstare gestiunt idololatræ) קלנדא סטורנורא Calenda Saturnalia, קרטיסים χρατησεις cùm primum imperium capesscerent. וגנוסא של מלכי Regum γυνσα ויום הליודי & dies nativitatis. Id est, cùm celebrant memoriam illius diei; quo ad regnum pervenerunt, & quo hanc lucem aspexerunt. Avoda Zarah c.1.v.3.
units.tr: These are the times of idolaters (that is, in these seasons idolaters are especially eager to render worship to their idols): the Calends and the Saturnalia, the kratēseis [κρατησεις], when they first took up rule; the genesis of kings [γενεσις], and the day of birth. That is, when they celebrate the memory of that day on which they came to the kingdom and on which they first saw this light (Avodah Zarah c. 1, v. 3).

units.la: §. Idololatriam fovebant tempore regni Graecorum כלילאי Calilai, qui solebant adferre coronas rosaceas, & eas suspendere ad fores fanorum,& ad ianuas tabernarum,cantare cantica idolis suis,inscribere fronti bovis & fronti Asini, nullam Dominis ipsorum esse partem in Deo Israelis; sed tandem illi ab Hasmonaeis cie-ti fuerunt, die 27. Mensis אייר, qui dies quoque deinde festivè celebratus fuit. Megillah Taanit cap. 2.
units.tr: Under Greek rule the Kalilai fostered idolatry. They used to bring rose garlands and hang them on the doors of temples and at the entrances of shops, sing songs to their idols, and write on the forehead of an ox and of an ass that their masters had no share in the God of Israel. At last they were stirred up by the Hasmoneans on the 27th day of the month Iyyar, which day was afterwards also celebrated as a festival (Megillat Taanit c. 2).

units.la: §. In universam apostasiam alicuius urbis ad idola, nemo animadvertere potuit praetor Senatum lxxi. virorum. Si urbs illa in limitibus sita sit ob apostasiam non plectitur, (nec licet ablato munimento in funibus, hostes commodius terram invadere possint.) Si plures urbes in hoc malum inciderunt, nunquam ternae eodem tempore, sed una, vel ad summum binae plectuntur. Sanhed. c.1.5. De Seductore ad Idololatriam vid. Seduclor.
units.tr: Concerning a general apostasy of any city to idols, no one could take action without the Sanhedrin of seventy-one men. If the city lies on the borders, it is not punished for apostasy; nor is it lawful, the defences having been removed, for enemies to invade the land more conveniently. If several cities have fallen into this evil, never three at the same time, but one, or at most two, are punished (Sanhedrin c. 1, 5). On the seducer to idolatry, see "Seductor."

units.la: IEHOVA: nomen sanctum יהוה nullibi nisi in Sanctuario, pronuntiabant sicuti scribitur, alibi vero semper per אדוני aut aliud cognomen efferebant, ne si ubique absque locorum discrimine protulissent, promiscuo tali usu, obfolescerent eius sanctitas, in qua religiose observanda, omni tempore ad nauseam usque superstitiosi fuere. Interim tamen nobis cavendum ne in defectu peccemus, est enim illud nomen augustissimum; audiatur antiquum TargumHierof. Deut. 32. Ait Moses, va iis qui in execrationibus proferunt nomen sanctum, si quidem nullis Angelis qui supernè sunt id licet enuntiare, nisi τοῖς τεσσαράκοντα πρεμίsso; Ab illis didicit Moses, ut non usurparet nomen Dei expres- sum עד זמן מחניה פוטיה בעשרה וחדה וחדה מילין ante- quam xxi.vocibus & 95.literis eos suum confecrasset. Quæ deinde de hoc nomine communiter ventilantur, hodie omnibus ita trita sunt, ut nemo non nasum Rhinocerotis sibi in illis habere videatur. Quare nos iis hic supersedemus.
units.tr: JEHOVAH. The holy name יהוה was pronounced nowhere except in the sanctuary, and there as it is written. Elsewhere they always pronounced it as Adonai or with some other epithet, lest, if they had uttered it everywhere without distinction of place, its holiness would have been worn away by such promiscuous use. In observing it religiously they were superstitious at all times, even to the point of nausea. Meanwhile we must take care not to sin by defect, for that name is most august. Let the ancient Targum of Jerusalem on Deuteronomy 32 be heard: "Moses says: woe to those who utter the holy name in curses, since no angels who are above are permitted to pronounce it, except [the forty-two?] ... From them Moses learned not to use the expressed name of God, until he had consecrated them with twenty-one words and ninety-five letters." What is commonly discussed about this name is now so worn out for everyone that no one fails to seem to have a rhinoceros's nose in these matters. Therefore we pass them over here.

units.la: Ieĥuda Sanctus יהודה הקדוש ' י Natus est eò die quò Akiba occubuit, inde orta illa Iudæorum sententia, Eò die occidit lux Israelis & iterum orta est. Postquam rebus administrandis admotus fuit, prima eius cura erat, Synedrium & Academiam in Tiberiada transferre. Quod etiam feliciter ipsi successit. Deinde operam contulit, ut omnia Mischnaiot in unum volumen compingeret; videbat enim (inquit Zemach David) prolongationem captivitatis, & discipulos pusillanimos redditos esse. Vim sapientiæ verò & legem orâlem attenuatam. Corrasit itaque omnia decreta, statuta, & dicta virorum doctorum, qui ante ipsum floruerunt, atque ea in hunc ordinem disposuit, quo illa hodierno die conspiciuntur.
units.tr: Judah the Holy [יהודה הקדוש] was born on the day Akiba died, and from this came the Jewish saying, On that day the light of Israel went out and rose again. After he was entrusted with the government of affairs, his first concern was to transfer the Sanhedrin and the Academy to Tiberias, and this succeeded for him. Then he set about gathering all the Mishnayot into a single volume, for he saw (as Zemach David says) that the captivity was being prolonged and that the disciples had become fainthearted, and that the power of wisdom and the oral law had been weakened. He therefore collected all the decrees, statutes and sayings of the learned men who had flourished before him, and arranged them in the order in which they are seen today.

units.la: §. Hic Doctor κατ' ἐξοχὴν vocatur Rabbi; aliquas de eo historiolas habes in Hierof. Sanhed. sol.18.3. ubi intercalatio malè cessit suis discipulis. Hierof.Erubbin sol.23.4. Vbi Magdalenses non exiguum beneficium ab ipso recipiunt. Hierof.Horaiot sol.47.1. Vbi Simeon Ben Lachisch ipsum quoque censuræ subiectum esse voluit. Hierof. Terumot sol.46.2. Vbi familiares eius וולקין Diocletianum porcarium male excipiunt.
units.tr: §. This teacher is called Rabbi par excellence. You have some little stories about him in Hierosolymitanum Sanhedrin fol. 18.3, where an intercalation turned out badly for his disciples. Hierosolymitanum Erubbin fol. 23.4, where the people of Magdala receive no small kindness from him. Hierosolymitanum Horaiot fol. 47.1, where Simeon ben Lakish wanted him also to be subject to censure. Hierosolymitanum Terumot fol. 46.2, where his household servants treat Diocletian, the swineherd, badly.

units.la: §. Mortuus est Rabbi Zippore quò se ante obitum 17. annis contulerat, at si pultus fuit in Beth Schaarim, moriens præcepit ne plorarētur in civitatibus parvis, sed in magnis. Gl.Bab. Sanhed. sol.47.1. Miracula facta iunt illo die quo civitates congregatæ erant ad ipsum plangendum. Hierof. Kilaim sol.32.2. Filium reliquit R.Gamalielem ultimum Synedrii Præsidem, cum illo enim Synedrialis potestas expiravit. Vid. Iuchafin.
units.tr: §. Rabbi Zippori died, to whom he had withdrawn seventeen years before his death; but if he was buried in Beth Shearim, he commanded on dying that he should not be mourned in small towns but in large ones. Gloss on Babylonian Sanhedrin fol. 47.1. Miracles were done on the day when the towns had gathered to mourn for him. Hierosolymitanum Kilaim fol. 32.2. He left a son, Rabban Gamaliel, the last president of the Sanhedrin, for with him the power of the Sanhedrin expired. See Iuchasin.

units.la: Ieiunia varia habuerunt Iudæi 1 Ieiunabat totus cætus & privati propter pluvias sementi necessarias. Taanit c.1. Præsente die octobris decimo septimo si adhuc nullæ pluviæ descenderint, incipiunt privati ieiunare tria ieiunia; si iam adsit initium Novembris, nec ullæ pluviæ segetes irrigaverint, Synedrium tria ieiunia Ecclesiæ decernit; Si illa ieiunia præterierint, nec tamen Deus ipsos exaudiverit, Synedrium tria alia ieiunia prioribus rigidiora decernit: Si nec tunc pluviam habuerint, à Synedrio septem alia ieiunia indicantur; privati verò ieiunare pergunt usque ad finem Martii: qui si ad exitum pervenerit absque pluvia, signum est maledictionis.
units.tr: The Jews had various fasts. (1) The whole congregation and private persons fasted on account of rains needed for sowing. Taanit chap. 1. If on the seventeenth day of October no rain has yet fallen, private persons begin to fast three fasts; if the beginning of November is already at hand and no rain has watered the crops, the Sanhedrin decrees three fasts for the Church. If those fasts have passed and God has still not heard them, the Sanhedrin decrees three other fasts, stricter than the earlier ones. If they still have no rain, seven other fasts are appointed by the Sanhedrin; private persons, however, continue to fast until the end of March, and if this end is reached without rain, it is a sign of curse.

units.la: §. 2. Indixerunt sibi ipsis non raro ieiunia eo fine ut felicia adipiscerentur insomnia, vel ut insomnii malum omen averterent. Hinc Phraseologia usitatissima תענית חלום Ieiunium pro insomnio, cuius causâ licet ieiunare in Sabbatho. Bab.Schabbat sol.11.1. cùm propter alia ieiunia id fuerit prohibitum.
units.tr: §. 2. They often appointed fasts for themselves so that they might obtain happy dreams, or so that they might avert the evil omen of a dream. Hence the very common phrase Fast for a dream [תענית חלום], on whose account it is lawful to fast on the Sabbath, Babylonian Shabbat fol. 11.1, although on account of other fasts this was forbidden.

units.la: §. 3. Ieiunarunt sæpè eo fine, ut desideria sua assequerentur Hierof. Kilaim sol.32.2. R. Iose ieiunavit oblogintₐ ieiunia, & R. Simeon Ben Lachisch trecenta, eo fine ut viderent R. Chaia Rubba.
units.tr: §. 3. They often fasted with this aim, that they might obtain their desires. Hierosolymitanum Kilaim fol. 32.2. Rabbi Yose fasted eighty fasts, and Rabbi Simeon ben Lakish three hundred, so that they might see Rabbi Hiyya Rabba.

units.la: §. 4. Ieiunarunt etiam,ut mala imminentia propellerent; sic ieiunavit R. Zádok per quadraginta annos, à tempore quo sponte templi portæ apertæ fuerunt, ut excidium urbis & templi avertere posset; Sic Seniores Hierosolymitani desce-nderunt in urbes suas, & indixerunt universale ieiunium, Quia Asca one visa fuerat uredo instar magnitudinis orifi ii furni. Ita cùm cis Iordanem lupi duos pueros devoraverant,exequias illorum infantum inter fletum & ieiunium fecerunt. Licet vito religioso ob spiritum malum fe ipsum ieiuniis afflig ere Bab. Taanit sol.22.2. Confer Matth.17.21. Vide Taanit.
units.tr: §. 4. They also fasted to turn away impending evils. Thus Rabbi Zadok fasted for forty years, from the time when the gates of the temple opened of their own accord, so that he might avert the destruction of the city and the temple. So the elders of Jerusalem went down to their towns and appointed a general fast, because a blight had appeared in Ascalon the size of the mouth of an oven. So too, when wolves had devoured two boys on this side of the Jordan, they performed the funeral rites for those infants amid weeping and fasting. It is lawful for a religious man to afflict himself with fasts on account of an evil spirit. Babylonian Taanit fol. 22.2. Compare Matthew 17:21. See Taanit.

units.la: §. 5. Si urbem aliquam Cuthæi obsederunt, aut si navis quædam in mari conquassata fuerit, imò etiam si unicus persecutionem patiatur à latronibus Cuthæis aut à spiritu malo, propter hæc ieiunarunt atque Divinam implorarunt misericordiam Maymon. de Ieiuniis cap.1.
units.tr: §. 5. If they besieged some city of the Cuthaeans, or if some ship was battered at sea, indeed even if a single person suffered persecution from Cuthaean robbers or from an evil spirit, on account of these things they fasted and implored the divine mercy. Maimonides, On Fasts, chap. 1.

units.la: §. Pharisæi ut ex Lucæ xviii.12. patet, solliti sunt ieiunare bis in unaquaque septimana, die scilicet secundo & quinto septimanæ. Ou a (ut Glossa notat ad Bab. Rava Kama sol.82.1) Moses die 5. ad Deum ascendit, & pa ato iam
units.tr: §. The Pharisees, as is plain from Luke 18:12, were accustomed to fast twice in every week, namely on the second and fifth days of the week. Ou a (as the Gloss notes on Babylonian Rava Kama fol. 82.1) Moses ascended to God on the fifth day, and pa ato already

units.la: Deo die hebdomadis secundo iterum descendit. De his diebus vide etiam Hieros. Megillah sol. 75. 1.
units.tr: On the second day of the week he came down again to God. On these days see also Hierosolymitanum Megillah fol. 75.1.

units.la: §. Non ieiunant Iudæi nisi antea in se sufceperint ieiunium cum dies est adhuc, alioqui non est ieiunium, Quomodo vero illud suscipiunt? Cum vespertinas preces ad Deum quis fundit, finitis precibus dicit, cras ero in ieiunio, atque sibi firmiter in corde suo proponit ieiunare die crastino. Maym. Taanit c. 1.
units.tr: §. The Jews do not fast unless they have undertaken the fast beforehand while it is still day; otherwise it is not a fast. But how do they undertake it? When someone pours out the evening prayers to God, when the prayers are finished he says, Tomorrow I will be in fast, and he firmly resolves in his heart to fast on the following day. Maimonides, Taanit chap. 1.

units.la: §. In ieiuniis oblinunt facies suas cineribus. Taanith cap.2. In publicis ieiuniis, accipit unusquisque cineres, & imponit capiti suo. Iuchafin sol. 59. de R. Iosua Ben Anania dicunt, quòd omnibus diebus vita sua הושחרו פני תעניות Nigra fuit facies eius pro ieiuniis &c. Ita Rabbinus quidem vocatus fuit Aschur, quia ieiunando הושחר niger factus fuit. Bab. Sotah folio 12.1.
units.tr: §. In fasts they smear their faces with ashes. Taanith chap. 2. In public fasts each one takes ashes and puts them on his head. Iuchasin fol. 59. They say of Rabbi Joshua ben Hananiah that all the days of his life his face was blackened for fasts [הושחרו פני תעניות], etc. So indeed he was called a rabbi, Ashur, because by fasting he was made black [הושחר]. Babylonian Sotah folio 12.1.

units.la: §. Ieiunantes nec se unxerunt nec lavarunt, ita in magno illo die Expiationum non solùm omnis cibus prohibitus erat, sed insuper nemini licuit aut se ungere, aut lavare, aut sandalia induere, aut coire cum uxore. Ioma cap.8.
units.tr: §. Those who fast neither anoint themselves nor wash. So on that great Day of Atonement not only was all food forbidden, but moreover no one was allowed to anoint himself, or wash, or put on sandals, or lie with his wife. Yoma chap. 8.

units.la: 1. Gemara in Ioma sol.77.2. Bab. Taanit sol.11. 2.13.2.
units.tr: 1. Gemara on Yoma fol. 77.2. Babylonian Taanit fol. 11.2, 13.2.

units.la: §. Ordo ieiunii publici hic est; Educunt arcam in plateam urbis, omnique populo convocato, saccis ciliciisve induti arcæ & libro legis inspergunt cinerem, eo fine ut uberiores populi lacrymas excitent & ad humilitatem illius animum inflectant. Postea senem sapientia clarum assurgere iubent, circa quem considerent, si haud praestò fuerit senex, viro tantùm sapienti id officii demandant; at si nec Senex, nec Sapiens illic praesens sit, constituunt virum morum vitaeq; integrum, ut orationem argutam & quae relinquat in animis populi aculeos (דברי שיבוש) habeat. Hic, Nec laccus, inquit, cilicium ve, nec ieiunium quid efficit, ô fratres; sed poenitentia ac bona opera. Exemplo nobis esto Ninive, de cuius civibus profectò non dicitur, respexisse Deum eorum cilicia & ieiunia; sed tantum legitur; Et vidit Deus opera eorum Ion.3.10. Sic ipse Deus in Prophetarum scriptis monet (Ioel.2.13.) Lacerate cor vestrum, & non vestimenta vestra. Atque huius argumenti plura alia, quantum ipse quidem potest, producit, usquedum humiliaverit tandem eorum animos, & resipiscant ac veram agant poenitentiam. Postquàm ille orationem suam absolvit surgunt ad praeces, & Ministrum Synagogae, vel illum ipsum qui orationem fudit, vel alium qui dignus habetur, ad precandum ordinant. De qualitatibus illi ad orandum requisitis. Vide Maymon. de Ieiunio. Ille porrò coràm ipsis xxiv. preces fundit, octodecim quidem quae singulis diebus dicuntur, & sex quas hic superaddit, de quibus Vide Taanit.c.2. Denique sub finem deprecationum ait. Is qui Abrahamo Patri nostro in monte Morija respondit, respondeat vobis & vocem hodie exaudiat clamoris vestri: Benedictus esto, ô Dominé Redemptor Israelis. His ita prolatis denuò sex benedictiones post invicem huic addit, in quarum unaquåq; verbis deprecatoriis & Scripturæ dictis ex libris Propheticis & Hagiographis depromptis, misericordiam Dei sollicitat, & quamlibet tandem his benedictionum clausulis obsignat. In 1. hanc ponit clausulam: Is qui Mosi & Patribus vestris ad mare rubrum respondit, idem vobis respondeat, & vocem clamoris vestri exaudiat hodie: Benedictus esto, ô Domine qui recordaris eorum quæ oblivione dudum sepulta. In 2. hanc: Is qui in Gilgal respondit Iosuæ, respondeat vobis & exaudiat hodie vocem clamoris vestri: Benedictus esto, ô Domine, qui clangorem audis. In 3. hanc: Is qui in Mitspa Samueli respondit, respondeat & vobis &c. Benedictus esto ô Domine qui clamorem exaudis. In 4. istam: Is qui Eliæ in monte Carmel respondit, respondeat &c. Benedictus esto ô Domine qui orationem exaudis. In 5. hanc: Is qui Ionæ in ventre piscis respondit, respondeat &c. Benedictus esto, ô Domine, qui tempore angustiæ respondes. In 6. hanc: Is qui Davidi eiusque filio Salomoni Hierosolymis respondit, respondeat &c. Benedictus esto, ô Domine, qui terræ miserëris. Cæterùm unicuique harum benedictionum universus populus reponit, AMEN. Maymon. de Ieiunio, ubi plura Vide. De Ieiuniis vid. Schindleri & Cl. Buxt. Lex. in ꝺ. Cofri 162. Synog. c. 30.
units.tr: §. The order of a public fast is this. They bring the ark out into the square of the city, and with all the people called together, dressed in sackcloth or hair shirts, they sprinkle ashes on the ark and on the book of the law, so that they may draw out more abundant tears from the people and bend their minds to humility. Afterwards they bid an old man, distinguished for wisdom, to rise, around whom they sit; if no elder is at hand, they entrust this duty only to a wise man; but if neither an elder nor a wise man is present there, they appoint a man of upright character and blameless life, so that he may have a lively speech which leaves goads in the minds of the people (divrei shibush). He then says: "Neither a sack nor a hair shirt, brothers, nor a fast accomplishes anything; but repentance and good works do. Let Nineveh be our example, of whose citizens it is certainly not said that God regarded their sackcloth and fasts, but only: And God saw their works, Jonah 3:10. So God himself warns in the writings of the prophets (Joel 2:13): Rend your heart, and not your garments." And he brings forward many other arguments of this kind, as far as he himself can, until at last he has humbled their minds and they come to their senses and do true repentance. When he has finished his speech, they rise to prayer, and they appoint as minister of the synagogue either the very man who gave the speech, or another who is considered worthy, to pray. Concerning the qualifications required of him for praying, see Maimonides, On Fasting. He then offers twenty-four prayers before them: eighteen indeed which are said on every day, and six which he adds here, concerning which see Taanit chap. 2. Finally, at the end of the supplications he says: "May he who answered our father Abraham on Mount Moriah answer you, and hear the voice of your cry this day: Blessed are you, O Lord, Redeemer of Israel." When these have been spoken, he again adds six blessings one after another, and in each of their words, drawn from the prophetic books and the Hagiographa, of petitionary words and sayings of Scripture, he entreats the mercy of God, and at last seals each with a closing formula of these blessings. In the first he puts this closing: "He who answered Moses and your fathers at the Red Sea, let him answer you likewise, and hear the voice of your cry today: Blessed are you, O Lord, who remember what was long buried in oblivion." In the second: "He who answered Joshua in Gilgal, let him answer you and hear the voice of your cry today: Blessed are you, O Lord, who hear the trumpet blast." In the third: "He who answered Samuel in Mizpah, let him answer you also, etc. Blessed are you, O Lord, who hear the cry." In the fourth: "He who answered Elijah on Mount Carmel, let him answer, etc. Blessed are you, O Lord, who hear prayer." In the fifth: "He who answered Jonah in the belly of the fish, let him answer, etc. Blessed are you, O Lord, who answer in time of distress." In the sixth: "He who answered David and his son Solomon at Jerusalem, let him answer, etc. Blessed are you, O Lord, who have mercy on the land." Moreover, to each of these blessings the whole people responds, AMEN. Maimonides, On Fasting, where more is to be seen. On fasts see Schindler and the learned Buxtorf, Lexicon under Cofri 162; Synagogue chap. 30.

units.la: IEPHTA quorsum fugerit vide Hierof. Schevift sol. 36. 1. IANNES & IAMBRES vid. Cl. Buxtorf. L. Talm. p. 945.
units.tr: Where Jephthah fled to, see the Jerusalem Talmud, Shevuot, fol. 36, col. 1. For Jannes and Jambres, see Cl. Buxtorf, Lexicon Talmudicum, p. 945.

units.la: Matth.27.9. contentio, quomodo salvâ integritate textus, explicanda sint verba Evangelistæ. n snsiv ds Ieremiæ ꝏ ꝏꝏ; cùm illa verba quæ citantur non extent apud ipsum Ieremiam sed apud Zachariam. Clariss. Leigtfootus pro eo acumine quo valet, ex Talmudico monumento elegantem nos extricandi rationem reperiit; propria ipsius verba adscribamus.
units.tr: Matthew 27:9. There is a dispute about how the words of the Evangelist can be explained while the integrity of the text is preserved, since the words cited are not found in Jeremiah himself but in Zechariah. The most distinguished Lightfoot, with the keenness for which he is known, has found from a Talmudic monument an elegant way of extricating the passage. Let us set down his own words.

units.la: Bab. Bava Batra. sol.14.2. Traditio Rabbinorum. Hic est ordo Prophetarum. Liber Iosuæ, Iudicum, Samuelis, Regum, Ieremiæ, Ezechielis, Esaiæ & duodecim. Et paulò post. Cùm autem tempore præcesserit Esaias Ieremiam, atque Ezechielem, præponendus ẏitè esset Esaias; כין Cùm verò liber Regum terminaret in excidio ירם הו כוליה חרבנה Ieremias que totus agat de excidio, cùmque initium Ezechielis sit de excidio, finiaturque in consolatione, cùmque totus Esaias sit de consolatione סמכינן Coniunxerunt excidium cum excidio, & consolationem cum consolatione. Id est, libros qui egerunt de excidio coniunxerunt, & libros coniunxerunt qui egerunt de consolatione.
units.tr: Bab. Bava Batra, fol. 14, col. 2. "Tradition of the Rabbis: This is the order of the Prophets: the book of Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah, and the Twelve." And a little later: "Since Isaiah preceded Jeremiah and Ezekiel in time, Isaiah ought to have been placed first. But since the book of Kings ends in destruction, and Jeremiah is wholly concerned with destruction, and the beginning of Ezekiel is about destruction and it ends in consolation, and all of Isaiah is about consolation, they joined destruction with destruction and consolation with consolation." That is, they joined the books which dealt with destruction, and they joined the books which dealt with consolation.

units.la: Traditionem hanc citatam habes à Davide Kimchio in præfatione ad Ieremiam. Unde patet aperte Ieremiam in volumine Prophetarum olim primum locum obtinuisse: atque hinc eius memoria præ omnibus aliis Prophetis Matth.xvi.14. Quia ille primus incessit in volumine Prophetarum, nominatur ille primus ; cùm ergò textum Zachariæ sub nomine Ieremiæ proferat Matthæus, verba è volumine Prophetarum citat tantùm, sub istius nomine, qui primum locum tenuit in volumine Prophetarum. Sic dicit Christus Luca xxiv. 44. Complenda sunt omnia quæ de me scribuntur in Lege, Prophetis, & Psalmis. In Psalmis, id est, in libro Hagiographorum, in quo primum locum obtinuit liber Psalmorum.
units.tr: You have this tradition cited by David Kimchi in his preface to Jeremiah. From it it is clear that Jeremiah once held the first place in the collection of the Prophets, and hence his name is mentioned before all the other Prophets in Matthew 16:14. Because he came first in the collection of the Prophets, he is named as "the first." Therefore, when Matthew brings forward a text of Zechariah under the name of Jeremiah, he cites only the words from the collection of the Prophets, under the name of the one who held the first place in that collection. So Christ says in Luke 24:44: "All things must be fulfilled which are written concerning me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms." "In the Psalms" means in the book of the Hagiographa, in which the book of Psalms held the first place.

units.la: Iericho, ab illa potuerunt audire portam templi cùm aperiebatur, vocem tintinabuli, strepitum Machinæ Ben Katin &c. Tamid cap.3.8. Bab. Ioma sol.20. 2. & 39.2. De his loquutionibus vid. Hyperbole. de eius ab Hierosolyma distantia, lege Iosephi de bell. I.4. c.27. Iericho est Deut. xxxiv. 3. Iericho iterum ædificari non debuit, Iosua vi. 6. nec Iericho nominari Hieros.Sanhed. sol.24.4.
units.tr: Jericho: from that place they could hear the gate of the temple being opened, the sound of the bell, the noise of the machine of Ben Katin, etc. Tamid, ch. 3, sec. 8. Bab. Yoma, fol. 20, col. 2, and fol. 39, col. 2. On these expressions see Hyperbole. For its distance from Jerusalem, read Josephus, Jewish War 1.4, ch. 27. Jericho is at Deut. 34:3. Jericho was not to be built again, Joshua 6:26, nor was Jericho to be named (Jerusalem Sanhedrin, fol. 24, col. 4).

units.la: §. Erat Icrichunte confessus Synedrii Hieros. Avoda Zarah sol.42.3. Memoratur maximè Camera Ben Gadiæ in Ierichunte. ibidem. Quamvis Iericho 24000 Viros stationarios producere potuisset, ut Hierosolyma ut tamen illi aliquâ ratione cederet, solùm 11000 habuit. Hieros.Taanit sol.67.4.
units.tr: Jericho had a council of the Sanhedrin, as in the Jerusalem Talmud, Avodah Zarah, fol. 42, col. 3. The Chamber of Ben Gadia in Jericho is especially mentioned (ibid.). Although Jericho could have produced 24,000 standing men, as Jerusalem could, yet for some reason it yielded to her, and had only 11,000 (Jerusalem Taanit, fol. 67, col. 4).

units.la: §. Viri Ierichuntini ob sex ab iis extraordinariè & contra communes regulas peracta celebres sunt; tria ipsis indulsit Synedrium, quæ sunt, ut possent omni die inoculare palmas & infitiones facere. Complicare Schema (v.f.1.) Metere & manipulos colligere antequam oblatum manipulum. In tribus autem non consensit cum ipsis Synedrium, quæ erant 1. Quòd fructus, germina, quæ patres ipsorum sacro usui devoverant, in communem usum abalienarent. 2. Quòd comederent Sabbatho fructus deciduos, incerti an Sabbatho decidissent nec ne. 3. Angulus horti pro oleribus concederent, eo modo quo conceditur angulus agri pro segetibus. Pesachim c.4. v.8.
units.tr: The men of Jericho are famous for six things done by them in an extraordinary way and contrary to the common rules. The Sanhedrin granted them three privileges: that they might every day anoint their palms and make a show of drawing near, to fold a [?] ..., to reap and gather sheaves before the offered sheaf. But in three things the Sanhedrin did not agree with them, which were: (1) that they should alienate for common use the fruits and shoots which their fathers had devoted to sacred use; (2) that they should eat on the Sabbath fallen fruits, though it was uncertain whether they had fallen on the Sabbath or not; (3) that they should grant a corner of the garden for vegetables, in the same way that a corner of a field is granted for crops. Pesachim, ch. 4, sec. 8.

units.la: §. Regio Ierichuntina fertilis erat שושן ורדנא Vnguenti Balsami, & hinc quoque à grato odore vocata fuit ירחו Vid. Gloss. Bab. Beracoi sol.43. 1.
units.tr: The region of Jericho was fertile, "Shushan Rederna," of ointment and balsam, and hence also it was called from its pleasant odour Yericho. See the Gloss on Bab. Berachot, fol. 43, col. 1.

units.la: IEROSOLYMA. Hunc locum Abraham vocavit Iireh, Semus verò Schalem, si Iudæi ipsum vocarent simpliciter Iireh disputaret illud Semo Iusto, si verò Schalem, disputaret Abrahamo iusto, Ergo ipsi nomen imposuerunt, quod ab utroque est compositum ירושלם יראה שלם Berefchit Rabba Sect.9. Aruch in ירושלם.
units.tr: Jerusalem. Abraham called this place "Yireh," but Shem called it "Shalem." If the Jews called it simply "Yireh," that would dispute with Shem the Just; if "Shalem," it would dispute with Abraham the Just. Therefore they gave it a name compounded of both: Yerushalayim = Yireh + Shalem. Bereshit Rabba, sect. 9; Aruch, under "Yerushalayim."

units.la: §. Sita est computante Aben Esra in Num. 13. in 33. gradu latitudinis. Non dividebatur Ierosolyma inter tribus, nec proinde mercede conducebantur domus Hierosolymitanæ, quia propriæ non erant, accedentes ad festum proinde gratis hospitia habebant, relinquebant tamen suis hospitibus coria sacrificiorum & cantharos suos testaceos. Bab.Ioma f.12.1. Megillah sol.16.1. Gloss. Divisa nihilominus est urbs, inter tribum Iudæ & Beniaminis, procedebatque linea disterminans per ipsum atrium templi. Bab. ubi supra.
units.tr: It lies, according to Aben Ezra on Num. 13, at the 33rd degree of latitude. Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes, and therefore its houses were not let for rent, since they were not privately owned. Those who came to the feast therefore had lodging free of charge, yet they left to their hosts the hides of the sacrifices and their earthenware pots. Bab. Yoma, fol. 12, col. 1; Megillah, fol. 16, col. 1; Gloss. Nevertheless the city was divided between the tribe of Judah and Benjamin, and the line marking the boundary ran through the very court of the temple (Bab., ubi supra).

units.la: §. Vrbs Hierosolymitana multa præclara habuit præ reliquis civitatibus. Erat sanctissima, in qua nullus mortuus poterat pernoctare
units.tr: The city of Jerusalem had many distinctions above the other cities. It was most holy, and in it no dead man could spend the night

units.la: re in ea comedi debebant sacra leviora & decimæ secundæ. Præter sepulchra Domus Davidis & Prophetissæ Huldæ nulla in ea permittebant. Nullum in ea debuit esse fimetum. In ea non faciebant Caminos, propter fumum. Nulli alebantur galli propter Sacra. Maymon.Hal Beth Habeeh c.7.
units.tr: ...in it the lesser holy things and the second tithe had to be eaten. Apart from the sepulchres of the House of David and of the prophetess Huldah, they permitted no burials in it. No dunghill ought to be in it. In it they did not make fireplaces, on account of the smoke. No cocks were kept, on account of the holy things. Maimonides, Hilkhot Beit Ha-Behirah, ch. 7.

units.la: § Nunquam serpens aut scorpio cuiquam nocuit intra Hierosolymam. Nec dixit unquam quisquam proximo suo, arctus nimis mihi est locus in quo Hierosolymis hospitor. Avoth cap 5. 5. Hierosolymæ non occurrit Anathema, nec titubavit quisquam. Nec evenit illic conflagratio nec ruina. Nullus unquam conquestus est, se non reperiisse clibanum pro Pascha te, aut lectum pro quiete. Non plantant in ea arbores & hortos; Qui ibi fuerunt, iam à tempore priorum Prophetarum plantati fuerant. Avot. Rabb. Nathan sol. 9. 1. Ratio autem cur hortos non plantare debuerint, extat Bava Kama c.7. v.ult. sc. propter fœtorem ab herbis malis & stercore.
units.tr: No serpent or scorpion ever harmed anyone within Jerusalem. Nor did anyone ever say to his neighbour, "The place where I lodge in Jerusalem is too cramped for me." Avot, ch. 5, sec. 5. No Anathema ever occurred in Jerusalem, nor did anyone stumble there. No conflagration or ruin happened there. No one ever complained that he had not found an oven for his Passover cake, or a bed for rest. They did not plant trees and gardens in it; those who were there had been planted since the time of the earlier Prophets. Avot de Rabbi Nathan, fol. 9, sec. 1. The reason why they ought not to plant gardens is found in Bava Kamma, ch. 7, last verse, namely on account of the stench from bad herbs and dung.

units.la: §. ירושלם בולה כרמל הית Hierosolyma tota erat Carmelith (vid. Lex. Talm. Buxt) quia erat sicut atrium commune. Gloss. in Erubhin sol.101.1.
units.tr: Jerusalem as a whole was "Carmelith" (see the Talmudic lexicon of Buxtorf), because it was like a common court. Gloss on Erubin, fol. 101, col. 1.

units.la: §. תני ק& ירושלמי opponebantur sicut Rusticus & Vranus. Vide Demai c.6. 2.
units.tr: The Tanna and the Jerusalem [Talmud] were set against each other as the rustic and the urban. See Demai, ch. 6, sec. 2.

units.la: §. Hierosolyma Herodoto in Thalia cap. 5. est Cadytis; A Phœnice usque ad montes Καδύτιος πόλις, qua est urbs eorum Syrorum qui Palæstini vocantur. Viderat Herodotus illam in nummis קרושת & Syrorum Dialecto קרותא
units.tr: Herodotus, in Thalia, ch. 5, calls Jerusalem "Cadytis": "from Phoenicia as far as the mountains, the city of Cadytis, which is the city of those Syrians who are called Palestinians." Herodotus had seen it named in coins and in the dialect of the Syrians as "Qarusht," and "Qarutha."

units.la: קרותף vocari: unde forsan ipsius Cadytis.
units.tr: "Qarutha," which perhaps gave the name Cadytis.

units.la: §. שוקי ירושלם עשויין להתכבר בכל יום [?] Platea Hierosolymitana verrebantur in dies. Pesachim sol.71. & Metzia sol.26.1. Celebris est illa platea quae ducebat a templo ad montem olivetum: in illa aestivo tempore propter umbram templi quâ refrigerabatur, sedit R. Iochan. Ben Saccai, & docuit populum per totum diem. Pesachim sol.26.1. Per illam exiit Sacerdos vaccam rufam combusturus in Oliveto, & illâ introiit in die Palmarum Dominus noster Christus Iesus. De aliis Plateis vid. Platea.
units.tr: "The streets of Jerusalem were made to be swept every day." Pesachim, fol. 71, and Metzia, fol. 26, col. 1. The famous street was the one which led from the temple to the Mount of Olives. In summer, because of the shade of the temple, by which it was cooled, R. Johanan ben Zakkai sat there and taught the people all day long (Pesachim, fol. 26, col. 1). Through it the priest went out to burn the red heifer on the Mount of Olives, and through it our Lord Christ Jesus entered on Palm Sunday. On the other streets see Platea.

units.la: §. Muris Hierosolymitanis nihil adiungunt aut addunt, nisi ex Regis, Prophetae, aut Synedrii iussu. Cùm amplianda urbs esset tali caeremonia utebantur; Primùm oraculum Vrim & Tummim consuluerunt. Mox postquàm Rex & Synedrium de interpretatione responsi divini consensissent, Senatores Synedrii carmina duo, in quibus erat gratiarum actio, recitarunt, panesque totidem fermentatos summere, atque cum cymbalis egressi, ad cuiusque vici flexuras & cippos constiterunt, & illa verba proloquuti sunt ארוממך יהוה כי דליתני [?] Exaltabo te Domine, quoniam exaltasti me. Tandem cùm ad locum illum venissent, quem idcircò consecrari oportuit, quòd pomeriorum finis esset futurus, substitêre omnes, atque illic ex duobus panibus, quos decantato gemino carmine acceperant, unum comederunt, alterum usserunt flammis. Maymon Hal.Beth Habech. cap. 6. sub med.
units.tr: To the walls of Jerusalem they add or attach nothing except by order of the King, the Prophet, or the Sanhedrin. When the city was to be enlarged they used this ceremony: first they consulted the oracle of Urim and Thummim. Soon after the King and the Sanhedrin had agreed on the interpretation of the divine answer, the senators of the Sanhedrin recited two songs, in which there was thanksgiving, and took as many leavened loaves, and went out with cymbals, and stood at the bends and boundary stones of each quarter, and uttered those words: "I will exalt you, O Lord, for you have lifted me up." Finally, when they had come to that place which had to be consecrated for this reason, because it would be the limit of the pomerium, they all halted, and there they ate one of the two loaves which they had received while the twofold song was chanted, and burned the other in the flames. Maimonides, Hilkhot Beit Ha-Behirah, ch. 6, near the middle.

units.la: §. Hierosolymis nemo suam domum in tantam altitudinem evehere debuit, ut ipsi illinc patuisset conspectus in Sanctum Sanctorum. Si vero alicui coenaculum tale tam altum esset, fas quidem illi fuit semel in hebdomada illuc ascendere, uti sarta tecta omnia servaret, ac saepius aut ob aliam causam non licuit. Maymon. l. c. cap. 7.
units.tr: §. In Jerusalem no one was to raise his house so high that a view into the Holy of Holies could be had from it. But if anyone's upper room was so high, he was permitted to go up to it once a week, to keep the whole roof in repair; he was not allowed to go up more often, or for any other reason. Maimonides, loc. cit., cap. 7.

units.la: §. Inter Hierosolymitanos hortos extra urbem plantatos praestantissimus erat גנת ורדים hortus Rosarum, in quo nascebantur ficus, quae singulae tribus aut quatuor assariis divendi poterant, & tamen de iis nunquam desumpta est vel תרומה vel decima. Cuius rei ratio est, quia propter rosas nemini ingredi permittebant. Maaserot c. 2 §.
units.tr: §. Among the gardens planted outside Jerusalem, the most excellent was the garden of roses [גנת ורדים], in which figs grew. Each of these could be sold for three or four assaria, and yet no terumah or tithe was ever taken from them. The reason was that, because of the roses, no one was permitted to enter. Maaserot, c. 2, §.

units.la: §. De differentia quae est inter Hierosolymas & Schiloh sequentia habentur in Megillah c. 1. 11. Gloss Quod in Schilunte Sancta leviora & decimae secundae comedi potuerint, ubicunque Schiloh conspici potuit; Hierosolymis vero debeant comedi intra murum: Siloh devastato, adhuc altaria in excelsis habere & exstruere licuit; At Hierosolyma semel devastata, alibi sacrificia offerre non licet.
units.tr: §. The differences between Jerusalem and Shiloh are set out in Megillah, c. 1, and 11, with the Gloss: the lesser holy things and second tithe could be eaten wherever Shiloh could be seen, but in Jerusalem they had to be eaten within the wall. When Shiloh was laid waste, it was still permitted to have and erect altars on high places; but once Jerusalem had been laid waste, it is not lawful to offer sacrifices anywhere else.

units.la: §. Mundus similis est oculo; cuius album est Oceanus, qui circumdat mundum; nigrum est ipse mundus; pupilla est Ierusalem, imago quae est in ea Sanctuarium. ירך ארץ c. 5.
units.tr: §. The world is like an eye. Its white is the Ocean, which surrounds the world; its black is the world itself; its pupil is Jerusalem, and the image within it is the Sanctuary. Yerach Eretz, c. 5.

units.la: Iob. Quomodo littera Iod cum Deuteronomio coram Deo apparuerit & conquesta sit, quod eam ex nomine Sarae abstulerit; Vid. Hierof. Sanhed. f. 10. 3. Bab. Sanhed. f. 107. 1.
units.tr: Job. How the letter Yod appeared before God together with Deuteronomy and complained that it had been taken away from the name of Sarah; see Jerusalem Sanhedrin, f. 10, col. 3; Babylonian Sanhedrin, f. 107, col. 1.

units.la: §. דרוקורת Vrbecula huius nominis pro-
units.tr: §. דרוקורת: a little town of this name, [called] …

units.la: propter pter parvitatem eius vocatur Iod in Gloff.B a b. Taanith sol. 21 2. Vide etiam de litera Iod. Midrafch Tillim in Pfal. cxiv.
units.tr: …on account of its smallness it is called Yod in the Gloss on b. Taanith, fol. 21, col. 2. See also concerning the letter Yod the Midrash Tillim on Psalm 114.

units.la: ISRAELITICA Regio. Vniversum terrarum orbem partiuntur scriptores Iudaici in ארץ ישראל terram Israelis & ארץ חוצה Extra terram id est Regiones Ethnicas. Vid. Extranei. In ישראל Israelitas, & אומות העולם Nationes Mundi. Vid. Phraseologias in l. F. Fit etiam aliquando distinctio in ארץ terram (subinde Israeliticam) & מדינת הים Regionem Maris; (v.fl.) Vid.R. Salomoh in Gittin c. I.
units.tr: THE ISRAELITE REGION. Jewish writers divide the whole circuit of the earth into Eretz Israel [ארץ ישראל], the land of Israel, and Chutz la-aretz [ארץ חוצה], outside the land, that is, the heathen regions. See Strangers. Among the Israelites [ישראל] and the Nations of the World [אומות העולם]. See Phraseology in l. F. Sometimes there is also a distinction between the land [ארץ], (at times the Israelite land), and the Region of the Sea [מדינת הים]; (perhaps). See R. Solomon in Gittin, c. 1.

units.la: §. Terram Israeliticam duplici sub notione vulgo definiunt: eam scilicet שהחזיקו בה עולי מצרים Quam possederunt ipsi qui exierunt ex Ægypto; atque eam שהחזיקו בה עולי בבל quam possederunt ipsi, qui exierunt è Babylone. Vide loca illa in quibus de מכוון limine terrae Israelitica agitur, qualia sunt, Maymon in Demai c.1. §.2. Scheviit 6.§.1. Hierof. 1'y sol.40.1. Terra Israelitica occupata ab ascendentibus è Babylone multò minores limites habuit, quàm illa quæ ascendentibus ex Ægypto cesserit; Samaria enim exclusa erat, plurimæ aliæ regiunculæ ab Ethnicis occupatæ fuerunt.
units.tr: §. The Israelite land is commonly defined in a double sense: first, as that which the ones who came up out of Egypt possessed; and second, as that which the ones who came up out of Babylon possessed. See those passages in which the border of the Israelite land [מכוון] is discussed, such as Maimonides on Demai, c. 1, §. 2; Shevi'it 6, §. 1; Jerusalem ... fol. 40, col. 1. The Israelite land, as occupied by those who came up from Babylon, had far smaller borders than that which was given to those who came up out of Egypt; for Samaria was excluded, and several small districts were occupied by the heathen.

units.la: §. In limitibus terræ suæ notandis accurati fuerunt, partim propter Oeconomiæ legalis ritus qui alibi fieri non poterant, partim verò propter plurimas alias actiones, quæ à Talmudicis intra limites restringebantur; verbi gratiâ; Manipulus primitiæ, duo panes ex nulla alia regione quàm Israelitica adduci potuerunt. Kelim c.1. v.6. Hierof.Schekalim sol.47.4.
units.tr: §. They were careful in marking the boundaries of their land, partly because of the rites of the legal economy, which could not be performed elsewhere, and partly because of many other actions which the Talmudists restricted within the borders. For example: the sheaf of firstfruits and the two loaves could be brought from no region other than the Israelite. Kelim, c. 1, v. 6; Jerusalem Shekalim, fol. 47, col. 4.

units.la: Non obtinet lex de decollatione iuvencæ, nisi in terra Israelitica, atque ultrà Iordanem. Maymon. in Rozeach c.1. Non statuunt aut determinant de Nomeniis nec intercalant annum, nisi in terra Israelitica: Sicut dicitur Prodibit Lex è Sione. Maymon. in קדוש cap. 1 Hierof. Nedarim sol.40.1. Non promovent ad Presbyteratum, extra terram Israeliticam &c. Maym. in Sanhed. c.4. Spiritus sanctus ab ipsis fere intra limites istius terræ circunscribitur; Schekina non habitat supra ullum extrà terram. Rab. Salomoh in Iona cap.1.
units.tr: The law concerning the breaking of the neck of the heifer applies only in the Israelite land and beyond the Jordan. Maimonides on Rozeach, c. 1. They do not fix or determine the new moons, nor do they intercalate the year, except in the Israelite land, as it is said: The Law shall go forth from Zion. Maimonides on Qiddush, c. 1; Jerusalem Nedarim, fol. 40, col. 1. They do not promote anyone to the eldership outside the Israelite land, etc. Maimonides on Sanhedrin, c. 4. The Holy Spirit is almost confined by them within the limits of that land; the Shekhinah does not dwell above anything outside the land. Rabbi Solomon on Jonah, c. 1.

units.la: Habet etiam Israelitica regio hoc peculiare, ut qui in ea habitet Deum habeat; Bab. Chetubhot sol. 110.2. Vt omnibus illis qui habitant intrà illam remittantur peccata; Vt ille qui intra eum sepultus sit, eadem ratione se habeat, ac sepultus esset sub altari. Ibid.sol.111. Imò ipsummet Clima sapientes reddit. Gl. in Bab. Sanhed. sol.51. Viri Israelitici sunt admodum sapientes, Namipsum Clima sapientificat. Vide etiam Maymon Beth Habechina cap. 7. Confer quæ suprà apud Ægyptios de terra Israelitica diximus.
units.tr: The Israelite region has this peculiarity as well: that whoever dwells in it has God; Babylonian Ketubot, fol. 110, col. 2. That all those who dwell within it have their sins forgiven; that whoever is buried within it is in the same position as one buried under the altar. Ibid., fol. 111. Indeed the very climate makes men wise. Gloss on Babylonian Sanhedrin, fol. 51. The men of Israel are exceedingly wise, for the climate itself makes them wise. See also Maimonides, Beth ha-Behirah, c. 7. Compare what we said above about the Israelite land among the Egyptians.

units.la: Israeliticam terram quam possederunt ascendentes è Babel dividunt in שלשה ארצות tres regiones; Iudæam, Transjordanicam, & Galilæam; quarum unaquaque iterum in tres regiones dividi potest; quæ recensentur in Scheviit c. 9 1. Vid. Galilæam.
units.tr: The Israelite land which those who came up from Babel possessed is divided into three regions [שלשה ארצות]: Judea, Transjordan, and Galilee; each of which can again be divided into three regions; these are listed in Shevi'it, c. 9, §. 1. See Galilee.

units.la: Limites terræ Israeliticæ describuntur in Hierof. Scheviit sol.36.3. sed admodum obscu-rè; rē; illis verbis tamen aliquam lucem attulit Cl. Leigtfootus in Cent. Chorog. p. 4. & seq. Nota tamen generales limites ibi poni מפרשת a parte meridium turris Sid, usque ad ... Cadesch Barneam & Ascalon. De his terrae limitibus etiam sic loquuntur Gemaristae ad loc. cit. Insulas vides in mari ac si linea ducta esset a Montibus Amanae ad fluvium Ægypti: quodcunque est intra lineam, est de terra Israelitica; quodcunque est extra lineam, est extra terram. Item Targum Hierosolymitanum in Num.34.4. Et linea vesper Occidentalis erit Mare magnum atque Insula eius. Hierof. Schevii sol.36.4. Quodcunque ascendit a monte Amana intus est terra Israelitica &c.
units.tr: The limits of the Israelite land are described in Jerusalem Shevi'it, fol. 36, col. 3, but very obscurely; yet the illustrious Lightfoot has shed some light on those words in Centuria Chorographica, p. 4 f. Note, however, that the general limits are there laid down from the southern side of the tower of Sidon, as far as ... Kadesh-Barnea and Ashkelon. The Gemarists also speak in this way about these borders in the passage cited: You see islands in the sea as if a line had been drawn from the Amanus mountains to the river of Egypt: whatever is within the line is of the Israelite land; whatever is outside the line is outside the land. Likewise the Jerusalem Targum on Num. 34:4: And the western boundary shall be the great sea and its island. Jerusalem Shevi'it, fol. 36, col. 4: Whatever rises from the Amana mountain is within the Israelite land, etc.

units.la: §. De insigni fertilitate terrae Israeliticae quamplurima habent Talmudici eaque satis hyperbolica, quam tamen in miseram sterilitatem olim immutatam fatentur. Hierof. Peah sol.20.1.2. variae adduntur historiae, inter alias has legimus. Dixit R. Iochanan, fructus vilissimus, quem comedimus in iuventute nostra, praestitit optimo, quem nunc comedimus in senectute: nam in diebus eius immutatus fuit mundus. R. Chaia Bar Ba dixit ... Modius Arbelitanus exhibuit olim modium similia, modium farina, modium furfuris, & modium furfuris crassioris, & adhuc modium furfuris crassissimi: at nunc vix unus modius ex uno modio conflat.
units.tr: §. Concerning the remarkable fertility of the Israelite land the Talmudists have very many things, and these quite hyperbolical; yet they confess that it was later changed into wretched barrenness. Jerusalem Peah, fol. 20, cols. 1–2. Various stories are added; among others we read: R. Johanan said: the poorest fruit that we ate in our youth was better than the best that we now eat in old age; for in his days the world was changed. R. Chiya bar Ba said ... The Arbelite modius once yielded a modius of fine flour, a modius of bran, a modius of coarse bran, and a modius of very coarse bran; but now scarcely one modius results from one modius.

units.la: §. Regio praecox terrae Israeliticae vocabatur Baal שלישה qualis apud Ioh.iii.23. Σαλείμ. Sanhed. sol.12.1. Non erat in tota terra Israelitica Regio aliqua qua citius maturavit, & decoxit fruges suas, quàm Baal Schalischa. Tales regiones verò in Menachot sol.85.1. Agros Australes appellant.
units.tr: §. The early region of the Israelite land was called Baal Shalishah [בעל שלישה], such as is mentioned in John 3:23, Σαλείμ. Sanhedrin, fol. 12, col. 1: There was no region in the whole Israelite land that ripened and cooked its crops more quickly than Baal Shalishah. Such regions, however, in Menachot, fol. 85, col. 1, they call southern fields.

units.la: §. Ifraelitica terra optima Simila erat ממכס & מזניחה ( forsan exponendum, illa quae veniebat ex ממס & זניחה Quoniam & sequentia à suis locis denominantur:) & deinde illa quae veniebat è valle Ephraim. Optimum triticum erat ex בחייים & כרחום LocisHierosolymis proximis. Optimum oleum venit ex Tekoah; Secundum ex רגן ultra Iordanem, tertium ex חלב וגו. Praestantissimum vinum erat ex קרחו ועתולין Korchaim & Atolin, secundum à Beth Rimma, & Beth Laban in montano, & pago Sigana in Convalle. Menachot cap.8. & in Tosiphta. Optimi ficus fuerunt in Keila, inde פעילית קעמ דבלת Palatha Keilitica in Bab.Sanhed. sol.70.2. Bab. Ioma sol.76.1. Terra Israel eo tempore quo inhabitabant eam, erat lata, cùm verò non inhabitant eam est angusta. Bab.Gittin f.57.1.
units.tr: §. The finest flour of the Israelite land came from Mekhas and Mezanichah (perhaps to be explained as that which came from Mes and Zanichah, since the following are also named from their places); and then that which came from the valley of Ephraim. The finest wheat came from Bechaiim and Krhum, places nearest Jerusalem. The finest oil came from Tekoa; the second from Regan beyond the Jordan, the third from Chelb etc. The most excellent wine came from Korchaim and Atolin; the second from Beth Rimma and Beth Laban in the hill country, and the village of Sigana in the valley. Menachot, c. 8, and in the Tosefta. The best figs were in Keila, whence the Palatha Keilitica [פעילית קעמ דבלת] in Babylonian Sanhedrin, fol. 70, col. 2; Babylonian Yoma, fol. 76, col. 1. The land of Israel, at the time when they inhabited it, was broad; but when they do not inhabit it, it is narrow. Babylonian Gittin, f. 57, col. 1.

units.la: §. De Ifraelitica regione vid. plura apud Iudaam. De variis eius locis vid. in L. apud Loca Israel.
units.tr: §. Concerning the Israelite region see more under Judea. Concerning its various places see under Places of Israel in L.

units.la: unà die à Iordane ad montem Gerizim venerunt. Gloff.in Sanhed sol.44.1. Ibique pro se invicem spoponderunt, inde quoque unus ob alterius culpam plectitur. Rascbi Deut.28.29. Sanhed. sol.27.2.
units.tr: They came in one day from the Jordan to Mount Gerizim. Gloss on Sanhedrin fol. 44.1. There they went surety for one another, and so one is also punished for another's fault. Rashi on Deut. 28.29. Sanhedrin fol. 27.2.

units.la: §. Israelis redemptio est aurorae similis בתחילה קיטאה קיטאה כל מה שהיא הולכת היא רבה Qua primùm tenui admodum lumine apparet, sed deinde veniendo crescit. Hierof. Beracot folio 1. cap.3.
units.tr: The redemption of Israel is like the dawn [בתחילה קיטאה קיטאה כל מה שהיא הולכת היא רבה]: at first it appears with very little light, but as it comes on it grows. Jerusalem Talmud, Berachot fol. 1, cap. 3.

units.la: §. Quando Israelitæ castrametabantur in longitudine & latitudine spatium 11. milliarum occuparunt. Targum Ionath. Num.11.2. Idem spatium exercitum tenuisse referunt, cum Iordanem transiret. Bab.Sotah sol.54.1. in Gloss.
units.tr: When the Israelites encamped, they occupied an area of 11 miles in length and breadth. Targum Jonathan on Num. 11.2. They are also reported to have held the same area when they crossed the Jordan. Babylonian Talmud, Sotah fol. 54.1, in the Gloss.

units.la: §. Tres sunt impudentes in Mundo, Israelita inter populos, Canis inter animantes, Gallus inter aves. Alii dicunt, Capra inter pecundes; צר (arbor quæ triplices fructus profert, ad Venerem excitandam idoneos Beracot 36. 1.) inter arboresBeza 25.12.
units.tr: There are three shameless creatures in the world: the Israelite among peoples, the dog among animals, and the cock among birds. Others say: the goat among cattle, and the tree [צר], which bears three kinds of fruit suitable for arousing lust, among trees. Berachot 36.1. Beza 25.12.

units.la: §. Tres pastores boni erant Israeli, Moses, Aaron, & Mirjam, & tria bona exhibita sunt per eorum manus. Fons & Nubes & Manna. Fons propter meritum Miriamæ. Columna nubis propter meritum Aaronis; & Manna כוכות משה per meritum Mosis.Taanit sol.9.1.
units.tr: Israel had three good ministers: Moses, Aaron and Miriam, and three good things were given through their hands: the well, the cloud and the manna. The well was given because of the merit of Miriam; the pillar of cloud because of the merit of Aaron; and the manna [כוכות משה] because of the merit of Moses. Taanit fol. 9.1.

units.la: §. De Israelitarum honoribus vid. Honores.
units.tr: §. On the honours of the Israelites, see Honours.

units.la: IMMARCALIN vid. אמרכדין in A.
units.tr: IMMARCALIN, see AMMARCADIN [אמרכדין] under A.

units.la: IMPOSITIO manuum seniorum סמיכת ידים (quâ vel potestatem iudicandi causas mulctatitias vel illam de qua Lev.4.13.15. mentio fit in aliquem contulerunt) non poterat nisi à tribus fieri. Sanhed.1.3. Neque poterat conferri nisi in terra Canaan, quamvis potestas per eam collata ultra eius fines se portigebat. Ibid. Gemara sol.14.col.2. Maymon Sanhed c. 4.
units.tr: The IMPOSITION of hands by the elders [סמיכת ידים], by which they conferred either the power of judging cases involving fines, or that power mentioned in Lev. 4.13, 15, upon someone, could be done only by three. Sanhed. 1.3. Nor could it be conferred except in the land of Canaan, although the power conferred by it extended beyond its borders. Ibid. Gemara, fol. 14, col. 2. Maymon Sanhed c. 4.

units.la: §. Romani in quadam persecutione contra Israelem sub pœna mortis prohibuerunt ne aliquis promoveret aut promotionem accipere-ret. Ico non considerato Baba Ben Butah quinque fecit presbyteros, sed deinde etiam miserè à militibus interfectus periit. Bab. Sanhed. sol.14. 1.
units.tr: During a certain persecution of Israel, the Romans forbade on pain of death that anyone should promote others or accept promotion. Rabbi Ben Batah, not considering this, ordained five elders, but was afterwards killed by soldiers and perished. Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin fol. 14.1.

units.la: §. Promotio duplex est; illa quæ manuum impositione fiebat, sicut fecit Moses Iosuæ Deut.xxxiv 9. Et illa quæ conceptis verbis sive sermone. Hac ratione Ego promoveo te Rabbinum: Ejlo promotus Magister Juchasin. sol 60.
units.tr: Promotion is twofold: that which was done by the imposition of hands, as Moses did to Joshua (Deut. 34.9), and that which is done by express words or speech. In this way: "I promote you as Rabbi"; "Be promoted as Master", Juchasin fol. 60.

units.la: §. Promotus quamdiu vixit promotor eius nominabatur הבר addito præceptoris vel promotoris nomine. Vt R.Simeon Ben Eliefer הבר R. Iehuda Sancti. Beracot 27. 2. Vid. etiam הבר in C.
units.tr: A man who was promoted was called, as long as his promoter lived, "son of" [הבר] with the name of his teacher or promoter added, as Rabbi Simeon ben Eliezer, "son of" Rabbi Judah the Holy. Berachot 27.2. See also [הבר] in C.

units.la: §. Olim omnes promoti promovêre poterant alios: Sed à temporibus Hillelis principis, nemo potest promovere nisi facultate acceptâ à Principe Synedrii magni. Hierof. Sanhed c.1. sol.19.1. Princeps Synedrii non potest promovere אלא אם כן היה אב בית דין עמו Nisi præsente patre Domus Iudicii (secundo à Principe.) Pater domus Iudicii quoque promovere non potest nisi ipsi adsit Princeps Synedrii. Alii vero qui promoti fuerunt, potestate à Principe accepta præsentibus duobus testibus promovere possunt. Si quis promovendus est, ambo promotor & promovendus in terra Israelitica esse debent; non autem necessario requiritur ut uno in loco sint, & ad promovendum sufficere potest, si promoveas scribit promovendo, illum esse סיוך promotum יש לסוכך לסבוך אפיל Promovêre etiam cen tum und vice promovêre possunt. David Rex 30000 unâ die promovit (id est potestatem iudicandi dedit.) Potestates possunt restringere; verbi gratia, possunt alicui dare potestatem solùm iudicandi,non autem dispensandi באסור והמותר in veritis & licitu: & vice versa. Sic etiam potestas promovendorum ad certum tempus restringi potest; v.g. tibi licet dispensare de votis, & de דיני קיסות Iudiciis multiplicatis iudicare quandiu in illa provincia versaberis; vel donec huc princeps Senatus Venerit &c. Maymon. Hal. Sanhed. c.4. vid. etiam de promotionis forma & ritibus Inchafin sol. 60. Abravanel cap.1. Avot. De Impositione manuum in Sacrificiis vid. Sacrificia. & Maym. in Corban. c. 3.
units.tr: Formerly all who had been promoted could promote others, but from the time of the prince Hillel onward, no one can promote except by permission received from the Prince of the great Sanhedrin. Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin cap. 1, fol. 19.1. The Prince of the Sanhedrin cannot promote [אלא אם כן היה אב בית דין עמו], unless the father of the house of judgment is with him present (this is the second case, under the Prince). The father of the house of judgment likewise cannot promote unless the Prince of the Sanhedrin is himself present. Others who have been promoted, having received the power from the Prince, can promote in the presence of two witnesses. If anyone is to be promoted, both the promoter and the one to be promoted must be in the land of Israel; but it is not strictly required that they be in one place, and it is enough for the promotion if the promoter writes that the one to be promoted is [סיוך], promoted. [יש לסוכך לסבוך אפיל] Promoters may also promote a hundred, and in turn be promoted. King David promoted 30,000 in one day (that is, he gave them the power of judging). Those who hold power can restrict it: for example, they may give someone the power only of judging, but not of dispensing [באסור והמותר], in forbidden and permitted things, and vice versa.
