units.tr: §. His coming will be unexpected. Sanhedrin, fol. 97a: "Three things come unawares: the Messiah, a found object, and the scorpion's sting" [הרעת כחסח]. The Messiah is called "bar nasheli" [בר נשלי] in Sanhedrin 96b, because his coming, both in the macrocosm and in the microcosm, will be when things are most collapsed. Indeed our Lord Jesus Christ came into this world when the affairs of the Jews were greatly weakened and their privileges taken away. Let us relate a few things that bear on this. In the time of Simeon the Just, who lived and flourished in the year of the world 3448, prophecy was taken away, as Yuchasin, fol. 15b, states expressly. The scapegoat on the Day of Atonement, cast down from the cliff, was no longer cut into pieces as before, but fled alive into the desert and was eaten by the Saracens. After the death of Simeon, the lot of God cast on the Day of Atonement no longer came up only for the right hand as before, but sometimes for the right and sometimes for the left. The western lamp was often extinguished, whereas before it had burned continually. The fire on the pile was not kept unless wood was supplied all day; the scarlet tongue sometimes turned white, and sometimes not. The blessing of the showbread was also taken away, for the priests were never satisfied with it, as had been the case before. Read more fully on these things in Jerusalem Yoma, fol. 43, col. 3. Shortly before the coming of Christ the number of murderers had so multiplied under that notorious brigand Ehesere son of Dinai (whom, for his crimes, they called the Murderer) that the beheading of the heifer (v.fl.) had to be abolished. Rabbi Johanan ben Zakkai would no longer permit wives suspected of adultery to be tested by the drinking of the waters, because the vice had so broken out that they could be neither punished, on account of the immense multitude, nor tested. With Jose son of Joezer the outstanding and pious men ceased. Purity being removed, fraud had taken away the taste and savour of fruits and tithes; fornication and sorcery had corrupted everything, including the richness of the grain. So you have the teachers confessing this in the most elegant tractate Sotah, last chapter. Let us add what is said in the Babylonian Sanhedrin, fol. 99a and 97a: "Rabbi Judah says: In that generation, when the son of David comes, the schools will be brothels, Galilee will be laid waste, Gablan will be destroyed, and the inhabitants of the land (the gloss: the Sanhedrin) will wander from city to city and will find no mercy; the wisdom of the scribes will be foul, those who fear sin will be despised, and the faces of that generation will be like the faces of dogs, and truth will fail," and so on. What, I ask, were not the dissensions between the Shammaites and the Hillelites, before and after the coming of Christ? What slaughters and robberies there were in the history of those forty years which ran from the death of Christ to the destruction of Jerusalem! (See Hillel.)

units.la: §. Secundùm Hierof.Beracot sol.5.1. Messias nasci debuit, statim post excidium urbis, quia post excidium denuntiatum Esai.x.33 34. Statim adiungitur Esai.xi.1. Orietur germen ēstirpe Iesse. Gemariastæ tamen loco citato non erubescunt fateri Messiam ante sua tempora natum esse Bethlehemæ; eorum verba adduxit in Hor. Heb. ad Matth. p. 23. Cl. Ligtfoot. De bello Gog & Magog immediatè adventum ipsius præcessuro vid. Berefch. Rabba sect. 41. Bab.Sanhed.sol.95.2. & sol.97.1. Cl. Leigtf. Ev. Mr.50.
units.tr: §. According to the Jerusalem Berakhot, fol. 5, col. 1: the Messiah ought to have been born immediately after the destruction of the city, because after the destruction Isaiah 10:33–34 is announced, and immediately joined to it is Isaiah 11:1: "There shall come forth a shoot out of the stem of Jesse." Nevertheless the Gemarists, in the passage cited, are not ashamed to confess that the Messiah was born at Bethlehem before their own times; Lightfoot cited their words in his Horae Hebraicae on Matthew, p. 23. On the war of Gog and Magog, which will immediately precede his coming, see Bereshit Rabba, sect. 41; Babylonian Sanhedrin, fol. 95b and 97a; Lightfoot on Mark, 50.

units.la: §. Doctrina Iudaica de adventu Messiæ porrò hæc tria ponit. 1. futuram tunc temporis resurrectionem iustorum מֵשִׁיחַ עָתִיד לְהַקִּיץ יְשֵׁנֵי עָפָר Messias resuscitabit dormientes in pulvere. Midrasch Tillin sol.42.1. Vid. etiam Bab. Sanhed.sol.92. ubi sic Glossa. Iusti quos suscitabit Deus à mortuis in diebus Messiæ, cum revixerint, non redibunt iterum in pulverem suum, nec in diebus Messiæ, nec infeculo consecuturo; sed caro eorum in ipsis est permansura, usquedum redeant & vivant לְבַד עֲתִיד in æternum. Et per iflos annos quibus renovaturus est Deus mundum suum, יְהִיה עוֹלָם זֶה חֹרֶב אֶלֶף שָׁנִים vastabitur mundus hic per mille annos, ubinam tandem per iflos annos erunt, iufli isti? Ex quibus 2. patet secundùm Iudæos, resurrectionem iustorum consecuturam Mundi huius desolationem. Et 3 post iflos mille annos æternitatem futuram. De hoc הבא עוֹלָם vid. in Formulis loq. disserit etiam de illa æternitate Tanchuma sol.9.2. Dicit S.Bened.Israeli, In hoc mundo vos timetis à transgressionibus, at in mundo futuro, feliciti eritis solùm de bono vobis reposito. Item sol.77.3. In hoc mundo nuntii mei fuerunt caro & sanguis ; at in mundo futuro ego mitto vobis nuntium meum &c.
units.tr: §. The Jewish doctrine concerning the coming of the Messiah further holds these three things. 1. That there will be a resurrection of the just at that time: "The Messiah will raise those who sleep in the dust" [מֵשִׁיחַ עָתִיד לְהַקִּיץ יְשֵׁנֵי עָפָר]. Midrash Tillim, fol. 42.1. See also Babylonian Sanhedrin, fol. 92, where the Gloss says: "The just whom God will raise from the dead in the days of the Messiah, when they have revived, will not return again to their dust, neither in the days of the Messiah nor in the age to come; but their flesh will remain in them until they return and live for ever" [לְבַד עֲתִיד]. And during those years in which God will renew his world, "this world will be laid waste for a thousand years" [יְהִיה עוֹלָם זֶה חֹרֶב אֶלֶף שָׁנִים]; where then, during those years, will these just ones be? From these points it is clear that, according to the Jews, (2) the resurrection of the just will follow the desolation of this world, and (3) after those thousand years there will be an eternity to come. On this "world to come" [הבא עוֹלָם] see in Formulae loquendi; he discusses that eternity also in Tanchuma, fol. 9.2: "The Holy One, blessed be he, says to Israel: In this world you fear transgressions, but in the world to come you will be happy only in the good laid up for you." Likewise, fol. 77.3: "In this world my messengers were flesh and blood; but in the world to come I send you my messenger, etc."

units.la: §. Restant adhuc alia de Messia referenda. Varia eius nomina legere potes in Bab.Sanhed. 98.2. Voisin in pug.fid.671. de eius excellentia sic loquitur Abarben. in c.53. Iesai. משיח ירום מאברהם נשא ממשה וגבה מאד ממלאכי שרת Messias exaltabitur pra Abrahamo, elevabitur pra Mose, & sublimis erit valde pra angelis ministerii. Haec deinde prolixe diducit. De doloribus eius plurima extant; propter illius infirmitates dicunt Magistri כי חוורתא דבי רב שמו Quod nomen eius sit leprosus e domo Rabbi. Bab. Sanhed. sol.98.2. Et paulo post, Quod si Messias sit e vivis, Rabbenu Hakkadosch (R. Iudah scil.) ille sit. Quia R. Iudah plurimis laboravit infirmitatibus vid, Hieros. Kilaim sol. 32.1. ibi enim inter alia dicitur, ipsum tredecim annos laborasse dolore dentium. Sanhed. sol.98.2. haec legimus. Dicit Vlla, adveniet Messias, sed non videbo eum i.e. Non videndus erit. Quare? משום חבלו של משיח Propter dolores Messiae. Gloss. חבלו i.e. terrores & dolores, qui erunt in diebus eius. Schabbat sol.118.1. Qui ter convivatur Sabbatho, liberabitur a tribus miseriis מחבלו של משיח a doloribus Messiae, a iudicio Gehennae & a bello Gog & Magog.
units.tr: §. Other things about the Messiah remain to be related. You may read his various names in Babylonian Sanhedrin, fol. 98.2; see Voisin in Pugio fidei, p. 671. Concerning his excellence Abarbanel, on Isaiah 53, speaks thus: "The Messiah will be exalted above Abraham, lifted up above Moses, and will be exceedingly sublime above the angels of ministry" [משיח ירום מאברהם נשא ממשה וגבה מאד ממלאכי שרת]. He then develops this at length. Much is recorded about his sorrows; on account of his infirmities the masters say "that his name is the leper of the house of Rabbi" [כי חוורתא דבי רב שמו], Babylonian Sanhedrin, fol. 98.2. And a little later: "If the Messiah is among the living, it is Rabbenu Hakkadosh (that is, Rabbi Judah)." Because Rabbi Judah suffered many infirmities, see Jerusalem Kilayim, fol. 32.1; for there, among other things, it is said that he suffered for thirteen years from toothache. In Sanhedrin, fol. 98.2, we read this: "Ulla says: The Messiah will come, but I shall not see him," that is, he will not be seen. Why? "Because of the pangs of the Messiah" [משום חבלו של משיח]. The Gloss: "pangs" [חבלו], that is, terrors and sorrows which will be in his days. Shabbat, fol. 118.1: "He who is feasted three times on the Sabbath will be delivered from three miseries: from the pangs of the Messiah [מחבלו של משיח], from the judgment of Gehenna, and from the war of Gog and Magog."

units.la: §. Messias plurimum in monte oliveti versabitur. Midrasch Tillim. per tres annos & dimidium, fieri שכינה in monte oliveti, & praedicavit. &c. De afflictionibus tempore Messiae sic loquitur Moses Alschech in Iesai. 52. 13. In
units.tr: §. The Messiah will dwell very much on the Mount of Olives. Midrash Tillim: "For three and a half years the Shekhinah will be on the Mount of Olives, and he will preach, etc." Concerning the afflictions in the time of the Messiah, Moses Alshech, on Isaiah 52:13, speaks thus: "In

units.la: Mundo sunt tres afflictionum triades, prima Davidi & Patriarchis contigit, secunda seculo excisionis, i.e. hodierna Iudaorum captivitati; tertia seculo Messiae. Etiam pauperes futuri erunt in diebus Messiae. Bab. Schabbat fol. 63. Non est discrimen inter hunc mundum & dies Messiae אלא שעבוד מלכיות Nisi quoad afflictionem regnorum Ethnicorum; sicut dicitur Deut. xv. ii. Non deerit pauper e medio terra, R. Salom. & Aben Esra, si obedieveris verbis Domini, non erit in te pauper, at non obedies, ergo nunquam deerit. Confer haec Marci 14. 7. de Messia vid. Hal. Melach. c.12 De Messia veniente super Afinum vid. Afinum.
units.tr: the world there are three triads of afflictions: the first befell David and the patriarchs, the second the age of the excision, that is, the present captivity of the Jews, and the third the age of the Messiah." The poor will also be in the days of the Messiah. Shabbat, fol. 63: "There is no difference between this world and the days of the Messiah except [the subjection of the kingdoms of the Gentiles]" [אלא שעבוד מלכיות], as it is said in Deuteronomy 15:11, "The poor will never cease out of the land". Rabbi Solomon and Aben Ezra: "If you obey the words of the LORD, there will be no poor among you; but if you do not obey, then the poor will never cease." Compare Mark 14:7 on the Messiah. See Hilchot Melachim, ch. 12. On the Messiah coming upon an ass, see Asinus.

units.tr: Harvest: see Agriculture and Sowing.

units.tr: Measure: see Schedas.

units.tr: Metatron: see the illustrious Buxtorf, Lexicon Talmudicum, p. 1192.

units.la: מגדל Migdal vid. Magdala.
units.tr: Migdal [מגדל]: see Magdala.

units.la: למעוטי Limgnute, Significat oppositè; ut in Comment. Maym. ad Peah cap.1.4. בשמר המקר למעוטי custoditum dicitur oppositè ad id quod publici iuris est. Vid. etiam Hal. Rozeach cap.II. למה נאמר גנך למעט כתי כנסיות Cur dicitur tectum tuum? oppositè ad tecta Synagogarum. Haec observatiuncula ad intelligentiam plurimorum locorum proderit.
units.tr: Limmu'ute [למעוטי] signifies "in contrast"; as in Maimonides' commentary on Peah, ch. 1.4: "What is guarded [בשמר המקר] is said in contrast to what is of public right." See also Hilchot Rotzeach, ch. 2: "Why is it said 'your roof' [גנך]? In contrast to the roofs of the synagogues [גגי כנסיות]." This small observation will help in understanding many passages.

units.la: Milliare vid. Mensurationes.
units.tr: Mile; see Measurements.

units.la: Ministri. נפל ביתא חבל לכוותא Si cadat domus ve feneftris. Ad varios usus poteft applicari, sed praecipuè Ministris, in luctuosissimis reipublicae ruinis, haec lumina pessimè tractantur. Ialkut in Exod. 75.3.
units.tr: Ministers. If a house or a window falls [נפל ביתא חבל לכוותא]. This may be applied to various uses, but it is especially applicable to ministers: in the most lamentable ruins of the commonwealth, these lights are very badly treated. Yalkut on Exodus 75.3.

units.la: Miracula, mira. Vid. Magia.
units.tr: Miracles, wonders. See Magic.

units.la: מלכות
units.tr: Kingdom [מלכות].

units.la: Malcujoth sunt quædam formulæ quas precibus inserunt. Vid. Hierof. Beracot p.3. col.4. linea 58.& pag.4.Col.1.l.4.Talm. Babyl. Rosch Hafchana c. ult. de formula recipere in se iugum שים מלכות Regni cœlorum vid. Beracot c.2.2. & Formulæ loq.
units.tr: Malcujoth are certain formulas that they insert into prayers. See Jerusalem Berakhot p. 3, col. 4, line 58, and p. 4, col. 1, line 4; Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah, last chapter, on the formula of taking upon oneself the yoke of the kingdom of heaven [שים מלכות]. See Berakhot ch. 2.2 and Formulae loq.

units.la: vel מודיעית est definiente Rafchi כיך locus munitus distans Hierosolymis 15. milliaribus. Chagigah c. 3.5. Cives urbis Modaith, dum intra civitatem sunt, creduntur esse נאמנים observatores puritatis in vasis fictilibus, dum extra sunt, non item.
units.tr: Or Modaith (מודיעית), as Rashi defines it, is a fortified place fifteen miles distant from Jerusalem [כיך]. Chagigah ch. 3.5. The citizens of the town of Modaith, while they are within the city, are believed to be trustworthy observers of purity regarding earthenware vessels; when they are outside, they are not.

units.la: De eo vid. Selden. de Diis Syris 166. Kirch.Oedip. 1.32.8.Lud.de Dieu Act.7.43.Quando patres illi infantem unum sacrificarunt, sibi imaginabantur reliquos liberos hoc sacrificio a morte ereptos iri, seque tota vita futuros progenitores. Bechai Lev.18. Qui Molecho semen suum dat, lapidationis non fit reus, nisi & per ignem traduxerit, nam si alterum tantum secerit, evadit hanc pœnam. Sanhed c.7.7.
units.tr: On this see Selden, De Diis Syris 166; Kircher, Oedipus 1.32.8; Ludovicus de Dieu on Acts 7.43. When those fathers sacrificed a single infant, they imagined that the other children would be saved from death by this sacrifice, and that they themselves would be the progenitors of the whole of their lives. Bechai on Leviticus 18. He who gives his seed to Molech is not liable to stoning unless he has also passed the child through fire; for if he has done only the one, he escapes this penalty. Sanhedrin ch. 7.7.

units.la: parva vocatur apud Iudæos פרוטה, estque vel ex argento vel ex ære. Kidduschin c.2.1. Pondus Pruta est dimidii grani hordacei. Maymon Hal. Schekalim c.1. Ad שמין Schemin faciendum requiritur Pruta duplex, Kiddusch. f.12.1. (unde constat Siclum valere quatuor Dinarim sive drachmas; דינר Dinar 6. מעה qui faciunt 12. פונדיונין, qui faciunt 24. Assaria, qui faciunt 48. מוסמיסין, qui faciunt 96. קונדרינק, qui faciunt 192 Prutas, qui numerus per 24. Assaria divisus, invenitur unum assarium valere 8 Pruta.) Si quis exigat mutuum licet ipse sit dives, & qui multa debet pauperrimus,tamen in iudicio non miserentur eius, sed exigunt ab eo debitum אחרונה עד פרוטה Vsq; ad ultimum Denarium. (Confer Matth. 5. 26.) Maim. Hal. Malveh cap.1.4.
units.tr: The small coin is called among the Jews pruta (פרוטה), and is either of silver or of bronze. Kiddushin ch. 2.1. The weight of a pruta is half a barley grain. Maimonides, Hilkhot Shekalim ch. 1. For making a shemin (שמין) a double pruta is required (Kiddushin f. 12.1); whence it is clear that a shekel is worth four dinarim or drachmas, a dinar six ma'ah, which make twelve pundiones, which make twenty-four assaria, which make forty-eight mosmisin, which make ninety-six kondrinak, which make 192 prutot; this number, divided by twenty-four assaria, shows that one assarion is worth eight prutot. If anyone demands a loan, even though he himself is rich, and the debtor is very poor, they nevertheless do not show him mercy in judgment, but exact the debt from him down to the last pruta (עד פרוטה), that is, to the last penny. (Compare Matthew 5.26.) Maimonides, Hilkhot Malveh ch. 1.4.

units.la: §. De Argento Sacro & provinciali vid. Argentum. De Siclis & Denariis vid. etiam f.1. de nummis in genere quaedam dixit Doft. Leusdenius Phil. Mix. p 196. In tribus rebus homo cognoscitur, in loculo suo, in poculo suo, & in ira sua. Erubbin sol. 65. col. 2. Tria gravia sunt corpori. Vulnus cordis durum est; dolor viscerum gravius: omnium autem molestissimum est defectus nummorum. Midrasch Cohelet cap.7.27.
units.tr: §. On sacred and provincial silver see Argentum. On shekels and denarii see also f. 1. Concerning coins in general, Dr. Leusden in Philologus Mixtus p. 196 has said some things. "A man is known by three things: by his purse, by his cup, and by his anger." Erubin fol. 65, col. 2. "Three things are heavy for the body: a wound to the heart is hard, pain in the bowels is heavier; but of all, the most troublesome is the lack of money." Midrash Qohelet ch. 7.27.

units.la: §. Habebant monetam non signatam quam vocant אסימון quasi ἀσημον. De ea loquuntur in Bava Metzia cap. 4. ab init. in Maaser Scheni cap.1. ab init. De Assario אסר loqui,habebant in usu, quando de minori ad maius argumentabantur; exemplum est in Cholin cap.ult. in Mischna ad verba Deut.22.6. Si in praecepto levissimo שהיא באיסור quod vix assarii est (quod de re minimi pretii agit) adjicit scriptura hanc promissionem, ut bene sit tibi & prolonges dies, quanto magis valebit hoc de praeceptis gravioribus quae sunt in lege? Confer Matth.10.29. De hac nummi specie vid. Talm. Kidduschin in princip. Bava Metzia sol.44.2. Waserum de nummis Hebraeorum lib.2.23. Notas Tremellii ad Marci 12. 42.
units.tr: §. They had uncoined money, which they called asimon, as if from ἀσημον. They speak of it in Bava Metzia ch. 4, at the beginning, and in Maaser Sheni ch. 1, at the beginning. They used the assar (אסר) when they argued from the lesser to the greater; an example is in the last chapter of Chullin, in the Mishnah, on the words of Deuteronomy 22.6: if Scripture attaches this promise, that it may go well with you and you may prolong your days, to a commandment of the very lightest kind (one which is scarcely worth an assarion, and so deals with a thing of the smallest value), how much more will this hold for the weightier precepts that are in the law? Compare Matthew 10.29. On this kind of coin see the Talmud, Kiddushin at the beginning, and Bava Metzia fol. 44.2; Wasserus, De nummis Hebraeorum lib. 2.23; the notes of Tremellius on Mark 12.42.

units.la: §. Siclus erat duplex Provincialis & Ecclesiasticus; Politicus sive Provincialis, erat duarum drachmarum; Ecclesiasticus sive templi erat drachmarum quatuor; Drachma Heb. aliquando vocatur שקל aliquando דינר dimidia Drachma איסתרא גריגא vocatur איסתרא Græcè σταμνος. (Ketubb. sol.64.2. Vid. notas Tremellii Matth.17.24.) Erat insuper Monetæ species quæ vocabatur בר־דייקש Menach. sol.29.1. Illi nummi qui appellabantur דרבנות vel דרכמנות erant aurei, usitati ante exilium Babylonicum, tempore Davidis : valor ipsorum erat שני סלעים unius Taleri vel Imperialis Gloss. in Schekalim cap.2. sol.3. quoniam obligabantur provinciales singulis annis magnam summam siclorum Hierosolymam deferre, hoc autem propter onus incommodum esset, à Magistris permissum est, ut siclos permutarent in Darbonoth, maioris commoditatis causâ. Mishna in Schekalim l. m. c. קפס quando in Sacra Scriptura absolutè ponitur denotat Siclum: ita illud expositum Onkelos Genes.xx.16. Sed sicuti hoc verum, ita falsum, קפס in Prophetiis libram, in Hagiographiis Centenarium designare, ut volunt Gemar. ad Bechorot sol.50.
units.tr: §. The shekel was of two kinds, provincial and ecclesiastical. The political or provincial shekel was of two drachmas; the ecclesiastical or temple shekel was of four drachmas. The Hebrew drachma is sometimes called shekel, sometimes dinar; a half drachma is called istara griga (איסתרא גריגא), in Greek σταμνος. (Ketubot fol. 64.2; see the notes of Tremellius on Matthew 17.24.) There was besides a species of coin called bar-daiqash (בר־דייקש). Menachot fol. 29.1. Those coins called darbonot or darkemanot were gold, in use before the Babylonian exile, in the time of David; their value was two selaim, that is, one thaler or imperial. Gloss on Shekalim ch. 2, fol. 3. Since the provincials were obliged each year to bring a great sum of shekels to Jerusalem, and this would be an inconvenient burden, the Masters permitted them to exchange their shekels for darbonot, for the sake of greater convenience. Mishnah in Shekalim, loc. cit. When the word (כסף) stands absolutely in Holy Scripture it denotes a shekel; so Onkelos expounded it at Genesis 20.16. But just as this is true, so it is false that it designates a pound in the Prophets and a centenarium in the Hagiographa, as the Gemara on Bekhorot fol. 50 maintains.

units.la: Priscorum Patrum númi vocabantur קשיטה, ab impressa figura agni; de iis prolixè disserit Cl.Heideggerus in ראשי אבו. In Talmud. sic inquiunt. Quando iter feci in Africam היו קורין למעה קשיטה audivi quod nummum vocarint קשיטה: ex quo hunc fructum habemus. Gen.33.19. Centum קשיטה esse centum nummos. Vid. Bereschb. Rabba. sect. 79. in fine.
units.tr: The coins of the ancient Fathers were called qeshita (קשיטה), from the figure of a lamb stamped upon them. Cl. Heidegger discusses these at length in Rashei Abu. In the Talmud they say thus: "When I made a journey into Africa, I heard that they called a ma'ah a qeshita; from which we have this fruit," (Genesis 33.19), that a hundred qeshitot are a hundred coins. See Bereshit Rabba, sect. 79, at the end.

units.la: §. מעה Rabbinorum respondet Biblico גרה quod obolus redditur. Siclus pendebat viginti Geras sive מעין. Denarius sex מעין. Meah sedecim grana hordei sive quatuor אסרים. Gerali sive Meah collata ad nostram monetam valuit quasi dimidium Baẑium. Vid. R. Salomoh Lev. 27.25. Maymon Maaser Scheni c.4. Kidduschin f.12.1. Bechorot f.50.1. Vid. etiam Waserum de nummis Heb. lib.2.19. פולי Græcè folleralis erat monetæ parvæ species, & respondet Latinorum Teruntio; de eo fit mentio in Hieros. Peah cap. 1. & Berefchit Rabba sect. 49. פונקיין etiam obolus verti potest; in siclo erant 48. פונדיונין vid. Rabbi Salomoh Lev.17.18. Bechorot f.37.2. Kelim c.17. Maymon in Peah c.ult. Consule de his etiam Cl. Buxt. Lex.Talm. p.2449. ad rad. שמן vel שמין.
units.tr: §. The rabbinic ma'ah (מעה) corresponds to the biblical gerah (גרה), which is rendered obolus. The shekel weighed twenty gerot, or ma'in (מעין). The denarius was six ma'in. A meah is sixteen grains of barley, or four asarim. The gerali or meah, compared with our money, was worth about half a batzen (baẑium). See R. Solomon on Leviticus 27.25; Maimonides, Maaser Sheni ch. 4; Kiddushin f. 12.1; Bekhorot f. 50.1. See also Wasserus, De nummis Hebr. lib. 2.19. Pouli (פולי), in Greek follaris, was a kind of small coin, and corresponds to the Latins' teruncius; mention of it is made in the Jerusalem Talmud, Peah ch. 1, and Bereshit Rabba sect. 49. Punqiin (פונקיין) may also be rendered obolus; in a shekel there were 48 pundiones. See Rabbi Solomon on Leviticus 17.18; Bekhorot f. 37.2; Kelim ch. 17; Maimonides on Peah, last chapter. On these, consult also Buxtorf, Lex. Talm. p. 2449, under the root שמן or שמין.

units.la: §. Quatuor sunt quorum Moneta in mundum exiit: Abraham, Iosua, David, & Mardochæus. Berefch. Rabba sect.39. Nummus Mardochæi ex una parte habuit saccum & pulverem, ex altera coronam auream vel secundum Medrasch Ester sub finem, מרדכי מכאן ואסתר מכאן Mardochai erat ex una parte, & Esther erat ex parte altera.
units.tr: §. Four are those whose coins went out into the world: Abraham, Joshua, David and Mordecai. Bereshit Rabba sect. 39. The coin of Mordecai had on one side a sack and dust, and on the other a golden crown; or, according to Midrash Esther near the end, "Mordecai was on this side, and Esther was on that side" (מרדכי מכאן ואסתר מכאן).

units.la: §. D.N.I.Christus Matth.22.20. insidiis quæstionis propositæ respondet ex ipsa Magistrorum determinatione, quæ exstat apud Maymon in Gezela cap.5. Ubicunque numisma Regis alicuius obtinet, illic incola Regem istum pro Domino agnoscunt. Illudque probatur exemplo Abigailis in Hieros.Sanhed.sol.20.2. Dixit Abigail Davidi, Quidnam ego mali feci, vel filii mei, vel pecora mea? Respondit ille, Maritus tuus regnum Davidis vilipendit. Tune ergo, inquit illa, Rex es? (ut ille, Nonne Samuel me unxit in Regem? Respondit illa עדיין מונטא דמרן שאול קיים Numisma Domini nostri Saulis adhuc obtinet, quasi diceret. Nonne Saul pro rege est habendus, cùm numisma eius vulgò adhuc apud omnes recipiatur.
units.tr: §. Our Lord Jesus Christ (Matthew 22.20), in answer to the snare of the question put to him, replies from the very determination of the Masters, which is found in Maimonides, Gezelah ch. 5: "Wherever the coin of some king is current, there the inhabitants acknowledge that king as their lord." And this is proved by the example of Abigail in Jerusalem Sanhedrin fol. 20.2. Abigail said to David: "What evil have I done, or my son, or my flocks?" He replied: "Your husband despises David's kingdom." "Then," said she, "are you king?" (as if to say: "Has not Samuel anointed me king?"). She replied: "The coin of our lord Saul still stands" (עדיין מונטא דמרן שאול קיים), as if she were saying: "Is not Saul to be regarded as king, since his coin is still commonly received by everyone?"

units.la: Monoceros non intravit in arcam Noachi, sed catuli eius intraverunt. R. Nehemiah dicit, nec ipse nec catuli eius intraverunt, verùm Noachus eum alligavit ad arcam, atque is sulcavit sulcos in undis tantùm quantum spatii est, à Tiberiade ad Sufitham. (i.e. xxx. Stad. quæ est Mensura Ioseph. in vit. sua. Berefch. Rabba fect. 3. 1.
units.tr: The unicorn did not enter Noah's ark, but its whelps did. R. Nehemiah says that neither it nor its whelps entered; rather Noah tied it to the ark, and it furrowed the waves as far as the distance from Tiberias to Sufitha (that is, thirty stadia, which is the measure of Josephus in his Life). Bereshit Rabba sect. 3.1.

units.la: Montes varii. Mons Moriah ita vocatur secundùm R. Levi שיצא ממנו הוראה לישראל Quòd inde prodiret instructio Israeli. Secundùm R. Chaninah verò שמורא לאומות העולם Quod inde prodiret timor nationibus Mundi. Bab. Taanith sol.16.1.
units.tr: Various mountains. Mount Moriah is so called, according to R. Levi, "because instruction went out from it to Israel" (שיצא ממנו הוראה לישראל); but according to R. Chanina, "because fear went out from it to the nations of the world" (שמורא לאומות העולם). Babylonian Taanith fol. 16.1.

units.la: Communis Traditio est, locum ubi David condidit altare in area Araunæ, fuisse locum ubi suum condidit Abrahamus cùm ligaret Isaacum; ubi suum condidit Noachus, cùm egrederetur ex arca. Item ibi creatum esse Adamum, ibi sacrificasse Cainum & Abelem. Maymon in Beth Habech.cap.2. Iuchasin sol.9.1. Midrasch Tillim sol.41.2. Meritò itaque huic loco etiam inædificatum fuit sanctuarium.
units.tr: It is the common tradition that the place where David built an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah was the place where Abraham built his altar when he bound Isaac, and where Noah built his altar when he came out of the ark. Likewise Adam was created there, and Cain and Abel offered sacrifices there. Maimonides in Beth Habechirah ch. 2. Yuchasin f. 9.1. Midrash Tillim f. 41.2. Rightly, therefore, a sanctuary was also built on this place.

units.la: §. Mons Moriah ita situs erat, ut civitas, theatri instar, templum ambiret. Ioseph. Antiq. lib. 5. c.14. locus ubi templi ædificia exstructa erant vocatur à Rabbinis הר הבית Mons templi; in specie autem illo nomine designant atrium gentium.(Vid.atria.)Mons ille templi erat quadraturæ quingentorum cubitorum. Middot c. 2. v.1. Maymon.Beth Habech.cap.2. Mons Moriah per totum spatium atriorum erat excavatus יהוה כניות וכיפין עלגבי הין Et tota area erat arcubus & columnis sustentata, ne ullo modo intra sacrum hoc spatium fieret sepulcrum, à quo populus vel sacra contaminari possent. Vide loca modò cit.
units.tr: Mount Moriah was so situated that the city surrounded the temple like a theatre. Josephus, Antiquities book 5, ch. 14. The place where the temple buildings stood is called by the rabbis "the Mount of the House" (Mons templi); by that name they designate especially the atrium gentium (the court of the Gentiles; see "courts"). That Mount of the Temple was a square of five hundred cubits. Middot ch. 2, v. 1. Maimonides, Beth Habechirah ch. 2. Throughout the whole extent of the courts Mount Moriah was hollowed out: Et tota area erat arcubus et columnis sustentata, so that by no means could a tomb be made within this sacred space, by which the people or the holy things might be defiled. See the places just cited.

units.la: §. Montem טוורום Taurus Ionathan ponit pro monte הור in quo fato suo functus est Aharon. Vocatur etiam Taurus Vinarum & ponitur in finibus Idumææ Vid. Plinium lib.5. c.52. Jonathan Num.34.7.8.11.
units.tr: Jonathan renders the "Taurus" as the mountain Hor, on which Aaron died. It is also called Taurus Vinarum (the Taurus of the Vines) and is placed on the borders of Idumaea. See Pliny, book 5, ch. 52. Jonathan on Num. 34:7-8, 11.

units.la: §. Mons Hermon vocatur à Talmud. טור תלגות Interpres Samaritanus Deut.iv. 48. טבר תלגא etiam ad Hermonem refert. Hierof. Sanhed. sol.28.4. Exstruxerunt filiabus Midianitarum craticulas à Beth Ieschimon, usque ad montem nivis. Vid.in Jonath.Num.xxxiv.11.
units.tr: The Talmud calls Mount Hermon "Tur Telgot" (the mountain of snows). The Samaritan interpreter on Deut. 4:48 also refers the phrase "Tabar Telga" (טבר תלגא) to Hermon. Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin f. 28.4: Exstruxerunt filiabus Midianitarum craticulas a Beth Ieschimon usque ad montem nivis. (They built lattices for the daughters of Midian from Beth Yeshimon up to the mountain of snow.) See Jonathan on Num. 34:11.

units.la: §. De Monte Oliveti V. Oliveti montem. De Monte Amorrhæo vid. Mappas.
units.tr: On the Mount of Olives, see "Olivet, Mount." On Mount Amorrhaeus, see "Mappas."

units.la: §. Quamvis Iudæa hic illic montibus plurimum extumuerit, præcipua tamen eius extuberatio emicuit in dorso montium, lato admodum, & excurrente ab ultima ora Australi ad Hebronem usque, ad ipsas fere Hierosolymas, quæ à sacra pagina הר יהודה ὄρεσιν Ἰουδὰ vocatur, Ioh.xxi.11. Luc.1.39. à Talmudicis verò הר המלך Mons Regalis in Hierof.Scheviit f.38.4. Quodnam est montanum Iudææ? Mons Regalis. Ratio huius Etymologiæ non ita est promptu, nisi forte Regalis dictus est, quia Regia familia Davidis, ex Hebrone montis huius oppido, oriunda eft.
units.tr: Although Judaea has risen high here and there with mountains, its chief elevation stands out in the broad ridge of the hills, which runs from the southern border up to Hebron and almost to Jerusalem itself. Scripture calls it "the hill country of Judah" (הר יהודה, ὄρεσιν Ἰουδά; Josh. 21:11; Luke 1:39). The Talmudists call it "the Royal Mountain" (הר המלך, Mons Regalis), as in Jerusalem Talmud, Sheviit f. 38.4: Quodnam est montanum Iudaeae? Mons Regalis. (What is the mountain country of Judaea? The Royal Mountain.) The reason for this etymology is not readily apparent, unless perhaps it was called "Royal" because the royal family of David came from Hebron, a town of this mountain.

units.la: §. Loca in quibus de Monte Regali mentio fit, ob ingentem multitudinem ita accumulare non licet. Iuvat pauca adduxiffe.
units.tr: The passages in which the Royal Mountain is mentioned are too numerous to gather together in this way; it is useful to adduce a few.

units.la: Habebat Debora Pulverem album (argillam figulinam) in monte Regis בטר מלכא Chald. Paraph. in Iud.iv.5. In diebus R. Hofchaiae, ambierunt quidam immunitatem montis regalis, à quibusdam decimis. Hierof. Demai fol. 24. 4. R. Simeon habuit vineam כהר הטלך in monte Regali. Hierof. Avoda Zarah fol.40.2. R.Chaja, R. Iffai, & R. Immai afcenderunt in montem Regalem &c. Hierof. Avoda Zarah fol.44.4. Myrias urbium exftitit in monte Regali, de quibus mille poffedit R. Eliefer Ben Harfum. Hierof. Taanith fol.69.1. Et tamen non obftante illa multitudine villarum Pfal.lxxv.6. Mons Regalis vocatur מרבר הריח desertum montium, quia hæc regio erat afperior & incultior. Rex Iannai habuit in monte regali fexaginta myriades urbium, & in unaquaque erat numerus æqualis exeuntibus ex Ægypto. Bab. Gittin fol.57.1. Eft לשון גנוא Hyperbole, & ingens incolarum multitudo innuitur. Caufa devaftationis montis Regalis erat, quia in celebratione quarundam Nuptiarum milites Romani Sponfi Gallum & Gallinam (vid. Nuptias) fuftulerant. Gittin ubi fup. שור שעיון Mons Simeonitidis produxit 300. utres fruftulorum panis pauperibus unaquaque feptimana. Devaftatus fuit ob fcortationem. Hierof. Taanith fol. 69.1.
units.tr: Deborah had white dust (potter's clay) on the royal mountain (Chaldee Paraphrast on Judg. 4:5, בטר מלכא). In the days of R. Hoshaiah, some sought exemption on the royal mountain from certain tithes (Jerusalem Demai f. 24.4). R. Simeon had a vineyard on the royal mountain (Jerusalem Avodah Zarah f. 40.2). R. Chaja, R. Iffai and R. Immai went up to the royal mountain, etc. (Jerusalem Avodah Zarah f. 44.4). There were a myriad of cities on the Royal Mountain, of which R. Eliezer ben Harsum owned a thousand (Jerusalem Taanith f. 69.1). And yet, notwithstanding that multitude of villages, the Royal Mountain is called "the desert of the mountains" (מדבר הרים), because this region was rougher and less cultivated. King Jannai had sixty myriads of cities on the Royal Mountain, and in each there was a number equal to those who came out of Egypt (Babylonian Gittin f. 57.1). This is hyperbole, indicating a huge multitude of inhabitants. The cause of the devastation of the Royal Mountain was that at the celebration of certain weddings Roman soldiers had carried off the bridegroom's cock and hen (see "Weddings"). In Gittin, loc. cit., the Mount of Simeonitis (שור שעיון) produced three hundred skins of bread crumbs for the poor each week. It was laid waste on account of fornication (Jerusalem Taanith f. 69.1).

units.la: MORBI. Morbus ille quo pervertitur & contorquetur corpus ut in epilepticis vocatur יוזין vid.Gloss. in Midrasch Cohelet cap.1. v.8. Ialkut part.1.sol.27.col.2. Dyssenteriam vocant כורדס: Dyssentericum non visitant (consolandi causâ) neque etiam recordantur nominis eius, (est enim morbus impurus.) Nedarim sol.41.2. Tres moriuntur interea dum adhuc loquuntur; aegrotantes יין מעי חולי Morbo cholico, חיה puerpera והדריקון & Hydrope affectus. Erubbin cap.4. ab init. Hydrops est signum singularis alicuius transgressionis. Schabbat sol.33.1. Apud Rabbinos passio vulgaris & momentanea vocatur שיחו; dolor quiabit & redit,ut dolor dentium nominatur כאב: Morbus verò inveteratus & difficilis est חלי Schabbat sol.11. Col.1. Decem res reducunt aegrotantem לחליו ad morbum suum, redduntque morbum graviorem, nempe Esus carnis bubulae, caro pinguis, caro assata, caro avicularum, ovum assatum, tonsio capillorum, lac, caseus, balneum & שיחלים five ficus immatura. Beracot f.57.2. Signum bonum pro aegroto est sternutatio, sudor, Diarrhaea, somnus, somnia, Gonorrhaea. Ialkut in leg.f.10. 1.
units.tr: DISEASES. The illness by which the body is twisted and contorted, as in epileptics, is called יוזין (see the gloss on Midrash Qohelet ch. 1, v. 8; Yalkut part 1, f. 27, col. 2). Dysentery they call כורדס. Dyssentericum non visitant (for the sake of consolation) neque etiam recordantur nominis eius (they neither visit a dysenteric person nor even mention his name), for it is an unclean disease. Nedarim f. 41.2. Three die while they are still speaking: one suffering from Morbo cholico (colic), a woman in childbirth, puerpera, and one Hydrope affectus (afflicted with dropsy). Erubin ch. 4, beginning. Dropsy is a sign of some particular transgression. Shabbat f. 33.1. Among the rabbis a common and momentary ailment is called שיחו; a pain that comes and goes, such as toothache, is called כאב; but a long-standing and difficult disease is called חלי. Shabbat f. 11, col. 1. Ten things bring the sick man back to his illness and make the illness worse: namely, eating beef, fatty meat, roast meat, the flesh of birds, a roasted egg, cutting the hair, milk, cheese, bathing, and שיחלים, that is, an unripe fig. Berakot f. 57.2. A good sign for a sick man is sneezing, sweating, diarrhoea, sleep, dreams, and gonorrhoea. Yalkut on the Law, f. 10.1.

units.la: §. Synanche vel angina erat morbus satis notus apud priscos, invadebat autem praecipue infantes die 4. nativitatis ipsorum, quare etiam parentes eo die instituebant ieiunia, ne scilicet ea infantes invaderet.Schabbat sol.27.2. apud R.Salom. de hoc morbo etiam mentio fit in Berachot sol.8.1. & sol.40.1. Schabbat f.33.1. Fabulantur in Bava Bathra sol.16.2. Abrahamum Patriarcham gestasse in collo lapidem pretiosum, quem cum aegrotus aspiceret statim convaconvulsit. At cùm moreretur Abraham, Deus lapidem istum impositit sphæræ solis; inde natum proverbium, Levato sole, levatur morbus.
units.tr: Synanche, or quinsy, was a disease well known to the ancients. It attacked especially infants on the fourth day after their birth, and for this reason parents also appointed fasts on that day, lest it attack the infants (Shabbat f. 27.2, according to R. Solomon). Mention of this disease is also made in Berakot f. 8.1 and f. 40.1, and Shabbat f. 33.1. In Bava Bathra f. 16.2 they fable that the patriarch Abraham wore a precious stone around his neck, which, whenever a sick man looked at it, immediately made him convulse. But when Abraham died, God placed that stone on the sphere of the sun. Hence the proverb: Levato sole, levatur morbus (when the sun rises, the disease is lifted).

units.la: §. In Babylonia non erant ulcerosi, quia ibi edebant blitum vel betam, & bibebant siceram veprium, id est ex lupulis confectam (de la biere) Ketubbot sol.77.2. Viginti quatuor מוכי שיחין percussi ulcere Ægyptiaco sunt, quibus gravis erit coitus, gravissimum autem ulcerum genus est quod vocant ראתן. Ketubbot ubi supra & Vajikra Rabba sect.16.
units.tr: In Babylon there were no people with ulcers, because they ate beet or chard and drank a beer made from hops (de la bière) (Ketubot f. 77.2). Twenty-four kinds of those percussi ulcere Aegyptiaco (struck with the Egyptian ulcer) will find intercourse painful, and the most grievous kind of ulcer is called ראתן. Ketubot, loc. cit., and Vayikra Rabba sect. 16.

units.la: §. De Morbis vid. Medicum. & Ægrotum.
units.tr: On diseases, see "Physician" and "Sick person."

units.la: MORS. Horâ illâ quâ iustus solvit ex hoc mundo,trium angelorum ministrantium כיתות Chori obviam illi procedunt. Primus dicit Ingreditur pacem. Secundus quisquis ambulat in integritate sua. Tertius, ingredientur pacem, requiescent. Iuchafin sol.60. Mortis sunt 903. genera; placidissimum est illud הנשיקה Osculi, quo mortuus est Moses,(Beracot f.8.1.) gravissimum vero mors per אסכרה Anginam, (vid. morbi.) Schab.f.27.2. §.Si quis moritur repente vocatur חשופה, si ægrotet per unum diem & moriatur, est כיתה רחוב, si per duos dies, & moriatur est מיתה דחויה; Si per tres dies est גערה, per quatuor נויפה, per 5. מיתה כל ארם Est Mors communis. Si quis moriatur intra 50.annos,est מותה כרת Mors excidii. Intra 52. est mors Sam.Prophetæ. Anno 60. est מיתה כידי שמים Mors per manus Dei. Anno septuagesimo est שיבה Senectus; anno 80. est גבורה Robur. Moed Katon f.28.1.
units.tr: DEATH. At the hour when the righteous man departs from this world, three companies of ministering angels come to meet him. The first says, Ingreditur pacem (he enters into peace); the second, quisquis ambulat in integritate sua (whoever walks in his integrity); the third, ingredientur pacem, requiescent (they shall enter into peace, they shall rest). Yuchasin f. 60. There are 903 kinds of death. The most placid is the death by kiss (הנשיקה, Osculi), by which Moses died (Berakot f. 8.1); the most grievous is death by quinsy (Anginam; see "Diseases"). Shabbat f. 27.2. If someone dies suddenly it is called חשופה; if he is sick for one day and dies, it is כיתה רחוב; if for two days, it is מיתה דחויה; if for three days, it is גערה; for four, נויפה; for five, it is the death of every man (Est Mors communis). If someone dies before fifty years, it is Mors excidii (death of cutting off). Before fifty-two it is the death of the prophet Samuel. At sixty it is Mors per manus Dei (death by the hand of God). At seventy it is Senectus (old age); at eighty it is Robur (strength). Moed Katon f. 28.1.

units.la: §. Homo lethaliter ægrotus, videatur sibi in oculis דין לגרדום כמי שהעלוהו Simili illi quem ascendere faciunt ad tribunal ut condemnetur: quicunque ascendit ad tribunal iudicii, ut iudicetur, si sint ipsi advocati magni liberari potest; sin minus, non liberatur. Advocati autem sunt pœnitentia & opera bona. Schaibat sol.32.1.
units.tr: A man mortally sick should see himself as one Simili illi quem ascendere faciunt ad tribunal ut condemnetur (like one whom they make ascend the tribunal to be condemned). Whoever ascends the tribunal of judgment to be judged may be freed if he has great advocates; if not, he is not freed. The advocates are repentance and good works. Shabbat f. 32.1.

units.la: §. Morti adiudicatis potandum dant Iudæi, granum thuris in poculo vini, ad turbandum eorum intellectum, ne præsentia mala tam vehementer sentiant. Sanhed.43.1.
units.tr: To those condemned to death the Jews give a grain of incense in a cup of wine to drink, to dull their understanding, so that they may not feel their present evils so keenly. Sanhedrin 43.1.

units.la: §. Si quis mortuus reperiatur vel in agro, vel sit peregrinus,alienus, vel non habeat qui sepeliant, dicitur מצוה מת præcepti mortuum, & tunc vi præcepti tum pietatis causâ, quilibet pius aut Magistratus ipsi legitimam sepulturam dare debet. Erubbin 17.2. Cl.Buxt. Synag.Iud. 698.De statu animæ post mortem vid.ibid.7.13. Angelus mortis plenus est oculis. Avoda Zarah f.20.2. Ielammedenu Sect. משנה את המסת הפ. Alcoran. Surat.VII.25.
units.tr: If a dead man is found either in a field, or is a stranger or foreigner, or has no one to bury him, he is called a "dead man of the commandment" (מצוה מת). Then, by virtue of the commandment and for the sake of piety, any pious person or the magistrate ought to give him a lawful burial (Erubin 17.2). Cf. Buxtorf, Synagoga Judaica 698. On the state of the soul after death, see ibid. 7.13. The angel of death is full of eyes (Avodah Zarah f. 20.2). Yalkut... section משנה את המסת הפ. Qur'an, Sura VII.25.

units.la: §. De Ceremoniis funeralibus vid. Iuetum.
units.tr: §. On funeral ceremonies see Iuetum.

units.la: Moses natus est die 7. mensis Februarii, & eodem die mensque denatus. Kidduschin 58. 1. Varia eius nomina habes apud Eusab. præpar. Ev. lib.9. Pesikta 11.2. Eius encomia, dignitas, privilegia, Rosch Hafchana pag.21. Nedarim cap.38. Nomen eius est in unaquaque Pentateuchi sectione, post descriptam nativitatem eius, excepta sect. שמות Exod.27.20. quia dixerat cap.32.32. Dele me &c. Baal Haturim. Ante iter Midianiticum testantur Chronica Hebræorum,eum in Æthiopia regnasse, atque uxorem duxisse Æthiopissam. Vid.Abravanel & Iosephi Antiq. An nomen eius sit Hebræum vid.Buxt.Differt.viii.486. Magna pars decalogi à Mose prius fuit in Mara data. Sanhed. cap.7.52.
units.tr: Moses was born on the 7th day of the month of February, and on the same day and month he died. Kidduschin 58.1. You will find various names for him in Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica, book 9. Pesikta 11.2. For his eulogies, dignity and privileges, see Rosch Hafchana p. 21 and Nedarim ch. 38. His name appears in every section of the Pentateuch after the account of his birth, except the section Shemot [שמות] at Exod. 27.20, because at ch. 32.32 he had said "Blot me out," etc. Baal Haturim. The Hebrew chronicles testify that before the journey to Midian he reigned in Ethiopia and married an Ethiopian woman. See Abravanel and Josephus, Antiquities. On whether his name is Hebrew, see Buxtorf, Dissertatio viii, p. 486. A large part of the Decalogue was given by Moses earlier, at Marah. Sanhedrin ch. 7.52.

units.la: §. Mosen ubique magna reverentia prosequuntur, non potuerunt tamen sibi temperare quin ipsum castigarent inVajikra Rabba f 179.
units.tr: §. Everywhere they treat Moses with great reverence, yet they could not refrain from censuring him in Vayikra Rabba f. 179.

units.la: 1. De tribus rebus iratus est Moses, & abscondita est ab eo traditio. I. circa Sabbathum Exod. xvi. 20. Cum irasceretur oblitus est, recitare iis traditiones de Sabbatho. II. Circa vasa metallica Num. xxxi. 14. Cum irasceretur oblitus est, recitare iis, traditiones de vasis metallicis. III. Circa lugentem Lev. x.16.Cum irasceretur abscondita est ab eo traditio; quâ prohibetur lugens comedere de Sacris.
units.tr: 1. Moses was angry about three things, and the tradition was hidden from him. (1) Concerning the Sabbath, Exod. 16.20: when he was angry, he forgot to recite to them the traditions about the Sabbath. (2) Concerning metal vessels, Num. 31.14: when he was angry, he forgot to recite to them the traditions about metal vessels. (3) Concerning the mourner, Lev. 10.16: when he was angry, the tradition was hidden from him, by which a mourner is forbidden to eat of the sacred things.

units.la: Mosen male cornutum fingunt quidam & pinguut, solâ ratione הקרין Exod.34 35. quod radios non cornua immittere significat.
units.tr: Some foolishly depict Moses as horned, and they grow fat on one argument alone: the word karan [הקרין] at Exod. 34.35, which means that he sent out rays, not horns.

units.la: מומחה סומייות; probatus, aliquando etiam vocatur מומחה בית דין & מומחה לרבי Beracot cap.4.§.4. Eius definitio est secundùm Maymonidem Cuius sapientia & eminentia in lege nota est vulgo. Secundùm R.Scheriram vero; Qui in Mischna & Gemara, & ponderanda sententia versatus, aliquot annos interfuit iudiciis, probatusque sit vicibus aliquot, nec errasse deprehendatur. Vid.Coccei Sanhed. pag.4.
units.tr: Mumcheh [מומחה]: one who is approved. Sometimes he is also called mumcheh beit din and mumcheh le-Rabbi. Berachot ch. 4 §4. According to Maimonides, his definition is: one whose wisdom and eminence in the law are known to the common people. According to R. Scheriram, however: one who is versed in the Mishnah and Gemara and in weighing opinions, who has attended judgments for some years, who has been approved on several occasions, and who is not found to have erred. See Cocceius, Sanhedrin p. 4.

units.la: Mulieres, de iis vid.fœminas. de muliebribus vestimentis & ornamentis, sequentia notavimus. Caput, fœminæ & virgines ornabant, ornamento quodam אטעבא Vocato, compositio ex diversis coloribus, gemmis & margaritis, illo fultentabant capillos, ne dilaberentur, aut diffluerent. De hoc ligamento tria dicuntur in Schabbat f.57.2. Non iudicatur esse ex heterogeneis : non polluit tactu : cum eo in Sabbatho mulieres non egrediuntur foras.
units.tr: Women: on them see women. On women's garments and ornaments we have noted the following. On the head, women and virgins adorned themselves with an ornament called atabba [אטעבא], a composition of various colours, gems and pearls, with which they held up their hair so that it would not fall down or flow loose. Three things are said about this band in Shabbat f. 57.2: it is not judged to be made of heterogeneous materials; it does not convey uncleanness by touch; and women do not go out of doors on the Sabbath wearing it.

units.la: §. Ad fragrantiam & bonum odorem portabant קופת הרוכלים Pyxidem aromatariorum, diversis aromatibus contusis, & ligno cinnamomi repletam. De his pixidibus sonat decretum Esrae in Bava Kama sol.82.1. & Hierof. Megillah f.75.1. quo permisit ut בעיירות מחוירי הרוכלין Aromatarii circumire possent per urbes, ad Israelitidarum decus, ut eo facilius ad se ornandas necessaria comparare possent. Tales pyxides in Sabbatho etiam seponere debebant. Schabbat sol.91.2.
units.tr: §. For fragrance and a pleasant smell they carried the pyxis of the perfumers [קופת הרוכלים], filled with various crushed aromatics and cinnamon wood. The decree of Ezra in Bava Kama f. 82.1 and Jerusalem Megillah f. 75.1 concerns these boxes. By it he permitted the perfumers to go round the towns [בעיירות], for the adornment of Israelite women, so that they could more easily obtain what was needed to adorn themselves. Women were also required to set such boxes aside on the Sabbath. Shabbat f. 91.2.

units.la: §. Pepla quibus ornabant caput vocabant כיצא. Bava Bathra f.146.1. Velum erat usitatum sponsis vid. Nuptias Patriarch. in N. meretrices etiam utebantur רדיד peplo, vid. Historiam Thamaris Genef 38.15. Crines etiam implicabant & funis instar intorquebant; hinc illas quae speciatim se ad hanc plicationem applicabant, vocabant מגדלות plicatrices; qualis fuit Maria.(v.f.l.) de hac plicatione crinium mentio fit in Kelim c.15. in Schabb. f.97.2.
units.tr: §. The veils with which they covered their heads they called kitza [כיצא]. Bava Bathra f. 146.1. A veil was customary for brides; see Nuptiae Patriarcharum on the New Testament. Prostitutes too used a veil, radid [רדיד]; see the story of Tamar, Gen. 38.15. They also braided their hair and twisted it like a rope. Hence those who devoted themselves especially to this plaiting were called megadelot [מגדלות], plaiters; Mary was one of these (v. f. l.). Mention of this plaiting of the hair is made in Kelim ch. 15 and in Shabbat f. 97.2.

units.la: §. Meretrices utebantur Camisia sive indusio Cancellato instar retis, ut corpus per illud conspiceretur; de hoc חלוק indusio loquitur Kelim cap.28.
units.tr: §. Prostitutes wore a shift or undergarment with a lattice like a net, so that the body could be seen through it. The chaluk [חלוק], this undergarment, is spoken of in Kelim ch. 28.

units.la: §. Collum etiam honestae matronae ornabant Catella vel fibula aurea, eaque scapulare sub collo colligebant; inaures & annuli etiam erant in usu. De his sonat prohibitio quæ legitur in Schabbat sol.571. Non licet egredi mulieribus in Sabbatho, לא בקשלא cum fibula, לא בנוים neque inauribus, ולט בטבעת neq; annulo &c. §.
units.tr: §. Honest matrons also adorned their necks with a small chain or a golden clasp, and fastened it under the neck over the shoulder blade. Earrings and rings were also in use. The prohibition in Shabbat f. 57.1 speaks of these: It is not permitted for women to go out on the Sabbath with a clasp [לא בקשלא], nor with earrings [לא בנוים], nor with a ring [ולא בטבעת], etc. §.

units.la: Mundus est duplex vel עולם הזה Mundus præsens, qui iterum distinguitur in inferiorem, qui continet mare, desertum, terram habitabilem &c. & medium, continens sphæras, stellas,&c. & supremum, qui est mundus animarum, & mundus spiritualis, (has mundi partes repræsentavit ex ipsorum opinione tabernaculum Mosaicum.) vel deinde עולם הבא Mundus futurus, qui est status rerum & personarum post diem iudicii; aliis est tempus Messiæ. V. Abrabenel in P. Avoth c.4.iii.108. Kirch.Oedip. ii.4.6. עולם הזה Mundus præsens similis est vestibulo respectu mundi futuri; præpara teipsum in vestibulo,ut possis ingredi in triclinium, Avoth c.416. An mundus æternus sit disputatur in Cosri Buxt.34.362.De fine mundi vid.Sanhed. sol.97.1. Fundamenta mundi tria sunt, Lex, oratio, pii; Eliefer (ap.fid.166.
units.tr: The world is twofold. There is the present world [עולם הזה], which is further divided into the lower, containing sea, desert and inhabitable land, etc.; the middle, containing the spheres, stars, etc.; and the highest, which is the world of souls and the spiritual world. (In their opinion the Mosaic tabernacle represented these parts of the world.) Then there is the future world [עולם הבא], which is the state of things and persons after the day of judgment; for others it is the time of the Messiah. See Abrabanel on Pirkei Avot ch. 4, iii, 108; Kircher, Oedipus ii.4.6. The present world is like a vestibule in relation to the future world: prepare yourself in the vestibule, so that you may enter the dining hall. Avot ch. 4.16. Whether the world is eternal is disputed in Cosri, Buxtorf 34.362. On the end of the world see Sanhedrin f. 97.1. The three foundations of the world are the Law, prayer and the pious; Eliezer (ap. Fid. 166).

units.la: §. De formula loquendi circa Mundum vid. formulas loq. Exspectarunt prisci Mundum esse renovandum sub adventu Messiæ. Sanhed. f.92.
units.tr: §. On the manner of speaking about the world, see formulas loq. The ancients expected the world to be renewed at the coming of the Messiah. Sanhedrin f. 92.

units.la: 2. Annis istis, quibus Deus renovaturus est mundum suum. Numerum autem illorum annorum Aruch & Gloss.proponunt millenarium.
units.tr: 2. In those years in which God is going to renew his world. The Aruch and the Gloss propose that the number of those years is a millennium.

units.la: § De mundi mutatione sic loquitur R. Salomoh in Machfchirin c. 6. עלמא מדמי לגלגלא ראנטליא דמילי מתרוקן ודמרוקן מתמלא Mundus hic similis est rotæ sicularum, (dum rota circumagitur) quod plenum est evacuatur, & quod vacuum est impletur. Sic in hoc mundo alter ascendit, alter descendit. Cabbalistæ in הנת אצ f.53. 1. triplex Mundi בליםות dominium constituunt; primum attribuunt domino universi, alterum intelligentiis cœlestibus, quæ movent stellas, & tertium ipsimet motui stellarum.
units.tr: §. On the change of the world R. Solomon speaks thus in Machshirin ch. 6: This world is like the wheel of buckets [עלמא מדמי לגלגלא ראנטליא], which, as it turns, what is full is emptied and what is empty is filled. So in this world one rises and another descends. The Cabbalists, in the work cited as Hanat Atz [הנת אצ] f. 53.1, set up a threefold dominion of the world: the first they attribute to the Lord of the universe, the second to the heavenly intelligences that move the stars, and the third to the motion of the stars themselves.

units.la: MUSICA. De divisione Musicorum vid. 1. (chron. 25. De fundamento Musices in lege disputant Gemaristæ in Erachin sol. 11. עיקר שירה בקור fundamentum (principalis cantus pars) musices (templi) debebat fieri voce, inquit Maymon in Kele Mikdasch cap.3. quo tamen instrumenta non exclulit, sed vult illa solummodo tanquam appendices ad voces accessisse. Quoad Cantores ipsos, refert nobis in 1. c. fuisse illos partim Levitas, partim vero Israelitas מיוחסין הכשיאין לכהונה Præstantes & qui coniugio iunctli erant Sacerdotibus; ad Cantorum enim scamna nullum accedere debuisse, nisi esset vir notabilis & ingenuus. Mischna in Erachin 1. modò cit. docet, Israelitas solummodò instrumentis lusisse, & Levitis Musicam vocalem reliquisse. Familias autem illorum Cantorum fuisse illam גרים Pegaraorum & צפורים & Zipporia in Emmaus. Idem etiam dicitur in Succah cap.5. in Gem.
units.tr: MUSIC. On the division of the musicians see 1 Chron. 25. The Gemarists dispute about the foundation of music in the law in Erachin f. 11. The principal part of song [עיקר שירה] in the temple [בקור] ought to be made by voice, says Maimonides in Kele Hamikdash ch. 3. Yet he does not exclude instruments; he holds that they were added merely as appendages to the voices. As for the singers themselves, he tells us in the same chapter that they were partly Levites and partly Israelites of pure descent, fit to be joined in marriage with priests (mewuchasin hakesherin lekehunah [מיוחסין הכשרין לכהונה]). No one ought to approach the singers' benches unless he was a notable and free-born man. The Mishnah in Erachin 1, just cited, teaches that the Israelites only played on instruments, and left vocal music to the Levites. The families of these singers were those of Pegarim [פגראים], Tzipporim [צפורים] and Zipporia at Emmaus. The same is said in Succah ch. 5 in the Gemara.

units.la: §. Quoad numerum vocum nunquam debebat ipsarum numerus minor esse duodecim, sed semper usque addere licet. Erachin ubi supra. Infantes Musicorum in atrium ad subsellia cantorum nunquam accedere debebant, nisi tempore quo cantabant patres ipsorum: collocabantur autem ibi ad pedes patrum ipsorum, ut notat Glossa in l. m. c. & eliciunt ex Efræ 3. 9.
units.tr: §. As to the number of voices, it was never to be less than twelve, but it is always permitted to add more. Erachin, ubi supra. The children of the musicians were never to approach the courtyard and the singers' benches, except at the time when their fathers were singing. They were placed there at their fathers' feet, as the Gloss notes in the place mentioned, and as they infer from Ezra 3.9.

units.la: §. Instrumenta quibus utebantur erant duplicia, vel illa quæ flatu vel illa qua fidibus agitabantur. Prioris generis erant tubæ quarum mentio fit 2.(chron.7.6. & 29.26. & in pluribus aliis locis: ipsarum numerus non debebat esse minor quàm duo, nec 120. superare. Maymon in Kele Mikdaschh cap. 2. Præceptum de clangendis tubis in festis solemnibus, & noviluniis exstat Num. 10. 10. Illi qui clangebant, erant Sacerdotes non Levitæ, secundùm Num.10.10. 1.Chron.15.24. non stabant propè Levitas sed in altero latere altaris, & clangentes facies observas habebant Levitis, hi autem & illi versus altare erant conversi. Locus stationis ipsorum erat Tabula pinguedinis, & ad minimum duo ibi stare & clangere debebant. Tamid c.7.
units.tr: §. The instruments they used were of two kinds: those sounded by breath and those played with strings. Of the first kind were the trumpets, mentioned at 2 Chron. 7.6, 29.26 and in many other places. Their number was not to be less than two, nor to exceed 120. Maimonides, Kele Hamikdash ch. 2. The command to sound trumpets at solemn feasts and new moons is found at Num. 10.10. Those who sounded them were priests, not Levites, according to Num. 10.10 and 1 Chron. 15.24. They did not stand near the Levites but on the other side of the altar. The trumpeters had their faces turned towards the Levites, while both were turned towards the altar. The place of their station was the Table of Fat, and at least two had to stand there and sound. Tamid ch. 7.

units.la: §. Modus clangendi ipsorum erat, ut primò lente sonum ederent, deinde celeriùs illum modificarent & diversificarent, tandem verò iterum lento sono clangendi finem facerent. Has soni mutationes vocat Mischna modò citata תקיעה, תריעה, תקיעה, de hoc clanctu hanc generalem habemus traditionem Non clangunt minus quam 11. vicibus in festivitatio, neque ultra 48. excedunt. Erachin cap.2, in Mischnah. & Succah cap. 5. de tribus illis tubâ clangendi diversis modis loquitur, loquuntur etiam Gemarista loc.mod.cit. f.53. & Gloss. Et sic exprimunt תרועה באמצע ופשוטה לפניה ולאחריה Bb 4 Vox infracta ( Galli Alarme ) debet esse in medio, illam autem sequi & precedere debet, vox clara, absq; scilicet inflexione & variatione notabili.
units.tr: The manner of their sounding was this: first they blew with a slow note, then they varied and diversified the sound more quickly, and at last they ended the blowing again with a slow note. The Mishnah cited just above calls these changes of sound תקיעה, תריעה, תקיעה [tekiah, teruah, tekiah]. Concerning this blowing we have the general tradition: "They do not sound fewer than 11 times on a festival, nor more than 48." Erachin ch. 2, in the Mishnah, and Succah ch. 5 speak of those three different ways of blowing the trumpet. The Gemara also speaks of them, loc. cit., f. 53, and the Gloss. And so they express תרועה [teruah] in the middle, with a plain note before and after it: Vox infracta (the French alarme) should be in the middle, and it must be preceded and followed by a clear note, that is, without any notable bending or variation.

units.la: §. Aliud Instrumentum flatûs erat חליל Chalil quod etiam אבוב Abhubh nominatur. Respondet Germanicorum Schalmeye / Latinorum Tibia; de tali instrumento loquuntur Gemarisle in Erach. in l. m. c. & Aruch in אבוב. Unam scilicet tibiam repertam fuisse in templo, quæ tempore Mosis iam confecta fuerat; Iussisse regem ut illa inauraretur; sed tunc non amplius tam suavem edidisse sonum: ita ut aurum iterum tolli debuerit. Notandum autem est, tibiam non fuisse ordinarium in omni cultu instrumentum, sicuti tubæ fuerunt, sed utebantur illis solummodo duodecim diebus in anno. Audiamus Mischnam in Erachin ubi supra. Semper debebant esse duæ חליל tibiæ, nec plures esse debebant quam duodecim. Illis autem ludebant duodecim diebus in anno coram altari, scilicet in paschate mensis prioris, & in paschate mensis posterioris; die primo festi Paschatis, die primo festi Pentecostes (Lev.23.21.) septem diebus festi tabernaculorum ולא היה מכה כאבוב של נחושת אלא באבוב של קנה Non autem ludebant tibiâ aneâ sed Cannea ערב שקיולי מפני quia sonum suaviorem edebat. Neque finem imponebant lusui tibiarum omnibus simul, sed una solum, quia ita suavius claudebatur.
units.tr: Another wind instrument was the חליל [chalil], which is also called the אבוב [abhubh]. It corresponds to the German Schalmeye, and to the Latin tibia. The Gemara in Erachin, loc. cit., and the Aruch under אבוב speak of such an instrument. They relate that a single pipe was found in the Temple, which had already been made in the time of Moses; the king ordered it to be gilded, but then it no longer gave so sweet a sound, so that the gold had to be removed again. It should be noted, however, that the pipe was not a standard instrument in every form of worship, as the trumpets were; they used it only on twelve days of the year. Let us hear the Mishnah in Erachin, where cited above: "There were always to be two pipes [חליל], and not more than twelve. They played on them twelve days in the year before the altar: namely, on the Passover of the first month and on the Passover of the second month; on the first day of the feast of Passover, on the first day of the feast of Pentecost (Lev. 23.21), and the seven days of the feast of Tabernacles." וְלֹא הָיָה מַכֶּה כְּאֲבוּב שֶׁל נְחוֹשֶׁת אֶלָּא בְּאֲבוּב שֶׁל קָנֶה [They did not play on a pipe of bronze, but on a pipe of cane], "because it gave a sweeter sound." Nor did they all stop playing the pipes together, but only one, because in this way the piping ended more sweetly.

units.la: §. Erant tria alia instrumenta, quæ perpetuò ad Musicam adhibebantur, & hæc tria erant נבל כנור צלצל Nebhel, Cinnor, Tsiltsel, & hæc indiscriminatim divisa erant filiis trium Cantorum Magistrorum, Asaph, Heman, & Ieduthun 1. Chron. 15. 19. 20. 21. 1. Chron. 16. 5. & 25. 1. De his Instrumentis sic Iosephus lib. 7. cap. 10. pag. Edit. Frob. 116. ut ‭בנור‬ ipsi sit Nabla, illamque sic definit, 'H δὲ Νάβλα δῶδε-κα φθόγγος ἔχουσα τῆς δεκατέσσαρος χορδῆς. ‭נבל‬ Graece ponit Κινύρα, illamque sic describit; Η μὲν Κινύρα δεκαχορδὸς ἔξημμένη τύπῳ πληκτρῳ. ‭כנור‬ Iosepho est Κύμβαλον, de illo sic inst Κύμβαλα τι ἐν πλατεῖα καὶ μικρὰ χαλκᾶ. In quae Iosephi verba sequentia notanda.
units.tr: There were three other instruments that were always used in music: these three were נבל, כנור, צלצל [nebhel, kinnor, tsiltsel]. These were divided without distinction among the sons of the three chief singers, Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun (1 Chron. 15.19, 20, 21; 1 Chron. 16.5; 25.1). Josephus, book 7, ch. 10, p. 116 of the Frobenius edition, on these instruments: he takes the nebhel to be the nabla, and defines it thus: "The nabla is a sound of twelve strings" [ἡ δὲ Νάβλα δωδεκάφθογγος, ἔχουσα τῆς δεκατέσσαρος χορδῆς]. He renders נבל in Greek as kinyra, and describes it thus: "The kinyra is a ten-stringed instrument, played with a plectrum" [ἡ μὲν Κινύρα δεκαχορδὸς, ἐξημμένη τύπῳ πληκτρῳ]. For Josephus the כנור is a kymbalon, and of it he says: "Cymbals are small bronze plates" [κύμβαλα τι ἐν πλατεῖα καὶ μικρὰ χαλκᾶ]. On Josephus' words the following points should be noted.

units.la: 1. Quod ‭נבל‬ & ‭כנור‬ quae optimè per Cytharam & Psalterium, (Germ. Harpfen) exponuntur, fuerint instrumenta fidibus instructa, oppositè ad illa instrumenta flatus, de quibus iam supra loquuti sumus.
units.tr: 1. That the נבל and the כנור, which are best rendered by cithara and psalterium (German Harpfen), were stringed instruments, as opposed to the wind instruments of which we have just spoken.

units.la: 2. Quamvis hæc duo instrumenta ambo fides sive chordas habuerint, nihilominus aliquam inter ipsa fuisse differentiam; nam primo unum percutiebatur aliquâ pennulâ, vel fructulo ligni vel arcu ut nostræ Citharæ & Violæ (Geigen.) Alterum verò percutiebatur digitis, ut Chelis (Lauten.) Secundò notas unius instrumenti diversificatas fuisse, per digitorum pulsus & motus, alterius verò per ipsam chordarum differentiam; talem enim vim habent nomina φθόγγος & χορδή. Nablium duodecim habebat chordas, & multitudine suarum chordarum diversos edere poterat sonos, ‭כנור‬ verò decem solùm habuit fides, & digitorum motu diversificabantur. De Cithara loquuntur etiam Gemarisse in Erachin ubi supra.
units.tr: 2. Although these two instruments both had strings, there was nevertheless some difference between them. For, first, one was struck with a little quill or a piece of wood, or with a bow, as our cithara and viol (Geigen) are; the other was struck with the fingers, as the lute (Lauten) is. Second, the notes of one instrument were varied by the pressing and movement of the fingers, but those of the other by the difference of the strings themselves; for the words φθόγγος and χορδή have this force. The nebhel had twelve strings, and by the number of its strings it could produce various sounds; but the kinnor had only ten strings, and its sounds were varied by movement of the fingers. The Gemara in Erachin, loc. cit., also speaks of the cithara.

units.la: 3. ‭צלצל‬ sive Cymbalum fuisse vas aliquod æneum, instar hodiernorum Cymbalorum, nisi forte quòd ita affabrè factum erat, ut multò suaviorem sonum ediderit. De cymbalo loquuntur in Erachin sol.10. & Talm. Hierof. in Succah sol.55. Erat Cymbalum in templo, confectum erat ex ære, sonusq; eius erat amœnissimus. Sed accidit ut fissurâ hiaret; Senatores miserunt Alexandriam, & inde opifices accersiverunt, qui illud repararunt, sed sonus eius non amplius tam gratus erat, ut fuerat antea. Sustulerunt, itaque illud quod opifices illi addiderant, & sonus tam suavis rediit, ut solito erat. Ad ordinariam Musicam suffecit unam adhibere; Maym. Kele Hammikdafch cap.3. & videtur Cymbalum Bassus vel vocis infimæ loco fuisse. Infra duo הרפס Psalteria (Harpfen) in Cantu non debebant descendere, neque plura habere quam sex. Erachin cap.2. in Mifchna. de כנורות vero non infrà novem, sed suprà quantum habere licet.Tosapht. in Erachin cap 2. De Instrumento Hydrauli vid Buxt. Lex. Talm p.629.
units.tr: 3. The צלצל or cymbal was some bronze vessel like today's cymbals, except perhaps that it was so skilfully made that it gave a much sweeter sound. The cymbal is discussed in Erachin fol. 10, and in the Talmud of Jerusalem, Succah fol. 55: "There was a cymbal in the Temple, made of bronze, and its sound was most pleasant. But it happened that it had a crack; the senators sent to Alexandria and summoned craftsmen from there, who repaired it, but its sound was no longer as pleasing as it had been before. So they removed what those craftsmen had added, and the sound returned as sweet as it had been." For ordinary music it was enough to use one; Maimonides, Kele Hammikdash ch. 3; and the cymbal seems to have been the bass, or lowest voice. Below, two הרפס [harpsim] psalteries were not to descend in the singing, nor to have more than six strings: Erachin ch. 2, in the Mishnah. As for the כנורות [kinnorot], they were not to have fewer than nine, but could have as many as one likes above that: Tosephta in Erachin ch. 2. On the water-organ, see Buxtorf, Lexicon Talmudicum, p. 629.

units.la: §. Sed satis inhæsimus instrumentis, videamus nunc ipsum Musices exercitium & praxin. Tubæ (Drummeten) suum חצוצרות Taratantara sonabant fungulis horis matutinis, cùm porta Nicanoris & reliquæ atrii portæ aperiebantur. Succah cap.5. in Mifchna & Gloss ibid. Hoc tubarum signo viri stationarii ad sua officia vocabantur, & populo campanarum instar indicium incipientis cultus divini dabatur. Clangebant duo Sacerdotes secundâ vice, tempore libationis vini. Vid. Tamid. cap.7. v.3. omnes etiam reliquæ Musices partes, tunc demum incipiecipiebant, cùm sacrificium holocausti & libamen oblatum erat; rationes habes in Erachin in Gem. sol.11. & Gloff.in Pefachin c.5. f.64.
units.tr: But we have dwelt long enough on the instruments; let us now see the practice and exercise of the music itself. The trumpets sounded their חצוצרות [chatsotserot] taratantara at certain hours in the morning, when the Gate of Nicanor and the other gates of the court were opened: Succah ch. 5, in the Mishnah, and the Gloss there. By this signal of the trumpets the watchmen were summoned to their duties, and the people were given, as with bells, a sign that divine worship was beginning. Two priests sounded a second time, at the time of the libation of wine: see Tamid ch. 7, v. 3. All the other parts of the music also began only when the burnt offering and the drink offering had been presented; you have the reasons in the Gemara in Erachin fol. 11, and in the Gloss on Pesachin ch. 5, f. 64.

units.la: §. Psalmi quos ordinariè cantabant sequentes erant. Die primo septimanæ Psal.xxiv. Die secundo xlviii. Psalm. Die tertio Psal.82. Die quarto94 Psalm. Die quintoPsal.81. 'Die sexto Psalm.93. Die sabbathi verò Psalm.92. Tamid ubi supra. Rationes cur hos elegerint Psalmos vid. in Rosch Hafchana sol.31. Maym. in Tamid. cap.6. Vnumquemque ex his Psalmis in tres partes Cantores dividebant, in quibus pausas faciebant, quas Talmudici פרקים nominant, in his pausis tubis canebant, & populus adorabat, secundùm illud על כל פרק תקיעה ועל כל תקיעה השתחויה In unaquaque Pausa erat taratantara tuba, & apud unamquamque taratantaram adoratio populi. Vid. Tamid. c.7. & Rosch Hafchana loc. mod. cit.
units.tr: The psalms they ordinarily sang were these. On the first day of the week, Psalm 24; on the second, Psalm 48; on the third, Psalm 82; on the fourth, Psalm 94; on the fifth, Psalm 81; on the sixth, Psalm 93; and on the Sabbath, Psalm 92: Tamid, loc. cit. For the reasons why they chose these psalms, see Rosh Hashanah fol. 31, and Maimonides on Tamid ch. 6. The singers divided each of these psalms into three parts, and made pauses between them, which the Talmudists call פרקים [perakim]; in these pauses they sounded the trumpets, and the people bowed down, according to the saying: "At every section a sounding, and at every sounding a bowing down." "At every pause there was a taratantara of the trumpet, and at every taratantara the people's worship." See Tamid ch. 7, and Rosh Hashanah, loc. cit.

units.la: §. Extraordinarios clanctus tubarum edebant in vespera Sabbathi ad populum à labore revocandum, & ad distinguendum diem insequentem à diebus profestis. Succah. c.5.
units.tr: They sounded extraordinary blasts of the trumpets on the evening of the Sabbath, to call the people back from their labour, and to distinguish the following day from the working days: Succah ch. 5.

units.la: §. In ipso Sabbatho tempore sacrificii additionalis de quo Num.28.9.10. Levitæ cantabant canticum Mosis (Deut. 32.) Maymon in Tamid. cap. 6. & Sacerdotes tubis suis tribus aliis vicibus, quàm in ordinariâ Musicâ solebant, clangebant. Succah ubi supra.
units.tr: On the Sabbath itself, at the time of the additional sacrifice mentioned in Num. 28.9, 10, the Levites sang the song of Moses (Deut. 32): Maimonides on Tamid ch. 6. And the priests sounded their trumpets three more times than they were accustomed to in ordinary music: Succah, loc. cit.

units.la: §. Ad Sacrificia additionalia primi diei anni (Num.29.1.2.) Levitæ cantabant Psal.81. & tubis etiam clangebant ad indicandum annum novum. Vesperâ verò huius diei cantabant
units.tr: At the additional sacrifices of the first day of the year (Num. 29.1, 2), the Levites sang Psalm 81, and they also sounded the trumpets to mark the new year. In the evening of this day they sang

units.la: Psal.19. In Psalmo vero canebant Hallel, de quo vid. suo loco.
units.tr: Psalm 19. In the Psalm they sang the Hallel, on which see in its place.

units.la: מצוה Mitsva. Occurrit non raro apud Rabbinos distinctio inter תורה & מצוה legem & praeceptum; Per posterius intelligunt speciale aliquem vel grandiorem (ipsis iudicibus) ritum; qualis erat Circuncisio, recitatio Phylacteriorum, Sabbatizatio. Haec recipit quaestio à Scriba proposita Marci 12. 28.
units.tr: מצוה [mitsvah]. The distinction between תורה [torah] and מצוה [mitsvah], law and precept, occurs not rarely among the rabbis. By the latter they understand some particular or more weighty rite (in the judgment of the rabbis themselves), such as circumcision, the recitation of the phylacteries, or the keeping of the Sabbath. This is the question that a scribe put forward in Mark 12.28.

units.la: N.
units.tr: N.

units.la: נאמן Neeman. Quis? Vid. Decimus. Vid. etiam Oleum.
units.tr: Neeman [נאמן]. Who? See Decimus. See also Oleum.

units.la: NARDINUM νάρδινον Marci xiv.3. Verti potest Nardinum Balanimum. Sic enim Plinius lib. 13. cap. 1. Nardinum conflat, omphacio, balanino, iunco, nardo, amomo, myrrha, balsamo &c. Et lib.12. cap.21. Myrobalanum, Troglodytis, & Thebaidi & Arabia qua Iudaam ab Aegypto disterminat, commune est, nascens unguentum ut ipso nomine apparet, quo item indicatur & glandem esse arboris. At glandem quam Graece vocant βάλανος Talmudici vocant בלנוס ; ut in Gittin sol. 69.1. לברסם ליתי כי פתקא רניששיד Pleuritidi recipe ad quantitatem glandis de Ammoniaco. Vid. Gloss. & Aruch in פתקא. Sicuti itaque vox Nάρδος Hebraizat, à voce נרד, ita & vox νάρδος Syriasat à voce פתקא, Ita ut hoc unguentum Balanimum vocari possit: In cuius confectione primas obtinuêre Nardus & Glans. Vid. Cl. LigtLigtfootum in loc.
units.tr: NARDINUM [νάρδινον] Mark xiv.3. It may be rendered "Nardinum Balanimum." For so Pliny, book 13, chapter 1: "Nardinum is compounded of omphacium, balaninum, rush, nard, amomum, myrrh, balsam," etc. And book 12, chapter 21: "Myrobalanum is common to the Troglodytes, to the Thebaid, and to Arabia, which divides Judaea from Egypt. It is a growing unguent, as the very name shows, and it likewise indicates that it is also the acorn of a tree." But the acorn, which the Greeks call βάλανος [balanos], the Talmudists call בלנוס [balanos], as in Gittin fol. 69.1: "For pleurisy, take ammoniac in the quantity of an acorn" (transliterated: lebarsam leyti ki patka ranishshid). See the Gloss and the Aruch under פתקא [patka]. Just as the word Νάρδος [Nardos] is Hebraized from the word נרד [nerd], so also the word νάρδος is Syriacized from the word פתקא [patka], so that this unguent may be called Balanimum, since nard and acorn obtained first place in its preparation. See Cl. Lightfoot on the passage.

units.la: NAZIRÆUS præcepto tenetur Comam alere, item omnium mortuorum contactum evitare, ne immundus fiat. Et tandem à vino & reliquis à vino confectis abstinère: Si autem hæc non observarit, flagellationem duplicem meretur, Alteram quòd votum ruperit; alteram quòd transgressus sit illud ad quod præcipuè vi voti Nazirætus tenebatur.
units.tr: A NAZIRITE is bound by precept to let his hair grow, and likewise to avoid contact with all the dead, lest he become unclean. And finally he must abstain from wine and from everything made from wine. If he does not observe these things, he deserves a double flogging: one because he has broken his vow, the other because he has transgressed that to which the Nazirite was especially bound by the force of the vow.

units.la: §. Qui dicit,non moriar nisi Naziræus fuero, iam tunc ut Naziræus æstimatur; ut etiam ille, qui dum Naziræum transire videt, dicit. Ego etiam ero Nazirœus, aut Crines suos prehendens dicit, Ego etiam talis Ero.
units.tr: §. He who says, "I will not die unless I am a Nazirite," is already then regarded as a Nazirite; likewise he who, seeing a Nazirite pass by, says, "I too will be a Nazirite," or who, taking hold of his own hair, says, "I too will be such."

units.la: §. כל כינוי נזירו כנזירות Omnia Nazireatus epitheta, plenum Nazireatum indicant; hinc qui dicit. Ecce, ego voveo me nucleos acinorum non comesturum, aut vovet, se libationes non facturum; aut dicit, Ecce ego Nazireus sum respectu impuritatis, non solum Nazireus est respectu harum rerum, sed etiam omnium reliquarum, quæ Nazireus evitare debet: Si scilicet illud cuius abstinentiam vovet, fit inter ea quæ Nazireo illicita sunt, qualia ea sunt, quæ modò adduximus. Maymon Hal. Nazir cap. 1.
units.tr: §. כל כינוי נזירו כנזירות [All the expressions of a Nazirite's vow indicate full Nazirite status]. Hence he who says, "Behold, I vow not to eat the seeds of grapes," or vows that he will not make libations, or says, "Behold, I am a Nazirite with respect to uncleanness," is a Nazirite not only with respect to these things but also with respect to all the rest that a Nazirite must avoid, if indeed the thing whose abstinence he vows falls among those things that are forbidden to the Nazirite, such as those we have just mentioned. Maimonides, Hilchot Nazir ch. 1.

units.la: §. Si quis voverit Nazirætum, & voti sui ipsum pœniteat, ille se conferre poterit ad sapientem (cui illa potestas data in impositione manuum. Vid. Impositio &c.) qui ipsi votum solvet; sicuti in usu habent, etiam omnia reliqua vota solvere.
units.tr: §. If anyone has vowed a Nazirite vow and regrets his vow, he may go to a wise man (to whom that power was given by the laying on of hands; see Impositio etc.), who will release him from the vow, as they customarily do in releasing all other vows.

units.la: §. Si duobus itinerantibus aliquis occurrat, quem ita bene agnoscere non possint, & unus dicat, Ecce me Nazi'raum, si hic Ruben sit, sed est Schimeon; Alter vero dicat etiam cum tali voto, non Schimeonem sed Rubenem esse, si ille advenerit, & Ruben sit, ille qui voto affirmavit Rubenem esse, revera Nazirææus est, & ita de cæteris.
units.tr: §. If someone meets two men who are travelling together, whom they cannot easily recognize, and one says, "Behold, I am a Nazirite, if this man is Reuben," but it is Simeon; and the other likewise says with such a vow that it is not Simeon but Reuben, if he has arrived and is Reuben: then he who affirmed by his vow that he was Reuben is truly a Nazirite, and so with the rest.

units.la: §. Mulieribus & servis etiam competit Nazirææatus, nisi servum dominus ad bibendum vinum, & ad mortuorum impuritatem impulerit, tunc enim cessat; mulier vero potest à marito suo, aut patre ut in cæteris votis absolvi.
units.tr: §. Women and slaves may also take the Nazirite vow, unless the master has made the slave drink wine and touch the uncleanness of the dead; for then it ceases. A woman, however, can be released by her husband or father, as in other vows.

units.la: §.
